2b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Perhaps the verse means sunrise the next morning, and that the person then becomes pure?
Rabba bar Rav Sheila answers: In that case the verse would say ‘and he shall become pure.’ Its wording means the day has cleared, as people say when the sun has set.
In the West they had not heard Rabba bar Rav Sheila’s explanation, so they raised the question themselves.
Does ‘the sun comes’ mean sunset and ‘it is pure’ the end of the day, or sunrise and the person’s purification?
They resolved it from a baraita.
The baraita gives the appearance of the stars as the sign.
Therefore the verse refers to sunset and the clearing of the day.
The master taught: From when the priests enter to eat terumah.
But another teaching says the evening Shema begins when a poor person comes to eat bread and salt, and lasts until the end of that meal.
The end of that teaching certainly disagrees with the mishnah.
Does its starting time also disagree?
No. The poor person and the priest refer to the same time.
But another baraita gives Rabbi Meir’s time as when people eat on Friday night, while the Sages say when priests may eat terumah, at the appearance of the stars.
The baraita cites the work from dawn until the stars appeared as a scriptural hint.
It adds that the night was for guarding and the day for work.
Why does it add a second verse?
One might say that night began at sunset, and the workers simply started early and finished late.
The second verse answers: the night was for guarding and the day for work.
The discussion initially assumes that the poor person and ordinary people eat at the same time.
If the poor person and priest also had the same time, the Sages and Rabbi Meir would agree, yet the baraita presents different views.
It appears that the poor person and priest have different times.
No. The poor person and priest can have the same time; the poor person and ordinary people need not.
Can the poor person and priest really have the same time?

Another baraita lists distinct views: Rabbi Eliezer says the start of Shabbat, Rabbi Yehoshua when priests are pure, Rabbi Meir when they immerse, Rabbi Hanina when a poor person eats, and Rabbi Ahai when most people recline to eat.
If the poor person and priest had the same time, Rabbi Hanina and Rabbi Yehoshua would agree.
So their times are indeed different.
Which time is later?
It is reasonable that the poor person’s time is later.
If it were earlier, Rabbi Hanina and Rabbi Eliezer would agree.
The poor person’s time is therefore later.
The master cited Rabbi Yehuda’s objection: priests immerse while it is still day.
Does Rabbi Yehuda not make a good point against Rabbi Meir?
Rabbi Meir answers that he means twilight as Rabbi Yosei defines it, rather than twilight as Rabbi Yehuda defines it.
Rabbi Yosei says twilight lasts as briefly as the blink of an eye; one period enters as the other leaves, and its exact moment cannot be determined.

ranges.en: The two reports of Rabbi Meir disagree.
Two tannaim transmit different accounts of Rabbi Meir’s view.
The two reports of Rabbi Eliezer also disagree.
Two tannaim likewise transmit different accounts of Rabbi Eliezer’s view.
Alternatively, the beginning of the mishnah may not be Rabbi Eliezer’s ruling.
The mishnah says: until the end of the first watch.
If Rabbi Eliezer holds that night has three watches, why not say four hours? If it has four watches, why not say three hours?
He holds that night has three watches; the language teaches that watches occur both in heaven and on earth.
A baraita says that night has three watches and God roars like a lion during each one.
The baraita cites Jeremiah’s description of God roaring from on high.
It gives signs for the three watches: a donkey brays, dogs bark, and later a child nurses while a woman talks with her husband.
Which point in each watch is Rabbi Eliezer counting?
If he means their beginnings, the first sign is unnecessary: that is nightfall.
If he means their ends, the last sign is unnecessary: that is daybreak.
He means the end of the first, the middle of the second, and the beginning of the last watch.
Alternatively, he may mean the end of all three watches.
Why, then, would the last watch need a sign?
It helps someone sleeping in a dark room know when to rise for the Shema.
Rav teaches that God roars during each of the three watches and laments the destruction and exile.
A baraita begins Rabbi Yosei’s account: he entered a ruin to pray, Elijah waited, and they exchanged greetings.
Elijah asks why Rabbi Yosei entered the ruin.
Rabbi Yosei says he entered to pray.
Elijah says he should have prayed on the road.
Rabbi Yosei explains that he feared passersby would interrupt him.
Elijah says he should have recited a short prayer.
Rabbi Yosei lists three lessons: avoid ruins, pray on the road, and use a short prayer there.
Elijah asks what sound Rabbi Yosei heard in the ruin.
Rabbi Yosei reports a heavenly voice lamenting the destruction and exile.
Elijah says that the voice laments three times every day.
He adds that God responds when Israel blesses His name in synagogues and study halls, lamenting the exile of His children.
The rabbis teach three reasons to avoid a ruin: suspicion, collapse, and harmful spirits.
Why mention suspicion when danger of collapse already forbids entering?

3b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The preceding case concerns a new ruin, without danger of collapse.
Why not prohibit entry because of harmful spirits?
The case involves two people.
If two people enter, why would there be suspicion?
Both may be licentious.
The teaching also mentions falling debris.
Why not rely on suspicion and harmful spirits instead?
This case involves two upright people.
The teaching also mentions harmful spirits.
Why not rely on suspicion and falling debris instead?
This case concerns a new ruin and two upright people.
With two people present, why would harmful spirits be a concern?
Their own haunt remains dangerous.
Alternatively, a lone person enters a new ruin in the fields; suspicion is unlikely there, but harmful spirits remain a concern.
A baraita records Rabbi saying night has four watches and Rabbi Natan saying three.
What is Rabbi Natan’s reason?
A verse calls one watch the middle watch, implying one before and one after it.
How does Rabbi explain “middle”?
It can mean one of the two middle watches.
Rabbi Natan objects that the verse says “the middle,” not “one of the middle ones.”
What is Rabbi’s reason?
A teaching contrasts verses about rising at midnight and eyes anticipating the watches.
How can both verses be true?
There are four watches in the night.
Rabbi Natan follows Rabbi Yehoshua: counting the hours until kings rise can still yield two watches after midnight.
Rav Ashi offers another answer: one and a half watches may also be called watches.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that one speaks before a deceased person only about matters of the deceased.
One version of Rabbi Abba bar Kahana limits this rule to Torah matters.
Another version applies it even to Torah matters, all the more so to ordinary talk.
Did David rise only at midnight?
A verse suggests he was awake from dusk.
How is “neshef” known to mean evening? A verse is cited.
Rav Oshaya explains that midnight never found David asleep.
Rabbi Zeira says David dozed until midnight, then rose with strength.
Rav Ashi says he studied Torah until midnight, then sang praises.
Another verse appears to use “neshef” for morning, challenging the evening reading.
Does the verse not mean from morning until night?
It could mean from one evening until the next.
Then why does the verse use two different words for evening?
Rava concludes that “neshef” can name either the fading of night or the fading of day.
How did David know exactly when midnight came?
Even Moses did not appear to know the precise time.
Moses said “about midnight.”
Could God have said “about midnight”? Surely there is no uncertainty before God.
God said “at midnight,” but Moses said “about,” showing his uncertainty.
How, then, did David know?
David had a sign.
A teaching says a north wind played the harp over David’s bed at midnight, and he then rose to study.
At dawn Israel’s sages came to David.
They told the king that the people needed a livelihood.
He advised them to support one another.
They replied that their own resources could not meet the need.
He told them to go out in military bands.
They consulted Ahithofel, the Sanhedrin, and the Urim and Tummim.
Rav Yosef asks which verse supports this account.
He begins citing a verse that identifies Ahithofel as the adviser.

ranges.en: Benayahu ben Yehoyada represents the Sanhedrin, and Evyatar the Urim and Tummim.
A verse identifies Benayahu with the Kereti and Peleti.
Why are they called the Kereti and Peleti?
They decide matters and are distinguished in their teaching.
Only afterward does Yoav appear as the king’s army commander.
Rav Yitzhak asks for a verse supporting the account of David’s harp.
He cites David’s call for his harp and lyre to wake the dawn.
Rabbi Zeira says that Moses and David both knew when midnight came.
If David knew, why did he need the harp?
It woke him from sleep.
If Moses knew, why did he say “about midnight”?
He feared Pharaoh’s astrologers might err and accuse him of falsehood.
A teaching counsels saying “I do not know” to avoid being caught in a false claim.
Rav Ashi offers another reading: Moses compared tomorrow’s midnight with the present midnight.
A psalm has David call himself pious.
Levi and Rabbi Yitzhak give two explanations.
The first explains that David rose at midnight to thank God while other kings slept.
The second points to David’s work on difficult purity rulings and his willingness to consult Mefivoshet without shame.
What verse supports the account of David’s lack of embarrassment?
David says he will speak of God’s testimonies before kings without shame.
A teaching says Mefivoshet’s name was Ish Boshet.
Why was he called Mefivoshet?
He embarrassed David in questions of halakha.
David therefore merited a descendant named Kilav.
Rabbi Yohanan says Kilav’s name was actually Daniel.
Why was he called Kilav?
He embarrassed Mefivoshet in halakha.
Two verses in Proverbs praise a wise son who answers those who taunt his father.
How could David call himself pious when a psalm appears to express doubt about his reward?
Why are dots placed over the word “luleh”?
David trusted that God would reward the righteous in the World to Come.
Yet he did not know whether he would share in that reward, fearing that sin could intervene.
Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi raises a similar contradiction about Jacob.
God promised to guard Jacob wherever he went.
Yet another verse says Jacob was very afraid.
Jacob feared that sin might undo the promise.
A baraita cites a verse about the people crossing over.
It interprets the repeated crossing as the first and second entries into the land.
The Sages conclude that Israel could have received a miracle in Ezra’s time as in Joshua’s, but sin prevented it.
The mishnah records the Sages’ limit of midnight.
Whose interpretation do the Sages follow? If Rabbi Eliezer’s, why not adopt his first-watch limit?

ranges.en: If the Sages follow Rabban Gamliel, why do they not say so directly?
They agree with Rabban Gamliel but set midnight as a precaution against transgression.
A baraita illustrates why the Sages made a safeguard: one should recite and pray before eating and sleeping.
The cited teaching warns against transgressing the Sages’ words.
Why does this teaching add the severe warning when others do not?
One answer points to the danger of falling asleep.
Another answer stresses that evening prayer is obligatory.
The Gemara recalls the earlier instruction to recite Shema and then pray.
That order supports Rabbi Yohanan’s teaching to join redemption to evening prayer.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi places the prayers between the two recitations of Shema.
What is the basis of their dispute?
The dispute may rest on a verse or on reasoning.
Their reasoning differs over whether the nighttime redemption counts as redemption.
A second account grounds both positions in one verse.
The verse about lying down and rising supplies their shared source.
Rabbi Yohanan reads the analogy as Shema followed by prayer in both periods.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi reads the analogy as Shema near the time of bed in both periods.
Mar son of Ravina objects that Hashkivenu interrupts the joining of redemption and prayer.
The Sages’ instituted Hashkivenu is treated as an extension of redemption.
Otherwise, how could the morning prayers join redemption and prayer?
Rabbi Yohanan’s rule also places an opening verse before the morning prayer.
An instituted opening counts as part of prayer; likewise Hashkivenu counts as part of redemption.
Rabbi Elazar citing Rabbi Avina praises reciting Psalm 145 three times daily.
What is the reason for its special standing?
Alphabetical order alone cannot explain it, since Psalm 119 has a fuller alphabetic pattern.
Its verse about God opening His hand offers a possible reason.
But the Great Hallel also contains a verse about feeding all creatures.
Psalm 145 has both the alphabetic pattern and the verse about sustenance.
Why does Psalm 145 omit a verse beginning with nun?
The letter would recall a verse about Israel’s fall.
The verse in Amos supplies the wording about falling.
A western interpretation reads the Amos verse as allowing Israel to rise again.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak cites a later verse in Psalm 145 about God supporting those who fall.
Rabbi Elazar bar Avina says Scripture describes Michael more greatly than Gabriel.
The contrasting scriptural descriptions of Michael and Gabriel support the distinction.
How is the unnamed seraph identified as Michael?
Rabbi Yohanan answers through an analogy using the word one.
The verses in Isaiah and Daniel each use one, with Daniel naming Michael.
A teaching compares the speed of Michael, Gabriel, Elijah, and the Angel of Death.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that Shema should also be recited at bedtime.
What verse supports reciting Shema at bedtime?
The verse about speaking on one’s bed is cited as support.
Rav Nahman begins a further statement that continues on the next daf.

ranges.en: A Torah scholar need not repeat the full bedtime recitation.
Abaye qualifies the exemption: even a scholar should say a verse of mercy.
A person should set the good inclination against the evil one.
The verse about trembling without sin supports resisting temptation.
If resistance fails, one should study Torah.
The verse about speaking in the heart supports Torah study.
If Torah study does not suffice, one should recite Shema.
The words about lying on the bed support reciting Shema.
If that fails, one should remember the day of death.
The verse’s closing call for stillness supports that final step.
What does the verse listing tablets, Torah, commandment, writing, and instruction mean?
Each phrase is read as a different part of the teaching given to Moses at Sinai.
Reciting Shema at bedtime is likened to holding a two-edged sword.
A psalm places praise in the throat beside a two-edged sword.
How does that verse indicate bedtime Shema?
The answer looks to the beginning of the psalm’s context.
The neighboring verses mention beds, praise, and the sword together.
Rabbi Yitzhak says bedtime Shema drives harmful spirits away.
Verses about flight and fiery harm are read to connect Torah with protection.
Reish Lakish says Torah study turns suffering away.
The same verses are interpreted with fiery harm referring to suffering.
Rabbi Yohanan challenges that teaching as already obvious to schoolchildren.
A verse in Exodus already promises protection from illness for obedience.
The teaching instead concerns harsh suffering brought by neglecting possible Torah study.
Psalms and Proverbs are cited to connect silence about the good with pain and Torah.
A comparison contrasts human reluctance in giving with God’s joy in giving Torah.
The verse about a good teaching supports that comparison.
One who suffers should first examine personal conduct.
The verse in Lamentations calls for examining one’s ways.
If no wrongdoing is found, one should consider neglect of Torah.
The verse about chastening and learning Torah supports that possibility.
If that too is absent, the suffering is understood as chastening of love.
Proverbs links divine rebuke with love.
Rav Huna teaches that God may afflict one in whom He delights.
Isaiah is cited for God’s delight and suffering.
Does this apply even when the sufferer does not accept it willingly?
The comparison to a guilt offering requires willing acceptance.
What reward follows acceptance?
Isaiah promises offspring and long days.
The teaching adds that the person’s learning endures.
The continuation of Isaiah is cited for enduring success.
Two sages dispute which sufferings count as chastening of love.
One opinion excludes suffering that interrupts Torah study.
A psalm joins chastening with learning Torah.
The other opinion excludes suffering that interrupts prayer.
A psalm praises God for not removing prayer.
Rabbi Yohanan reconciles both views: both types can be sufferings of love.
The verse in Proverbs links rebuke and love.
What is learned from the psalm’s reference to teaching from Torah?
The wording is reinterpreted as learning the matter from Torah itself.
An argument from a slave’s tooth or eye infers the greater cleansing power of suffering.
Reish Lakish compares the covenant of suffering with the covenant of salt.
Verses call both salt and suffering a covenant.
As salt sweetens meat, suffering is said to cleanse sins.
A baraita names Torah, the land of Israel, and the world to come as gifts through suffering.
What is the source concerning Torah?
A psalm connects chastening with learning Torah.
What is the source concerning the land of Israel?
Deuteronomy connects divine chastening with entering the good land.
What is the source concerning the world to come?
Proverbs connects reproof and instruction with the way of life.
A tanna begins a further teaching on Torah and acts of kindness.

5b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The preceding teaching concludes that burial of one’s children is associated with forgiveness.
Rabbi Yohanan accepts the links to Torah and acts of kindness.
Verses connect kindness and truth with atonement, and identify truth with Torah.
What is the source for the claim about burying children?
An elder cites a word analogy taught in Rabbi Shimon bar Yohai’s name.
Two verses using the word iniquity are joined to support the claim.
Rabbi Yohanan says plagues and childlessness are not sufferings of love.
A baraita calls plague symptoms an altar of atonement, apparently challenging the ruling.
Atonement does not make the suffering a chastening of love.
One resolution distinguishes the local teaching from another community’s teaching.
Another resolution distinguishes hidden from publicly visible affliction.
If childlessness includes children who died, Rabbi Yohanan’s own example challenges the claim.
The teaching concerns one who never had children, not one whose children died.
Rabbi Yohanan visits the ill Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba.
He asks whether the suffering is cherished.
The patient rejects both the suffering and its reward.
Rabbi Yohanan takes his hand and raises him.
Rabbi Hannina visits Rabbi Yohanan during his illness.
He asks whether the suffering is cherished.
Rabbi Yohanan rejects both the suffering and its reward.
Rabbi Hannina takes his hand and raises him.
Why could Rabbi Yohanan not raise himself?
A prisoner cannot free himself from prison.
Rabbi Yohanan visits the ill Rabbi Elazar, brings light, and sees him weeping.
He asks why Rabbi Elazar is weeping.
He offers consolation concerning limited Torah study.
He notes that material provision is not given equally to everyone.
He invokes his own loss of children.
Rabbi Elazar says he weeps for beauty that will decay.
Rabbi Yohanan agrees that this is a reason to weep, and they weep together.
The conversation turns back to Rabbi Elazar’s suffering.
Rabbi Yohanan asks whether the suffering is cherished.
Rabbi Elazar rejects both the suffering and its reward.
Rabbi Yohanan takes his hand and raises him.
Four hundred jars of Rav Huna’s wine sour, and the sages visit him.
They urge him to examine his conduct.
Rav Huna asks whether they suspect him of wrongdoing.
They answer by asking whether God acts unjustly.
Rav Huna asks them to state what they have heard against him.
They report that he withheld his tenant’s share of the vines.
Rav Huna replies that the tenant stole the produce.
They counter with a proverb that stealing from a thief is still theft.
Rav Huna accepts the criticism and promises to give the tenant his share.
The tradition gives alternative accounts of how the financial loss was reversed.
A baraita records Abba Binyamin’s two concerns about prayer and bed placement.
What does it mean for his prayer to be before his bed?
Could it mean praying in front of the bed itself?
A ruling against barriers between a worshipper and the wall challenges that reading.
The verse about Hezekiah turning to the wall supports the no-barrier rule.
The phrase means praying near the time of going to bed.
The second concern places the bed between north and south.
A teaching associates that orientation with male children.
A verse mentioning the north and children is cited.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak adds that this orientation prevents miscarriage.
A word shared by verses in Psalms and Genesis supports the addition.
A baraita says one who leaves a fellow worshipper alone has his prayer torn up.
The verse in Job about tearing one’s soul is cited.
The teaching adds that leaving causes the Divine Presence to depart.
Verses about the Rock are read as referring to God.
What reward follows when one waits for the other worshipper?

6a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina answers with the blessings earned by waiting.
The verse in Isaiah promises peace, righteousness, and descendants to one who heeds the commandments.
Abba Binyamin teaches that visible harmful spirits would overwhelm people.
Abaye says the spirits outnumber and surround people.
Rav Huna describes their multitude at each person’s sides.
Rava attributes crowding, fatigue, worn clothing, and stumbling to them.
A method is given for detecting their footprints.
A further method is given for seeing them, with precautions.
Rav Bibi’s experience and recovery illustrate the danger.
Abba Binyamin teaches the importance of prayer in a synagogue.
A verse about hearing song and prayer is read as linking prayer to the place of song.
From where is it known that God is present in a synagogue?
The verse about God standing in the congregation is cited.
From where is the Presence with ten people at prayer?
The same congregation verse is cited for ten.
From where is the Presence with three who sit in judgment?
The verse about judging among judges is cited.
From where is the Presence with two studying Torah?
Malachi describes two who speak together and are heard.
What does Malachi mean by those who think upon God’s name?
An intended commandment prevented by force is credited as performed.
From where is the Presence with one person studying Torah?
A verse promises God’s arrival and blessing wherever His name is recalled.
Why mention two if the Presence is with one?
The words of two are recorded in a book of remembrance.
Why mention three if the Presence is with two?
One might think judging is only civic peace; the teaching establishes its Torah status and the Presence.
Why mention ten if the Presence is with three?
The Presence arrives before ten, but waits for three to sit.
From where is it derived that God wears tefillin?
Isaiah mentions God’s right hand and arm of strength.
The right hand is identified with Torah.
A verse in Deuteronomy places fiery teaching at God’s right hand.
The arm of strength is identified with tefillin.
A psalm says God gives strength to His people.
How are tefillin a strength for Israel?
A verse about God’s name upon Israel is joined to a teaching identifying head tefillin.
What is written in the tefillin of the Master of the world?
A verse praising Israel as a unique nation is named.
Does God take pride in Israel’s praise?
Verses in Deuteronomy speak of Israel and God declaring one another special.
The reciprocal declaration is explained as each making the other unique.
Shema is cited for Israel declaring God one.
The verse about Israel’s uniqueness is cited for God’s declaration.
What is written in the other tefillin compartments?
Several scriptural praises of Israel are listed.
That list seems to require too many compartments.
Related verses are grouped together so the passages fit the compartments.

6b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The discussion of God’s tefillin concludes with the passages on the arm.
One who regularly attends synagogue but misses a day is sought by God.
A verse about one walking in darkness is cited.
Absence for a commandment is distinguished from absence for ordinary business.
The difference is explained by whether the person trusted in God.
Rabbi Yohanan says God is angered when a synagogue lacks ten worshippers.
Isaiah’s question about finding no one is cited.
One who fixes a place for prayer has the God of Abraham as a help.
The person is praised after death as a humble disciple of Abraham.
How is it known that Abraham fixed a place for prayer?
Verses about Abraham returning to a place and standing in prayer support the claim.
One should not take large steps when leaving a synagogue.
Abaye limits this to leaving; hurrying to enter is a commandment.
Hosea’s call to pursue knowledge of God supports hurrying in.
Rabbi Zeira initially thought the sages’ Sabbath haste was improper.
A teaching says to run to a matter of law even on the Sabbath.
The verse about following God supplies support.
Rabbi Zeira then adopted the same practice.
The reward of a study session is the haste to reach it.
The reward of a public discourse is its crowded attendance.
The reward of study is the reasoning it produces.
The reward of a house of mourning is respectful silence.
The reward of a fast is charity.
The reward of a eulogy is raising a voice in lament.
The reward of attending a wedding is speaking to celebrate the couple.
Prayer behind a synagogue is described as wicked.
A psalm about the wicked walking around is cited.
Abaye limits the criticism to one who does not face the synagogue.
An encounter with Elijah illustrates the criticism of praying away from the synagogue.
What does the verse about vileness exalted among people mean?
It refers to lofty matters that people treat with contempt.
Needing others changes a person’s face, according to two sages.
The same verse about vileness is applied to that condition.
What is the meaning of the word kerum?
A changing-color bird named kerum explains the image.
Two sages compare dependence on others to suffering both fire and water.
A psalm mentioning fire and water is cited.
Rav Huna urges care with the afternoon prayer, when Elijah was answered.
The verse about Elijah at the afternoon offering is cited.
Elijah’s repeated plea is explained as asking for fire and for recognition that it was not magic.
Rabbi Yohanan adds that the evening prayer also requires care.
A psalm compares prayer to incense and to the evening offering.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak adds the morning prayer.
A psalm repeats the appeal to God in the morning.
One who enjoys a wedding meal without gladdening the groom transgresses five voices.
Jeremiah lists voices of joy, groom, bride, and thanksgiving.
What reward comes from gladdening the groom?
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says the person merits Torah.
Verses at Sinai describe the voices accompanying the giving of Torah.
Another verse about voices at Sinai appears to make the count too large.
Those additional voices preceded the giving of Torah.
Rabbi Abbahu compares gladdening the groom to bringing a thanksgiving offering.
Jeremiah mentions bringing thanksgiving offerings.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak compares the act to rebuilding a ruin of Jerusalem.
Jeremiah’s promise of restoration supports the comparison.
A God-fearing person’s words are heard.
Ecclesiastes joins fear of God to all being heard.
What does the verse mean by calling this the whole person?
One answer says the world was created for such a person.
Another says such a person is equal in worth to the world.
A third says the world was created to accompany such a person.
One should greet first a neighbor who normally offers a greeting.
A psalm commands seeking and pursuing peace.
Failing to return the neighbor’s greeting is likened to robbery.
A verse about robbing the poor is cited.

ranges.en: R. Yoḥanan asks how we know that the Holy One prays.
Isaiah speaks of bringing people to “My house of prayer.”
The verse calls it “My prayer,” implying God’s own prayer.
What does God pray?
Rav says God prays that mercy overcome anger and that He treat His children beyond strict justice.
R. Ishmael recounts entering the innermost sanctuary and being asked by God to bless Him.
R. Ishmael blesses God with the same wish that mercy prevail over anger and strict justice.
God nods, teaching that even an ordinary person’s blessing should not be slighted.
R. Yoḥanan asks how we know not to appease a person while that person is angry.
God’s words to Moses, “My face shall go, and I shall give you rest,” are cited.
God tells Moses to wait until His angry countenance has passed.
Can anger exist before the Holy One?
The answer is yes.
The verse says that God expresses indignation every day.
How long does that anger last, and what is a moment?
A moment is described as an extremely small fraction of an hour.
Only Balaam could identify that instant, as implied by the verse calling him one who knows the knowledge of the Most High.
How could Balaam know God’s mind when he did not understand his own donkey?
His special knowledge was the ability to pinpoint the moment of divine anger.
Micah calls Israel to remember Balak’s plan and Balaam’s response.
What are the “righteous acts of the Lord” mentioned there?
God’s kindness was that He did not become angry during Balaam’s days, saving Israel from his curse.
Balaam’s words to Balak say he cannot curse whom God has not cursed.
This teaches that God did not express anger during those days.
How long is the moment of God’s anger?
R. Avin says it lasts only as long as saying the word “moment.”
What shows that God’s anger lasts only a moment?
Psalms contrasts the moment of His anger with a lifetime of favor.
Isaiah also says to hide for a moment until indignation passes.
When does that anger occur?
Abaye places it in the first three hours, when a rooster stands on one foot with a white comb.
But the rooster’s comb is always white.
At other times it has red streaks; at that moment it does not.
R. Joshua ben Levi tries to identify that moment to curse a troublesome neighbor, but falls asleep.
He concludes that issuing such a curse is improper.
The verse says God’s mercy extends over all His works.
Proverbs says that punishment is not good for the righteous.
R. Meir teaches that God becomes angry when kings crown themselves and worship the rising sun.
R. Yoḥanan says a single inner rebuke is better than many lashes.
Hosea depicts a person deciding to return to her first husband.
Reish Lakish says the inner rebuke surpasses a hundred lashes.
Proverbs contrasts a rebuke to the wise with a hundred blows to a fool.
R. Yoḥanan says Moses made three requests of God and was granted them; the first concerned the divine presence with Israel.
Moses asks whether God will go with Israel.
Moses also asks that the divine presence not rest on other nations.
The verse says that Moses and Israel will be distinguished.
Moses further asks to know God’s ways.
Moses says, “Make Your ways known to me.”
Moses asks why righteous and wicked people each sometimes prosper and sometimes suffer.
The first answer ties each person’s fortunes to whether the father was righteous or wicked.
The discussion restates that a righteous person’s fortunes were attributed to the father.
But verses about visiting parents’ sins on children and not punishing children for parents appear to conflict.
The verses are reconciled: the punishment applies when children continue their parents’ deeds.
Instead, prosperity and suffering are explained through the degree of a person’s own righteousness or wickedness.
R. Meir disputes this account, saying Moses received only two of his three requests.
The verse says God may grant grace and mercy even to someone undeserving.
But God tells Moses that he cannot see His face.
R. Joshua ben Korḥa says Moses declined an earlier opportunity, so God declined this request.
Another teaching disputes that account and links three merits of Moses to three rewards.
Moses’ hiding his face, fearing, and refraining from looking each correspond to a later divine reward.
God’s promise that Moses will see His back is cited.
Rav Ḥana explains that God showed Moses the knot of His tefillin.
R. Yoḥanan teaches that God does not retract a favorable pronouncement, even if conditional.
What is the source for this?
God tells Moses that He might destroy Israel and make Moses into a greater nation.
Although Moses averts the decree, the promise is fulfilled through his descendants.
Chronicles names Moses’ descendants and says Reḥavyah’s sons became very numerous.
Rav Yosef interprets “numerous” as more than six hundred thousand.
A shared word for increase links the verse about Moses’ descendants to Israel’s growth in Egypt.

7b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: R. Yoḥanan says Abraham was the first to call God “Lord.”
Abraham addresses God as Lord in the verse about inheriting the land.
Rav says Daniel was answered for Abraham’s sake.
Daniel’s prayer asks God to favor the desolate sanctuary “for the Lord’s sake.”
Why does the prayer say “for the Lord’s sake” instead of “for Your sake”?
It means for Abraham’s sake, because Abraham first called God Lord.
R. Yoḥanan asks why one should not appease someone in a moment of anger.
God tells Moses that His face will pass before granting him rest.
R. Yoḥanan says Leah was the first person to thank God.
Leah says, “This time I shall thank the Lord.”
R. Elazar interprets Reuben’s name as Leah saying, “See the difference between my son and my father-in-law’s son.”
Esau sold his birthright willingly.
Even so, the verse says Esau hated Jacob.
Esau also complained that Jacob had supplanted him.
By contrast, Joseph took Reuben’s birthright against Reuben’s will.
Chronicles says Reuben’s birthright passed to Joseph’s sons.
Even so, Reuben did not envy Joseph.
Genesis says Reuben rescued Joseph from his brothers.
What is the meaning of the name Ruth?
Ruth merited David as a descendant, who delighted God with songs and praises.
How do we know that a name can shape a person’s course?
A verse about God making desolations is read instead as referring to names.
R. Yoḥanan says a wayward child at home is harder than the wars of Gog and Magog.
The psalm about David fleeing Absalom says his adversaries have multiplied.
The psalm about Gog and Magog lacks that wording.
Why is David’s flight from Absalom called a psalm rather than a lament?
A parable says a debtor worries before a debt is paid but rejoices afterward.
David feared that the calamity promised from his household might come through someone without pity.
When he saw that it was Absalom, he rejoiced and sang a psalm.
R. Yoḥanan says one may contend with the wicked in this world.
Proverbs contrasts those who praise the wicked with those who contend with them.
R. Dostai teaches the same permission and cites the same proverb.
Someone may object that Psalms says not to contend with evildoers or envy them.
The verse means not to become like evildoers or imitate their wrongdoing.
Another proverb says not to envy sinners but to fear God.
R. Yitzḥak says not to contend with a wicked person enjoying good fortune.
Psalms says that such a person’s ways prosper.
The psalm also says judgment remains distant from that person.
It further says that person overcomes adversaries.
One ruling concerns personal matters, the other religious matters.
Alternatively, both concern religious matters, but distinguish a wicked person whose fortune is favorable from one whose fortune is not.
Alternatively, both concern a fortunate wicked person, but distinguish a completely righteous opponent from one not completely righteous.
Rav Huna reads Habakkuk’s question about a wicked person swallowing someone more righteous.
Can the wicked swallow a righteous person when Psalms says God will not abandon the righteous?
Proverbs also says no evil befalls a righteous person.
A wicked person may swallow someone more righteous than himself, but not the completely righteous.
Another answer makes the wicked person’s favorable fortune the exceptional case.
R. Yoḥanan says a person who establishes a fixed place for prayer sees enemies fall.
The verse promises Israel a place where oppressors will no longer afflict them.
Rav Huna contrasts “afflict them” here with “destroy them” in the parallel verse.
The sequence is first affliction, then destruction.
R. Yoḥanan says serving a Torah scholar is greater than studying under one.
Elisha is identified as one who poured water on Elijah’s hands.
The verse says “poured,” not “studied,” emphasizing service.
R. Yitzḥak asks Rav Naḥman why he does not come to synagogue to pray.
Rav Naḥman says he is unable to come.
R. Yitzḥak suggests gathering ten people to pray with him.
Rav Naḥman says that is burdensome.
R. Yitzḥak then suggests asking the prayer leader to notify him when the congregation prays.
Rav Naḥman asks why so much effort is needed.
R. Yitzḥak begins to answer with a teaching of R. Yoḥanan, continued on the next daf.

8a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: What does the verse about praying at an acceptable time mean?
When is the acceptable time?
It is when the congregation prays.
R. Yose cites Isaiah’s promise of an answer at an acceptable time.
R. Aḥa cites Job’s declaration that God does not reject the mighty.
He also cites a psalm linking redemption in peace with the many who were with the speaker.
R. Natan teaches that God does not reject the prayer of a group.
He cites the verses about God not rejecting the mighty and redeeming the speaker in peace.
God credits one who studies Torah, does kindness, and prays with the congregation as if redeeming Him and His children from exile.
Reish Lakish calls one who has a synagogue nearby but does not pray there a bad neighbor.
Jeremiah speaks of God’s bad neighbors near Israel’s inheritance.
Reish Lakish adds that this neglect brings exile on the person and his children, citing Jeremiah.
R. Yoḥanan hears that there are elderly people in Babylonia.
He wonders how they live long outside the land named in the promise of lengthened days.
He learns that they attend synagogue early and late, and attributes their long lives to this.
R. Yehoshua ben Levi similarly instructs his sons to enter synagogue early and leave late to live longer.
R. Aḥa asks for a scriptural source.
Proverbs praises those who wait at God’s doors daily and then promises life.
Rav Ḥisda says one should enter two doorways into a synagogue before praying.
Does he mean literally passing through two doors?
He means entering a distance equal to two doorways before prayer.
The discussion quotes the verse about the godly praying at a “time of finding.”
R. Ḥanina interprets that time as finding a wife.
Proverbs says that finding a wife is finding good.
In the West, a groom was asked whether his experience was “finding” or “I find.”
The favorable expression comes from Proverbs’ verse about finding a wife.
The unfavorable expression comes from Ecclesiastes’ verse about finding a woman more bitter than death.
R. Natan interprets “time of finding” as finding Torah.
Proverbs says that finding Torah is finding life.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak interprets the phrase as referring to death.
He cites the verse about the “issues of death.”
A teaching counts 903 kinds of death from the numerical value of the word for “issues.”
Croup is described as the harshest death and a kiss as the easiest.
The teaching compares the painful and gentle kinds of death to physical experiences.
R. Yoḥanan interprets “time of finding” as finding burial.
Job speaks of people rejoicing when they find a grave.
Rabbah bar Rav Sheila applies this to praying for peace through the final shovelful at burial.
Mar Zutra interprets “time of finding” as finding a privy.
Teachers in the West prefer Mar Zutra’s interpretation.
Rava asks Rafram bar Pappa to share Rav Ḥisda’s teachings about synagogues.
Rav Ḥisda cites the psalm saying God loves the gates of Zion more than Jacob’s dwellings.
He reads this as preference for gates distinguished by halakhic study over synagogues and study houses.
R. Ḥiyya teaches that since the Temple’s destruction, God’s world contains the four cubits of halakhah.
Abaye formerly studied at home and prayed in synagogue.
After hearing that teaching, Abaye prayed where he studied.
R. Ammi and R. Assi likewise prayed in their place of study despite many synagogues in Tiberias.
R. Ḥiyya says a person who enjoys the work of his hands is greater than one who fears Heaven.
The verse about one who fears Heaven calls that person happy.
The verse about one who eats from his labor says both “happy” and “good for you,” understood as this world and the next.
The second blessing is absent from the verse about fear of Heaven.
R. Ḥiyya says one should live near one’s teacher.
While Shimei lived, Solomon did not marry Pharaoh’s daughter.
But another teaching says not to live near one’s teacher.
The ruling depends on whether the student submits to the teacher.
A verse condemns those who leave God; whom does it describe here?
It refers to one who leaves while a Torah scroll is open.
R. Abbahu would leave between readers.
Rav Pappa asks whether one may leave between verses.
The question remains unresolved.
Rav Sheshet turned away and studied, saying each group had its own subject.
Rav Huna teaches that one should complete the weekly portion with the congregation, twice in Hebrew and once in translation.

8b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The twice-Hebrew, once-Targum reading requirement includes even the place names Atarot and Divon.
Completing one’s weekly portions with the congregation is said to lengthen life.
Rav Beivai planned to finish the entire year’s portions on the eve of Yom Kippur.
Ḥiyya cites the verse that speaks of self-affliction on the ninth of the month.
Is the fast not actually on the tenth?
Eating and drinking on the ninth is credited as though one fasted on both days.
Rav Beivai then planned to read early, but an elder taught that the reading should be neither advanced nor delayed.
R. Yehoshua ben Levi tells his sons to finish the weekly portions with the congregation, twice in Hebrew and once in Targum.
He also tells them to attend to the veins in slaughter according to R. Yehuda.
The mishnah quotes R. Yehuda’s requirement to cut the veins.
He further tells them to honor an elder who forgot learning involuntarily.
Both the intact tablets and the broken tablets were kept in the Ark.
Rava advises his sons not to cut meat on their hands.
Two reasons are offered: personal danger and spoiling the meal.
Rava also warns against sitting on an Aramean woman’s bed or walking behind a synagogue while people pray.
The discussion asks what the warning about the bed means.
Three readings are offered: do not sleep without the Shema, do not marry a convert, or avoid a literal Aramean woman’s bed.
In the story, Rav Pappa has a bed lifted and a dead child is found beneath it.
The story is used to restate the warning against sitting on such a bed.
The warning about passing behind a synagogue is restated.
R. Yehoshua ben Levi likewise forbids passing behind a synagogue while the congregation prays.
Abaye limits the prohibition to a synagogue without another entrance.
It is also limited to a place without another synagogue.
Carrying a load, running, or wearing tefillin also removes the objection.
R. Akiva praises three Median practices: cutting meat on a table, kissing on the hand, and consulting in a field.
Rav Adda asks for a scriptural source for consulting in a field.
Jacob calls Rachel and Leah into the field to speak with them.
Rabban Gamliel praises three Persian practices of modesty in eating, in the privy, and in intimacy.
Isaiah’s phrase “My consecrated ones” is quoted.
Rav Yosef applies it ironically to Persians destined for Gehinnom.
The mishnah’s ruling that the evening Shema lasts until dawn is recalled.
Shmuel rules according to Rabban Gamliel.
R. Shimon ben Yoḥai says one can read Shema before and after dawn to satisfy night and day obligations.
The teaching calls both readings “night,” implying that after dawn is still night.
Yet it says one reading fulfills the daytime duty, implying that after dawn is day.
It remains night in one sense, but people begin to rise then, so it can count as day for Shema.
Rav Aḥa says the law follows R. Shimon ben Yoḥai.
Some attach Rav Aḥa’s ruling to a different teaching of R. Shimon ben Yoḥai in R. Akiva’s name.
That teaching allows one Shema before sunrise and one after sunrise to fulfill both night and day.
It calls both readings “day,” implying that before sunrise is day.
Yet it says one reading fulfills the nighttime duty, implying that before sunrise is night. The resolution continues on 9a.

9a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Before sunrise is already day for this reading, although some people are still asleep then, so the teaching calls it night.
R. Aḥa reports that the law follows R. Shimon ben Yoḥai speaking in R. Akiva’s name.
R. Zeira adds that the bedtime blessing Hashkivenu is not recited at that time.
Rav Yitzḥak says R. Aḥa’s ruling was inferred from an incident, not stated explicitly.
Two scholars who missed Shema after becoming drunk at a wedding came before R. Yehoshua ben Levi.
He says R. Shimon’s opinion may be relied on in pressing circumstances.
The mishnah’s account of Rabban Gamliel’s sons returning from a feast is recalled.
Had the sons not known their father’s teaching before?
They wanted to know whether the majority disagreed with him or set midnight only as a safeguard.
He says the sages agree that they remain obligated; midnight protects people from transgression.
The mishnah says the same rule applies beyond this case.
Why would it say this if Rabban Gamliel himself never set a midnight deadline?
He explains that even the sages’ midnight limit is a safeguard; the underlying obligation lasts until dawn.
The mishnah’s example of burning sacrificial fats is recalled.
Why does it omit eating the Paschal offering?
Another teaching includes the Paschal offering among obligations lasting until dawn.
Rav Yosef assigns the two rulings to R. Elazar ben Azarya and R. Akiva.
The baraita quotes the command to eat the Paschal meat “on this night.”
R. Elazar ben Azarya compares “this night” with the night of the Egyptian plague and limits eating until midnight.
R. Akiva objects that the verse about eating in haste already marks the deadline.
The phrase “at night” instead teaches that the offering cannot be eaten by day.
R. Elazar needs “this” for his comparison; what does R. Akiva do with that word?
R. Akiva uses “this night” to exclude the next night, despite a possible analogy to other lesser holy offerings.
How does R. Elazar exclude the next night?
He uses the command not to leave any of the offering until morning.
R. Akiva objects that “morning” could mean the second morning.
R. Elazar takes an unqualified “morning” to mean the first one.
A parallel baraita interprets the verse about the time of the Passover sacrifice and the Exodus.
R. Eliezer assigns evening to slaughter, sunset to eating, and the time of departure to burning the remainder.
R. Yehoshua reads the time of departure as the endpoint of eating instead.
R. Abba says all agree Israel’s redemption began at night.
Deuteronomy says God brought Israel out at night.
They actually left Egypt by day.
Numbers says they went out the day after Passover.
What, then, is the point of dispute?
They disagree whether the haste refers to the Egyptians’ haste or Israel’s haste.
A supporting teaching quotes the verse about God bringing Israel out at night.
But another verse says Israel left openly on the following day.
Redemption began during the preceding evening.
The next discussion quotes God’s command to speak to the people about borrowing valuables.
R. Yannai’s school reads the word “please” as a request.
God asks Moses to ask Israel to borrow silver and gold from the Egyptians; the reason continues on 9b.

9b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The request for Egyptian valuables ensures that the promise of great wealth is fulfilled along with the promised servitude.
The Israelites would rather escape with their lives.
A prisoner wants immediate release even when promised wealth on the following day.
R. Ammi says the Egyptians lent Israel valuables against someone’s will.
Was it against the Egyptians’ will or the Israelites’ will?
The view that it was against the Egyptians’ will cites the verse about dividing spoil.
The view that it was against the Israelites’ will points to the burden of carrying the valuables.
R. Ammi says Israel emptied Egypt like a storehouse without grain.
Reish Lakish compares it to a fishless pool.
God’s name “I will be” means He will accompany Israel in this servitude and later exiles.
Moses objects that the present suffering is enough for them to hear about now.
God tells Moses to say only “I will be has sent me.”
Why did Elijah repeat “Answer me” twice?
He sought a heavenly fire to consume the altar offering.
He also sought to prevent the people from dismissing the event as sorcery.
Elijah’s plea concerning the turning of their hearts is cited.
The morning Shema begins when blue can be distinguished from white.
R. Eliezer requires distinguishing blue from green and sets sunrise as the end.
R. Yehoshua allows until the third hour, when kings commonly rise.
Reading afterward still counts as reading Torah, though the designated time has passed.
What does distinguishing blue from white mean?
Does it mean telling a blue lump of wool from a white one?
Those can be distinguished even at night.
It means distinguishing the blue and white portions within the same object.
R. Meir sets the time when one can distinguish a wolf from a dog.
R. Akiva sets it when one can distinguish a donkey from a wild donkey.
Others set it when one recognizes an acquaintance four cubits away.
Rav Huna rules like the “others.”
Abaye applies that measure to tefillin but follows the early pious worshipers for Shema.
R. Yoḥanan says those worshipers finished Shema at sunrise.
A baraita confirms they finished at sunrise so redemption could be joined to prayer in daylight.
R. Zeira cites the verse about fearing God with the sun.
The holy congregation of Jerusalem taught that joining redemption to prayer protects one throughout the day.
R. Zeira objects that he did join them yet experienced misfortune.
The supposed misfortune was carrying myrtle to the palace, a privilege worth paying for.
R. Yoḥanan says one should run even to see foreign kings, to compare their honor with Israel’s future kings.
R. Ilai asks Ulla to greet his brother before the academy, praising his joy in commandments.
His brother once joined redemption to prayer and remained joyful all day.
How can they be joined when prescribed verses come at the beginning and end of prayer?
R. Elazar first assigns that practice to evening prayer.
But R. Yoḥanan praises joining evening redemption to evening prayer too.
R. Elazar then assigns it to afternoon prayer.
Rav Ashi says the introductory verse is part of the prayer as instituted by the sages.
Evening prayer likewise inserts Hashkivenu between redemption and prayer.
Hashkivenu counts as an extension of redemption, just as the introductory verse counts as part of prayer.
Why place “May the words of my mouth be acceptable” after the Eighteen Blessings when it could also begin them?
David said that verse after eighteen psalms, so the sages placed it after the Eighteen Blessings.
But are there not nineteen psalms before that verse?
Psalms 1 and 2 are counted as a single unit.
David is said to have composed 103 psalms before first saying Hallelujah upon seeing the downfall of the wicked.
The cited psalm calls for sinners to cease and concludes with Hallelujah.
But the current count has 104 psalms.
Again, Psalms 1 and 2 must count as one unit.
A further teaching of R. Shmuel bar Naḥmani begins and continues on 10a.

10a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: David opened and closed a favored psalm with “Happy.”
Psalm 1 begins with “Happy is the man.”
The next psalm ends with “Happy are all who take refuge in Him.”
R. Meir prayed for troublesome neighbors to die.
Beruriah challenges his reading of the verse: it says sins, not sinners, should cease.
The verse then says the wicked will be no more, which can follow when their sins cease.
Beruriah urges him to pray for their repentance instead.
He prays for them and they repent.
A sectarian asks why a barren woman should sing because she has not borne children.
Beruriah cites the end of the verse about the desolate woman having many children.
She reads the barren woman as Israel, which has not borne children destined for Gehinnom.
A sectarian asks why the psalm about fleeing Absalom precedes the psalm about fleeing Saul, though Saul came first.
R. Abbahu says the order invites interpretation through the juxtaposition of passages.
R. Yoḥanan cites the verse describing scriptural passages as joined forever.
Why is the Absalom psalm placed beside the psalm about Gog and Magog?
A rebellious son makes it easier to understand the possibility of a servant rebelling against his master.
R. Yoḥanan asks whom Proverbs means by the mouth of wisdom and teaching of kindness.
He applies it to David, who sang from five stages of life.
David sang while still in his mother’s womb.
The psalm calls on all that is within him to bless God.
After birth, he saw the heavenly bodies and sang.
The psalm calls on the mighty heavenly servants to bless God.
David also sang while nursing at his mother’s breast.
The psalm tells his soul not to forget God’s benefits.
What benefit is meant by “all His benefits”?
R. Abbahu points to the placement of the breasts.
Why are they placed there?
One answer is so the child does not gaze at nakedness.
Another is so the child does not nurse from an unclean place.
David saw the downfall of the wicked and sang.
The psalm asks that sins cease and ends with Hallelujah.
He contemplated death and sang.
A psalm praising God’s greatness is cited.
How is that psalm understood to concern death?
Its continuation speaks of God withdrawing breath and creatures perishing.
Rav Shimi bar Ukva is described studying aggadah before R. Yehoshua ben Levi.
He asks about the verse calling on his soul and all within him to bless God.
A human artist draws an outer form but cannot give it life and organs; God forms life within life.
Hannah’s words that none is holy like God and no rock is like Him are cited.
“Rock” is read as “artist”: none creates as God does.
What is meant by “none beside You”?
A wordplay teaches that human works outlast their makers, while God outlasts His works.
The original question is clarified: to whom do David’s five calls to bless God refer?
As God fills the world, the soul fills the body.
As God sees without being seen, the soul sees without being seen.
As God sustains the world, the soul sustains the body.
As God is pure, the soul is pure.
As God dwells in inner chambers, the soul dwells within the body.
One bearing these five traits should praise the One bearing them in the greater sense.
Rav Hamnuna reads Ecclesiastes as asking who can make peace between two righteous people, Hezekiah and Isaiah.
Hezekiah expected Isaiah to visit him, citing Elijah’s visit to Ahab.
Isaiah expected Hezekiah to visit him, citing Joram’s visit to Elisha.
God brought illness upon Hezekiah and instructed Isaiah to visit him.
Kings recounts Isaiah’s visit and his warning that Hezekiah will die.
The warning is read as death in this world and loss of life in the world to come.
Hezekiah asks why the punishment is so severe.
Isaiah says he failed to have children.
Hezekiah says divine insight showed him that his children would be unworthy.
Isaiah replies that Hezekiah must do what he was commanded and leave hidden outcomes to God.
Hezekiah asks to marry Isaiah’s daughter, hoping their combined merit will yield worthy children.
Isaiah says the decree has already been issued.
Hezekiah rejects Isaiah’s finality and sends him away.
Hezekiah cites his family’s teaching: even with a sword at one’s neck, one must not give up on mercy.
R. Yoḥanan and R. Elazar transmit the same teaching.
Job says he will hope in God even if God kills him.

10b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: R. Ḥanan says one must not give up on mercy even after a dream predicts death.
Ecclesiastes warns that dreams can contain vanity and directs one to fear God.
Hezekiah immediately turned to the wall and prayed.
What does the “wall” mean?
Reish Lakish reads it as the chambers of Hezekiah’s heart.
Jeremiah uses “walls of my heart.”
R. Levi instead says Hezekiah invoked the Shunammite woman’s wall and the greater merit of his ancestor’s Temple covering.
Hezekiah’s prayer recalls walking before God faithfully and doing what was good.
What good deed did Hezekiah mean?
Rav says he joined redemption directly to prayer.
R. Levi says he hid the Book of Remedies.
A teaching lists six acts of Hezekiah: three approved and three disapproved.
The approved acts were hiding the Book of Remedies, breaking the bronze serpent, and dragging his father’s bones on a rope bed.
The disapproved acts were stopping Gihon’s waters, sending Temple doors to Assyria, and adding a month of Nisan within Nisan.
Did Hezekiah not know that the designated month is Nisan and no later month may replace it?
He misapplied Shmuel’s rule against intercalating on the thirtieth of Adar, a day that might become Nisan.
R. Yoḥanan says invoking one’s own merit brings an answer in others’ merit, and invoking others’ merit brings one’s own.
Moses appeals to the merit of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel.
A psalm credits Moses himself with standing before God to avert destruction.
Hezekiah invokes his own faithful conduct.
God promises to save Jerusalem for David’s sake.
R. Yehoshua ben Levi reads Hezekiah’s suffering as bitter even when peace was sent to him.
The Shunammite woman’s proposal for a small upper chamber is quoted.
Rav and Shmuel disagree whether it was an open room later roofed or a large portico later divided.
“Wall” fits the divided portico; how does the roofed-room view explain it?
It refers to putting a roof on the room.
“Upper chamber” fits a room; how does the portico view explain it?
It was the finest of the rooms.
The verse lists a bed, table, chair, and lamp for Elisha.
A scholar may accept hospitality like Elisha or decline it like Samuel.
Samuel’s return home is read to mean his household provisions accompanied him everywhere.
The Shunammite woman calls Elisha a holy man of God.
R. Yose says a woman recognizes a guest’s character more readily than a man.
How did she know Elisha was holy?
One explanation mentions no fly over his table; another mentions the unstained linen on his bed.
The wording suggests Elisha was holy but his attendant was not.
The story of Gehazi pushing the woman away is cited and interpreted as improper touching.
Hosting a Torah scholar and sharing one’s means is credited like offering the daily sacrifices.
One should pray in a low place rather than on an elevated platform.
The psalm says, “From the depths I called to You.”
A baraita likewise forbids praying from a chair, stool, or height because pride is out of place before God.
Verses about calling from the depths and a poor person’s prayer support the teaching.
One who prays should align the feet.
Ezekiel describes the heavenly beings’ feet as straight.
What does “Do not eat with the blood” teach here?
Do not eat before praying for your life.
Another teaching applies a verse about casting God behind one’s back to one who eats and drinks before prayer.
A wordplay reads it as pride: after satisfying oneself, the person accepts heavenly kingship.
Shmuel rules like R. Yehoshua that the morning Shema ends at the third hour.
The mishnah says a later reader has not lost out.
Rav Ḥisda initially says that person must omit the blessing over light.
A baraita says the late reader still recites two blessings before Shema and one afterward.
This refutes Rav Ḥisda’s initial statement.
Another version has Rav Ḥisda say “no loss” means no loss of the blessings.
A baraita explicitly preserves the two blessings before and one after.
R. Mani infers that reading Shema at its proper time surpasses ordinary Torah study.
Beit Shammai require reclining for evening Shema and standing for morning Shema, citing lying down and rising.
Beit Hillel allow reading in one’s usual manner, citing walking on the way.
What then does “when you lie down and when you rise” mean?
It refers to the usual times people lie down and rise.
R. Tarfon recounts reclining while traveling, following Beit Shammai, and being endangered by robbers.
The sages say he brought the danger on himself by disregarding Beit Hillel.

11a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Why do Beit Shammai reject Beit Hillel’s reading of the Shema posture verses?
Beit Shammai say the Torah could have said “morning and evening”; “lying down” and “rising” require those actual postures.
What do Beit Shammai do with “when you walk on the way”?
They use it with “when you sit at home” to exempt someone occupied in a commandment and a bridegroom.
Thus a man marrying a virgin is exempt from Shema, while one marrying a widow remains obligated.

The possessive wording “your sitting” and “your walking” limits it to one’s own voluntary activity.
Then why is a man marrying a widow not exempt too?
A virgin’s bridegroom is preoccupied; a widow’s is not in the same way.

Yet a mourner remains bound by commandments except tefillin, which are called an ornament.

Beit Shammai also use the wording to exempt messengers on a commandment.
Beit Hillel infer that an ordinary traveler can still read Shema.
Beit Hillel permit Shema while standing, sitting, reclining, traveling, or working.
R. Yishmael and R. Elazar ben Azarya change postures in opposite directions when Shema time arrives.
R. Elazar asks why R. Yishmael sat upright exactly when he reclined, treating the change as a conspicuous protest.
R. Yishmael followed Beit Hillel and feared students might take R. Elazar’s change as precedent for Beit Shammai.
What does his added concern about students mean?

Rav Yosef says one who follows Beit Shammai has not fulfilled it.

Beit Shammai reply that the elders did object and said the person had never properly fulfilled sukkah.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak says following Beit Shammai’s Shema posture incurs grave danger.

The next mishnah prescribes two blessings before and one after morning Shema, and two before and two after evening Shema.

Which blessings precede the morning Shema?
R. Yaakov begins to answer in R. Oshaya’s name; the answer continues on 11b.

ranges.en: The first morning blessing uses Isaiah’s wording, “forms light and creates darkness.”
Why not say “creates brightness” instead?
The blessing follows the wording of the verse.
But another clause of that verse says “creates evil,” while prayer changes it to “creates all”; wording can be softened.
Why not similarly replace “darkness” with “brightness”?
Rava says each prayer mentions the character of both day and night.
The morning blessing mentions night through darkness; where does the evening blessing mention day?
Abaye cites its wording about rolling light before darkness and darkness before light.
What is the second blessing before morning Shema?
Shmuel and R. Elazar prescribe the blessing “Abounding Love.”
A baraita likewise prefers “Abounding Love” over “Everlasting Love.”
Other sages prescribe “Everlasting Love,” citing Jeremiah’s verse about everlasting love.
Shmuel says someone who studies before Shema recites the Torah blessing; the Shema blessing of love can otherwise cover it.
Rav Huna requires a blessing for Scripture study but not Midrash.
R. Elazar requires it for Scripture and Midrash but not Mishnah.
R. Yoḥanan includes Mishnah but excludes Talmud.
Rava includes Talmud as well.
Rav Ḥiyya reports Rav washing, blessing, and then teaching Sifra.
What blessing is said?
Shmuel gives the blessing over engaging in words of Torah.
R. Yoḥanan adds a prayer that Torah be sweet to Israel and their descendants and closes with praise of God who teaches Torah.
Rav Hamnuna gives the blessing that God chose Israel and gave the Torah.
He calls this the finest of the blessings.
Rav Pappa concludes that all the formulations should be said.
A mishnah describes the Temple priests saying one blessing, reciting the Decalogue and Shema passages, and adding further blessings.
Which single blessing did they say before the reading?
Several sages were asked and passed the question onward until Rav Yehuda answered.
Shmuel identifies it as “Abounding Love.”
Another report identifies it instead as “Forms Light.”
Rav Yitzḥak says that report was inferred rather than stated explicitly.
The inferred teaching says the blessings do not prevent one another’s fulfillment.
If the priests said “Forms Light,” omission of “Abounding Love” would support independent validity; the analysis continues on 12a.
