ranges.en: If the priests first said “Abounding Love,” that alone would not show that the two blessings are independent.
They might have delayed “Forms Light” until its proper time and then recited it.
What difference does it make that the report was only inferred?
The original inference might concern only the order of the blessings, since both could ultimately have been said.
The Temple service included the Decalogue, Shema passages, and specified blessings.
Shmuel says a proposal to add the Decalogue outside the Temple was dropped because of sectarian objections.
A teaching of R. Natan confirms that the proposed practice was dropped.
Rabbah bar Rav Huna proposed it in Sura, but Rav Ḥisda cited the earlier abolition.
Amemar proposed it in Nehardea, but Rav Ashi gave the same response.
On Shabbat the outgoing priestly watch added a blessing.
What was that blessing?
The outgoing watch wished the incoming watch love, fellowship, peace, and friendship from God.
The mishnah’s rule about long and short blessings is recalled.
A person holding wine but initially thinking it beer still fulfills the blessing by concluding correctly for wine.
Even the general “everything came to be by His word” formula would suffice for wine.
What if one holds beer, initially thinks it wine, and concludes with the formula for beer?
Does the opening intention or the concluding formula control?
A baraita judges the morning light blessing by whether it ends with the proper morning formula.
It likewise judges the evening blessing by whether it ends with the proper evening formula.
The baraita states a general rule that the conclusion controls.
That case may differ because the conclusion explicitly names the Creator of lights.
Rav requires the divine name in a blessing, which would make that explanation work.
But R. Yoḥanan requires divine kingship; what answers his view?
The opening names God and His kingship while invoking both day and night, so the conclusion can still decide.
The baraita’s general rule may seem to include the original beer-and-wine question.
Instead, it may include the case of bread and dates.
How would that case differ from the original question if bread was eaten but dates were expected?
The case is eating dates after starting as if for bread; even the bread conclusion could work.
Dates are nourishing, explaining why the bread formula could apply.
Rav says the morning and evening Shema blessings must use their proper “true and firm” and “true and trustworthy” forms.
The psalm contrasts declaring kindness in the morning with faithfulness at night.
Rav says to bow at “Blessed” and rise at the divine name.
Shmuel cites the verse that God raises those who are bent down.
A verse about fearing before God’s name seems to oppose rising at the name.
The verse says “before My name,” not “at My name.”
Shmuel invites Ḥiyya to hear the teaching of Ḥiyya’s father, Rav.
The teaching again says to bow at “Blessed” and rise at the divine name.

12b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Sheshet bent quickly when bowing and straightened slowly when rising.
Rav prescribes “the holy King” and “the King of judgment” during the ten days from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur.
R. Elazar says “the holy God” still fulfills the obligation.
Isaiah uses “the holy God” in a passage about divine judgment during those days.
What is the practical ruling?
Rav Yosef retains “the holy God” and “the King who loves righteousness and judgment.”
Rabbah requires “the holy King” and “the King of judgment”; the law follows Rabbah.
One able to pray for a neighbor who fails to do so is called a sinner.
Samuel says refraining from praying for the people would be a sin.
Rava says one should also grieve for a Torah scholar in distress.
Might the proposed proof from Saul’s complaint apply only to a king?
A psalm about becoming ill while others suffered supplies another source.
Rav says shame after sin can lead to forgiveness of all sins.
Ezekiel links remembering and shame with God’s forgiveness.
Perhaps that verse applies only to a community.
Saul’s account to Samuel omits the Urim and Thummim while listing other ways he sought an answer.
Saul’s omission shows shame over his destruction of Nob, city of the priests.
How do we know he was forgiven?
Samuel says Saul and his sons will be “with me”; R. Yoḥanan reads this as sharing Samuel’s place.
Another verse calls Saul “chosen of the Lord,” affirmed by a heavenly voice.
The sages considered including the Balak passage in Shema.
They did not include it because its length would burden the congregation.
Was inclusion proposed because the passage mentions the exodus?
Other passages on usury and weights mention the exodus too.
Its distinctive verse says Israel lies down and rises like a lion.
Why not recite that verse alone?
A passage not divided by Moses is not divided for this recitation.
Why was the fringes passage included in Shema?
It contains five themes: fringes, the exodus, commandments, heresy, and improper desire and worship.
The verse explicitly links looking at the fringes with remembering commandments.
It also explicitly commands making fringes.
Another clause explicitly recalls the exodus.
Where are the other themes found?
“After your heart” is connected with heresy through a psalm denying God in the heart.
“After your eyes” is connected with improper desire through Samson’s words.
“You stray” is connected with idolatry through the verse about Baal worship.
The next mishnah requires mentioning the exodus at night.
R. Elazar ben Azarya says Ben Zoma taught him the scriptural basis for the nighttime mention.
Ben Zoma reads “all the days of your life” to include nights.
The sages instead read “all” as including the messianic era.
Ben Zoma asks whether the exodus will be mentioned in the messianic era.
Jeremiah anticipates a future redemption so prominent that the older exodus will no longer be the usual formula.
The sages say the exodus remains remembered, but later deliverance becomes primary.
The change from Jacob’s name to Israel illustrates a new name taking priority without erasing the old.

13a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Israel became Jacob’s primary name, while Jacob remained in secondary use.
Isaiah speaks of no longer remembering former things.
The former events are interpreted as prior servitude and the exodus.
Isaiah then announces that God is doing something new.
Rav Yosef interprets the new event as the war of Gog and Magog.
A parable describes someone remembering each successive rescue from wolf, lion, and snake more strongly than earlier rescues.
Likewise, later troubles can displace earlier ones in Israel’s account.
Chronicles says Abram is Abraham.
His changed name expands his role from father of Aram to father of the world.
Sarai is likewise called Sarah.
Her changed name expands her role from princess of her people to princess of the world.
Bar Kappara says calling Abraham “Abram” violates a positive command.
God says his name shall be Abraham.
R. Eliezer calls it a prohibition.
God says he shall no longer be called Abram.
Would calling Sarah “Sarai” likewise violate a rule?
That instruction was addressed specifically to Abraham.
Would calling Israel “Jacob” likewise be forbidden?
Scripture itself later calls him Jacob again.
Nehemiah also calls Abraham by his old name, Abram.
There the prophet recounts God’s earlier choice using the name from that time.
The first chapter ends, and the next discussion begins.
One reading the Torah when Shema time arrives fulfills Shema if the heart is directed appropriately.
R. Meir permits greetings between sections out of respect and within a section out of fear.
R. Yehuda distinguishes initiating and returning greetings, with broader permission between sections.
The mishnah lists the boundaries between blessings and Shema sections.
R. Yehuda forbids interruption between the fringes passage and “True and firm.”
Why does the first Shema passage precede the second?
One accepts divine kingship before accepting the other commandments.
Why does the second passage precede the fringes passage?
The second applies day and night, while the fringes passage applies by day.
Does the mishnah imply that commandments require intention?
If “directed his heart” merely means intending to read, he was already reading.
It excludes someone merely correcting the text.
Rabbi requires Shema in its written language; the sages allow any language.
Rabbi reads “these words shall be” as requiring their original form.
The sages read “Hear” as allowing a language the reciter understands.
But Rabbi too must account for “Hear.”
For Rabbi, it requires hearing one’s own utterance.
The sages allow fulfillment even without audible recitation.
But the sages too must account for “these words shall be.”
For them, it forbids reciting the Shema verses out of order.
Where does Rabbi derive the order requirement?
He derives it from the extra wording “the words.”
The sages do not derive anything from that wording.
Does Rabbi’s need for “these words shall be” imply that the rest of Torah can be read in any language?
No; “these words” is needed because “Hear” might suggest otherwise.
Does the sages’ need for “Hear” imply that the rest of Torah must remain in Hebrew?
No; “Hear” is needed because “these words shall be” might suggest otherwise.
A baraita derives the ban on reading Shema out of order from “these words shall be.”
Does “upon your heart” require intention for the entire passage?
R. Eliezer limits the requirement to the initial portion.
R. Akiva begins a challenge that continues on 13b.

13b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: R. Akiva argues that the verse’s mention of the heart requires intention throughout the first Shema passage.
R. Yoḥanan rules like R. Akiva.
Another version places R. Yoḥanan’s ruling after a teaching that Shema needs intention.
R. Aḥa says intention in the first passage is enough.
R. Yoḥanan rules like R. Aḥa in that version.
A baraita derives the ban on reading Shema out of order.
R. Zutra assigns intention to the first passage and recitation to what follows.
R. Yoshiah reverses the emphasis, assigning recitation first and intention afterward.
Why does R. Zutra require recitation afterward?
The first passage also says to speak the words.
He means both recitation and intention first, but recitation alone afterward.
The first passage mentions both the heart and speaking.
The next passage also mentions heart and speaking.
The later heart wording is used for the placement of tefillin against the heart.
The discussion restates R. Yoshiah’s allocation of recitation first and intention afterward.
Why require intention afterward?
The first passage also mentions the heart.
R. Yoshiah means both recitation and intention first, but intention alone afterward.
The first passage mentions both the heart and speaking.
The next passage also mentions the heart and speaking.
There “speaking of them” refers to teaching children Torah so they can recite it.
R. Meir requires intention through the opening verse of Shema.
Rava rules like R. Meir.
Symmachus says prolonging “one” in the opening verse lengthens life.
The lengthening belongs especially on the final dalet, without clipping the ḥet.
R. Yirmeya prolonged the word exceedingly in front of R. Ḥiyya bar Abba.
He was told that once he affirmed God’s rule in every direction, further lengthening was unnecessary.
Rav Yehuda says one stands through “upon your heart.”
This means from the opening through those words, but not necessarily beyond.
R. Yoḥanan requires standing through the whole first passage.
His ruling fits his view that intention is required throughout that passage.
Rabbi Yehuda ha-Nasi’s regular Shema was the opening verse.
Rav asks when Rabbi accepted divine kingship during his teaching.
R. Ḥiyya points to Rabbi covering his face with his hands.
Did Rabbi later complete the Shema?
Bar Kappara says no; R. Shimon son of Rabbi says yes.
Bar Kappara asks why Rabbi reviewed teachings mentioning the exodus if he later completed Shema.
It allowed the exodus to be mentioned at its proper time.
One who says the opening verse and then falls asleep has fulfilled the basic obligation.
Rav Naḥman tells his attendant to rouse him for the first verse, but not trouble him beyond it.
Rav Yosef reports a similar practice for Rabbah.
Rav Yosef forbids reading Shema while lying on one’s back.
Is merely sleeping on one’s back permitted? R. Yehoshua ben Levi condemned it.
A slight turn allows sleeping, but still does not permit Shema in that posture.
Yet R. Yoḥanan read Shema while inclined.
His large body made that case different.
The mishnah’s rule on greetings between sections is recalled.
Why explicitly permit returning a greeting if initiating one out of respect is already allowed?
The phrase may mean returning any person’s greeting.
The same problem arises for greetings within a section: why state a weaker permission to reply?
If replying is allowed out of respect, that sounds like R. Yehuda’s view, not the view under discussion.
The mishnah is expanded: R. Meir allows initiating for respect between sections and for fear within, with replies implicit.
R. Yehuda’s distinct rule for replying out of respect within a section follows.

14a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: R. Yehuda allows greeting out of respect between sections and returning anyone’s greeting.
A baraita confirms R. Meir’s rules for initiating and returning greetings during Shema.
The baraita also states R. Yehuda’s broader permissions for returning greetings.
May one interrupt Hallel or Megillah to greet someone?
Does an inference from interruptible Shema permit it, or does publicizing the miracle carry greater weight?
R. Ḥiyya says interruption is permitted.
Rabbah limits interruption on full-Hallel days to breaks between paragraphs.
On days when Hallel is not completed, interruption is allowed even within a paragraph.
But Ravina did not interrupt an incomplete Hallel when Rav bar Sheva visited.
Ravina did not regard that visitor as sufficiently distinguished for the greeting.
During a fast, may one taste food without eating or drinking it, or does the accepted fast exclude enjoyment too?
R. Ammi permits tasting.
A baraita says a person tasting food need not bless and a fasting person may taste.
How much may be tasted?
R. Ammi and R. Assi tasted up to a quarter-log.
Rav likens greeting a neighbor before prayer to making that person an altar.
He reads Isaiah’s question “of what account is he?” through a wordplay on “altar.”
Shmuel asks why one esteems the person before God.
Rav Sheshet cites the permission to greet during breaks in Shema.
R. Abba confines the prohibition to going specially to someone’s door before prayer.
R. Yonah similarly warns against pursuing personal business before prayer.
When challenged on the altar comparison, he states the more precise rule as a prohibition.
Rav Idi cites a verse that places righteousness before one’s journey.
One who prays before setting out receives divine help with worldly affairs.
The same verse puts righteousness before the person’s path.
R. Yonah says seven nights without a dream mark a person as evil.
A wordplay on the verse about sleeping satisfied without evil supports this reading.
R. Aḥa transmits another reading: one who fills oneself with Torah before sleep avoids bad tidings.
He cites the verse about sleeping satisfied and not meeting evil.
The mishnah’s list of breaks between Shema sections is recalled.
R. Yoḥanan rules like R. Yehuda that one must not pause between “your God” and “True and firm.”
R. Yoḥanan begins to ask the scriptural reason; the answer continues on 14b.

14b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Jeremiah’s verse links the divine name with “true.”
Should “true” be repeated at the start of the following blessing?
R. Yoḥanan says to repeat it.
Rabbah says it should not be repeated.
Rabbah objects when a prayer leader says “true” twice.
Rav Yosef praises the western evening custom of reciting the end of the fringes passage with “I am the Lord your God, true.”
Abaye questions it using Rav’s rule: one need not begin the passage, but must finish it once begun.
Another report says “and say to them” already counts as a beginning.
Rav Pappa says western practice counts the beginning only when “they shall make fringes” is reached.
Abaye concludes that their beginning prompts his community to complete the entire passage under Rav’s rule.
Ḥiyya says saying “I am the Lord your God” requires adding “true”; otherwise it need not be added.
But the exodus must still be mentioned.
A separate thanksgiving for redemption from Egypt can supply that mention.
R. Yehoshua ben Korḥa’s question about the order of Shema passages is recalled.
R. Shimon initially orders the passages as learning, teaching, and doing.
The first passage also mentions teaching and action.
The second passage also mentions action.
He means the first has learning, teaching, and action; the second teaching and action; the third action alone.
Is the earlier reason of R. Yehoshua ben Korḥa not enough?
Both reasons apply: accept divine kingship before commandments, and also follow the progression of themes.
Rav washed, recited Shema, put on tefillin, and prayed.
A baraita concerning a grave digger appears to place tefillin before Shema.
Its later clause has a worker wash, put on tefillin, recite Shema, and pray.
But the baraita seems internally inconsistent, first exempting the worker and then obligating him.
One clause concerns a lone worker; the other concerns two workers.
The apparent conflict with Rav’s sequence remains.
Rav may follow R. Yehoshua ben Korḥa’s priority of divine kingship before commandments.
That priority concerns the order of readings, not necessarily reading before performing tefillin.
Moreover, Rav Ḥiyya reports Rav blessing over study and putting on tefillin before Shema.
If Shema time had not yet arrived, what does that report establish?
It establishes that a blessing is needed even for Mishnah study.
The discrepancy in Rav’s order still remains.
The messenger bringing tefillin was late.
Ulla likens reading Shema without tefillin to giving false testimony about oneself.
R. Yoḥanan likens it to offering a sacrifice without its accompanying meal or libations.
R. Yoḥanan begins describing full acceptance of heavenly kingship; the procedure continues on 15a.

ranges.en: Full acceptance of heavenly kingship proceeds through bodily preparation, handwashing, tefillin, Shema, and prayer.
R. Yoḥanan credits this sequence as though one built an altar and offered a sacrifice.
The psalm joins clean hands with circling God’s altar.
Rava asks whether the verse should instead credit the person as though immersed, given its language of washing.
Ravina reports a western scholar’s ruling that one without water may clean the hands with earth, pebbles, or wood.
Rava approves because the verse requires cleanliness, not water specifically.
Rav Ḥisda even objected to searching for water when prayer time arrives.
The exception is prayer, for which one does seek water.
How far must one travel for water?
Up to a parasang forward, but not a full mile backward.
The wording implies that less than a mile backward is required.
The mishnah says inaudible Shema fulfills the duty, but R. Yose disagrees.
For unclear articulation, R. Yose permits fulfillment while R. Yehuda rejects it.
Reading paragraphs out of order fails; after an error, the reader returns to where it occurred.
Why does R. Yose require audible Shema?
He reads “Hear” as hearing one’s own words.
The first tanna instead reads “Hear” as permitting any understood language.
R. Yose derives both rules from the word.
A separate mishnah disallows a speaking but deaf person from separating terumah initially, yet validates it afterward.
Whose view permits that act only after the fact?
Rav Ḥisda assigns it to R. Yose, contrasting his strict rule for inaudible Shema with R. Yehuda’s leniency.
Shema is a Torah obligation, while the audible blessing over terumah is rabbinic and does not determine the separation.
Perhaps the terumah rule is R. Yehuda’s, who might also allow inaudible Shema only after the fact.
The mishnah’s phrasing highlights R. Yose’s strictness even after the fact; R. Yehuda would allow it initially.
A baraita on silent Grace after meals permits it after the fact but not initially.
That seems to fit neither R. Yehuda, if he permits it initially, nor R. Yose, if he rejects it even afterward.
The reply assigns it to a view of R. Yehuda allowing only after-the-fact fulfillment.
But another teaching permits a speaking but deaf person to separate terumah initially.
That initially permitted act seems to fit neither the just-assigned R. Yehuda nor R. Yose.
R. Yehuda’s own view allows it initially; his reported teacher’s view is stricter.
R. Yehuda quotes R. Elazar ben Azarya as requiring the reader to hear the Shema.
R. Meir answers that the words being “upon your heart” center intention rather than hearing.
Even if R. Yehuda follows his teacher, the opposing baraita can be R. Meir’s view.
A mishnah excludes a deaf person, mentally impaired person, and minor from reading Megillah, though R. Yehuda allows a minor.
Rav Mattena assigns the strict exclusion of a deaf reader to R. Yose’s Shema ruling.
How do we know that attribution establishes invalidity even after the fact? The challenge continues on 15b.

15b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Perhaps the Megillah rule is R. Yehuda’s, with inaudible reading invalid only initially.
The deaf reader is grouped with those whose reading fails even after the fact.
Perhaps each excluded group has a different rule.
The mishnah names R. Yehuda separately at the end, suggesting the opening exclusion is not his.
Alternatively, the entire mishnah could be R. Yehuda’s, distinguishing minors who have reached educational age.
If that attribution makes R. Yehuda permit only after the fact, how can another teaching permit a deaf person to separate terumah initially?
That permission seems to fit neither R. Yehuda’s supposed limited view nor R. Yose’s strict one.
R. Yehuda can allow the act initially.
But another baraita permits silent Grace only after the fact.
That seems to fit neither R. Yehuda’s initial permission nor R. Yose’s total rejection.
R. Yehuda’s own view permits it initially, while his teacher’s view is stricter.
R. Yehuda quotes R. Elazar ben Azarya’s requirement that Shema be audible.
R. Meir instead reads “upon your heart” as making intention decisive.
Even if R. Yehuda agrees with his teacher, the lenient teaching can be R. Meir’s.
Rav Ḥisda transmits two complementary rulings about R. Yehuda and the teacher he quotes.
The teacher’s ruling shows that audible recitation is preferred initially, beyond the basic leniency.
R. Yehuda’s ruling shows that an inaudible reading still has a valid after-the-fact remedy.
Rav Yosef first says the audible-reading dispute applies only to Shema, not other commandments, citing a verse about hearing.
Silent Grace after meals is valid after the fact, opposing that broad claim.
The corrected report says other commandments are valid after the fact even when inaudible.
What then of the verse requiring Israel to hear?
That verse concerns Torah study.
The mishnah’s issue of imprecise pronunciation is recalled.
R. Tavi rules according to the lenient view in both pronunciation disputes.
A proverb pairs the grave and the womb; what is their connection?
Both receive and later bring forth what entered them.
If a womb that receives quietly brings forth with cries, a grave receiving with cries will certainly bring forth again.
This is offered as a scriptural answer to denial of resurrection.
R. Oshaya interprets “write them” as including even the commands in the written Shema passages.
Rava associates that reading with R. Yehuda’s distinction between curses and commands in the sotah text.
The sotah verse limits writing to “these curses,” while the Shema verse says “write them” more broadly.
Is R. Yehuda’s sotah rule really based on “write”? It is based on “these curses.”
The broad wording in Shema blocks an analogy that would exclude commands there too.
Rav Ovadya reads “teach them” as requiring clear articulation between adjoining words.
Rava lists adjacent word pairs whose sounds could run together.
R. Ḥama says distinct Shema pronunciation brings relief from Gehinnom.
He reads a psalm about snow in Zalmon through wordplays on separating sounds and the shadow of death.
A further teaching of R. Ḥama begins and continues on 16a.

16a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Balaam’s verse places tents beside streams.
As streams bring purification, houses of study bring a person from guilt toward merit.
The mishnah’s rule against reciting Shema out of order is recalled.
R. Ammi and R. Assi were preparing R. Elazar’s wedding chamber while he went to hear a teaching.
A teacher says an uncertain error in Shema requires returning to the relevant paragraph or first repeated phrase.
R. Yoḥanan limits the rule: after “that your days may be multiplied,” habitual continuation can be assumed.
R. Elazar reports this back, and the others say the lesson alone justified the visit.
The mishnah permits workers to read Shema atop a tree or scaffold, but not to pray there.
A bridegroom is exempt from Shema through the following Sabbath until the marriage is consummated.
Rabban Gamliel nevertheless read on his wedding night, prompting his students’ objection.
He would not forgo accepting heavenly kingship even for an hour.
A baraita allows workers to read Shema aloft and to pray atop olive or fig trees.
For other trees they descend before prayer.
The employer descends regardless, because focus is lacking aloft.
Rav Mari asks how workers reading aloft fits the requirement of focused intention.
Another teaching explicitly requires Shema to be read with attentive intention.
Raba is silent and is asked whether he has heard a resolution.
Rav Sheshet says workers pause their labor to read.
Beit Hillel say they may continue working while reading.
The pause applies to the first passage; continued labor is allowed during the second.
A baraita requires hired workers to read Shema with blessings, eat with blessings, and pray the full Amidah.
They do not lead communal prayer or give the priestly blessing.
Another teaching prescribes only an abridged Amidah.
Rav Sheshet first assigns the teachings to Rabban Gamliel and R. Yehoshua.
R. Yehoshua’s abridged prayer applies to everyone, so why single out workers?
Both teachings can follow Rabban Gamliel, distinguishing wage workers from those working for meals.
A further baraita has workers pray and say only two blessings after eating.
It explains how the shortened Grace combines Jerusalem’s blessing with the blessing for the land.
That shortening applies to wage workers; workers paid in meals or eating with the employer say full Grace.
The bridegroom’s exemption is recalled.
“When you sit” and “when you walk” exclude commandment activity and the newly married virgin’s groom.
Rav Pappa explains that ordinary walking is a voluntary undertaking.
But the verse might also cover walking to perform a commandment.
The possessive “your walking” limits it to one’s own affairs, exempting travel for a commandment.

16b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If a groom is exempt, why distinguish a virgin bride from a widow?
The first groom is preoccupied; the second is not.
If preoccupation alone exempts, a person whose ship sank should also be exempt.
Rav teaches that a mourner remains obligated in the commandments, apart from phylacteries.
Phylacteries are called an ornament in Ezekiel’s verse.
Worry about a ship is voluntary business; this groom’s preoccupation concerns a mitzvah.
Rabban Gamliel bathed on the first night after his wife died.
His students object that he had taught mourners must not bathe.
He says his exceptional physical sensitivity makes his case different.
Rabban Gamliel accepted condolences when his servant Tavi died.
His students recall his rule against accepting condolences for slaves.
He says Tavi was unusually worthy.
A groom who wishes may recite Shema on the first night.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says not everyone may claim this distinction.
Why did Rabban Gamliel bathe during mourning?
Nighttime mourning is a rabbinic obligation.
The verse describes mourning ending like a bitter day.
The sages did not impose the nighttime restriction on an exceptionally sensitive person.
The discussion turns to Tavi’s death.
A baraita denies slaves the mourning row, mourners’ blessing, and condolences.
When R. Eliezer’s female slave died, his students followed him through several rooms to console him.
He rebukes the students for ignoring his teaching.
He repeats the baraita withholding the usual mourning rites from slaves.
What, then, is said when a slave dies?
One wishes that God will fill the owner’s loss, as when an animal dies.
Another baraita says slaves are not eulogized.
R. Yose permits words of praise for a worthy slave.
The others object that such praise leaves no distinction for upright free people.
A baraita reserves the titles Patriarchs for three and Matriarchs for four.
Could the reason be uncertainty about which son of Jacob is one’s ancestor?
The same uncertainty would apply to descent from Rachel or Leah.
Only the earlier figures have the special standing of Patriarchs and Matriarchs.
A baraita forbids addressing slaves as Father or Mother, yet Rabban Gamliel’s slaves received those titles.
The example of Rabban Gamliel’s slaves appears to contradict the rule.
Those slaves were especially esteemed.
R. Elazar asks how to understand the verse about blessing God in life and raising hands in His name.
He interprets the first clause as Shema and the second as prayer.
A further verse promises satisfaction to the person who does this.
Such a person also inherits both this world and the world to come.
The Psalm’s closing phrase supports the further reward.
R. Elazar’s post-prayer supplication asks for love, peace, students, good company, reverence, and a good future.
R. Yoḥanan’s post-prayer supplication asks God for mercy, protection, kindness, and humility.
R. Zeira prays to avoid sin and shame before the ancestors.
R. Ḥiyya prays that Torah be their occupation and that heart and eyes not fail.
Rav prays for long, peaceful, prosperous lives filled with Torah, reverence, and fulfilled good wishes.
Rabbi prays for rescue from arrogance, harmful people, bad impulses, harsh judgments, and hostile litigants.
He said this even while the authorities’ agents stood near him.
Rav Safra begins a post-prayer supplication for peace that continues on the next daf.

17a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Safra’s prayer continues with a wish for peace and for Torah students to study for its own sake.
R. Alexandri prays for light and for an undimmed heart and eyes.
Another tradition attributes that prayer to Rav Hamnuna and gives R. Alexandri a different prayer.
That prayer begins by affirming the desire to do God’s will.
What prevents people from doing God’s will?
The evil inclination and foreign rule.
The prayer asks deliverance from these barriers and a wholehearted return to God’s will.
Rava’s post-prayer confession expresses human frailty and shame before God.
He asks to avoid further sin and to have past sins cleansed mercifully without severe suffering.
The same words served as Rav Hamnuna Zuti’s Yom Kippur confession.
Mar son of Ravina asks for guarded speech and patience toward those who curse him.
He asks for devotion to Torah and protection from harm, temptation, and hostile plans.
He closes by asking that his words and thoughts find favor before God.
Rav Sheshet recites a supplication after praying on a fast day.
He recalls that in Temple times a sinner’s offering brought atonement through its fat and blood.
He asks that the fat and blood diminished by his fast count as an offering and bring divine favor.
R. Yoḥanan’s closing words after Job observe that humans and animals alike face death.
He praises one who lives with Torah, pleases the Creator, and leaves with a good name.
Ecclesiastes values a good name and the day of death over fine oil and the day of birth.
R. Meir’s habitual saying urges wholehearted Torah study, reverence, purity, and confidence in God’s presence.
The sages of Yavne say both scholar and laborer are God’s creatures, each with his own work.
Could the scholar claim superiority because he studies more?
Both the one who does much and the one who does little are valued if their intent is toward Heaven.
Abaye urges a person to be discerning in reverence for God.
Proverbs says a gentle answer turns away wrath.
Abaye urges peace with relatives and all people, even a stranger in the market.
Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai always greeted others first, even a stranger in the market.
Rava says wisdom aims at repentance and good deeds, without contempt for parents or teachers.
The Psalm links the beginning of wisdom with reverence and doing.
The verse’s wording emphasizes deeds done for their own sake.
Rava strongly condemns performing such deeds for an improper motive.
Rav describes the world to come as free of bodily needs and rivalry, with the righteous enjoying the Divine Presence.
The verse about beholding God and eating and drinking supports his image.
The Gemara says God’s promised reward for women is especially great.
Isaiah addresses women with a promise of ease and confidence.
Rav asks R. Ḥiyya by what merit women attain that reward.
They bring children to study, encourage husbands to learn, and wait for their return.
Sages leaving R. Ami’s or R. Ḥanina’s study hall would offer a blessing.
They bless him with good in this life and the next, wisdom, Torah’s light, and eagerness to learn.
Sages leaving Rav Ḥisda’s or R. Shmuel bar Naḥmani’s school also offered a blessing.
Their blessing invokes the Psalm about leaders bearing a burden.
Two pairs of sages are named in variant reports of a dispute over that verse.
One reading praises leaders learned in Torah and laden with mitzvot.
The other reads leaders learned in Torah and mitzvot as bearing suffering.

17b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The blessing asks that this group have no traitor like Ahitophel in David’s circle.
It asks that none emerge like Doeg from Saul’s circle.
It asks that none emerge like Gehazi from Elisha’s circle.
It asks that no child or student publicly disgrace the group.
A dispute is introduced over Isaiah’s phrase about the stubborn-hearted far from righteousness.
One interpretation says the world lives by charity, while the righteous are sustained by their own claim.
The other says the world lives by the righteous, though they themselves scarcely benefit.
Rav’s teaching says the world is sustained for Ḥanina’s sake while he subsists on a small weekly measure of carobs.
Rav Yehuda disagrees and identifies the stubborn-hearted as the people of Gova’ei.
Rav Yosef notes that none of them had converted.
Rav Ashi similarly describes Mata Meḥasya’s residents, who saw Torah’s glory twice yearly yet did not convert.
The discussion recalls the mishnah about a groom wishing to recite Shema.
Do Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the sages really differ over concern for presumptuousness in this way?
The Ninth of Av rule seems to put their views in the opposite order regarding refraining from work.
Both the sages’ positions and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel’s positions now seem contradictory.
R. Yoḥanan resolves this by reversing the attribution in one source.
Rav Sheisha says the attributions can stand and begins distinguishing the cases.
A groom reading Shema along with everyone else does not appear presumptuous.
Refusing work while everyone works on Ninth of Av does appear presumptuous.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel’s two statements can also be reconciled.
A groom’s inability to concentrate is evident, making his Shema a claim to unusual devotion.
An idle person on Ninth of Av may simply lack work, so idleness need not appear presumptuous.
The chapter on one who was reading ends.
A mourner with an unburied relative is exempt from Shema, prayer, phylacteries, and positive commandments.
Pallbearers and replacements needed before the bier are exempt from Shema.
Those behind the bier must read Shema, but both groups are exempt from prayer.
After burial, one starts Shema only if there is time to finish before reaching the condolence row.
People in the inner condolence row are exempt; those in the outer row are obligated.
The mishnah also lists women, slaves, and minors as exempt from Shema and phylacteries but obligated in other duties.
Does the exemption depend on the deceased literally lying before the mourner?
A baraita describes the mourner moving away, using another house, a partition, or averted face to eat.
The baraita also restricts festive eating and blessings, continuing the apparent challenge to a literal reading.

18a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The baraita continues: a mourner before burial is exempt from blessings, Shema, prayer, phylacteries, and other commandments.
On Shabbat the mourner resumes ordinary meals, blessings, and commandment obligations.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel extends the Shabbat obligation to all duties.
What practical difference remains between his view and the first view?
The difference concerns conjugal relations.
The baraita’s broad exemption seems to conflict with the mishnah’s wording about a corpse lying before him.
Rav Pappa limits that exemption to the case of eating while facing away from the corpse.
Rav Ashi says responsibility for burial makes the dead person count as lying before the mourner.
Abraham speaks of his dead as being before him even when arranging burial elsewhere.
The exemption lasts while the burial remains his responsibility.
Does this exemption apply only to one’s own deceased relative and not to a watcher?
A baraita exempts one who watches the dead even when the deceased is unrelated.
Watching the dead and being responsible for one’s own dead each independently give the exemption.
Would someone merely walking through a cemetery then remain obligated?
A baraita forbids displaying phylacteries or a Torah scroll there, lest one mock the dead.
That rule concerns the four cubits around a grave; beyond them a passerby is obligated.
A mourner or watcher remains exempt even farther away.
The baraita’s rule exempting a watcher of the dead is repeated.
When two people watch, they alternate guarding and reciting Shema.
Ben Azzai permits both to pray away from the dead when traveling by boat.
What difference explains the two views?
Ravina says they disagree whether mice are a concern even on a boat.
One transporting bones may not ride on them packed in a saddlebag, which disrespects the remains.
Danger from outsiders or robbers permits this manner of transport.
The baraita applies the same rule to a Torah scroll.
Does this parallel refer to the obvious ban on disrespect, or something else?
It refers to the permission in a dangerous situation.
One who fails to escort a dead person violates the verse against mocking the poor.
What reward is promised to one who does escort the dead?
Rav Asi cites verses likening kindness to the poor to lending to and honoring God.
R. Ḥiyya and R. Yonatan walk in a cemetery while R. Yonatan’s fringes drag near the graves.
R. Ḥiyya tells him to lift them so the dead will not feel insulted.
R. Yonatan asks whether the dead really know this.
He cites Ecclesiastes: the dead know nothing.
R. Ḥiyya says R. Yonatan has not understood the verse as taught.
He interprets the living as the righteous, who remain called living after death.
The account of Benayahu, called a living man, is cited in support; the discussion continues.

18b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Does calling Benayahu a son of a living man imply that everyone else is descended from the dead?
He is called living because even after death he is regarded as alive.
His mighty deeds are read as gathering people for Torah.
The two lion-hearted men are read as the two Temple eras, in which no equal to him appeared.
The verse’s account of killing a lion on a snowy day is considered.
One interpretation says he broke ice and immersed.
Another says he studied the Sifra on a winter day.
“The dead know nothing” is applied to the wicked, who are called dead even while alive.
Ezekiel calls a living wicked ruler slain.
Another proof is the verse calling the condemned person “the dead.”
He must be called dead in advance because of his wickedness.
R. Ḥiyya’s sons forgot their learning and struggled to recall it.
One asks whether their deceased father knows their distress.
The other cites Job to argue that a dead parent does not know a child’s state.
The first counters with Job’s depiction of the dead feeling pain and mourning.
R. Yitzḥak likens the pain of decay for the dead to a needle piercing living flesh.
The dead may know their own pain without knowing the suffering of others.
A baraita is brought against that distinction.
A pious man gives to a poor person during famine, is rebuked by his wife, and sleeps in a cemetery.
He hears one spirit invite another to learn what calamity is coming.
The other cannot leave her reed-mat burial and asks to be told what is heard.
The traveling spirit reports that hail will harm crops sown in the first rainy period.
The man sows later; other crops are damaged but his are spared.
The following year he again hears the spirits discuss seeking news of coming calamity.
The spirit in the reed mat again asks her companion to bring back the news.
The traveling spirit reports that blight will harm crops sown in the second rainy period.
The man sows early; others’ crops wither while his do not.
His wife asks why his crops escaped disaster in both years.
He tells her the entire account.
After quarreling with the buried woman’s mother, his wife reveals the reed-mat burial.
The man returns to the cemetery the next year and hears the spirits begin talking again.
One spirit refuses, saying their private words have become known among the living.
This suggests that the dead know events among the living.
Perhaps someone else died and told them what had happened.
Ze’iri’s innkeeper dies while holding his deposited money, and he seeks her at the cemetery.
She identifies where the money is and asks her mother to send personal effects with someone arriving tomorrow.
Her knowledge of tomorrow’s arrival seems to prove awareness of the living.
Perhaps Duma announces each new arrival to the dead beforehand.
Shmuel’s father dies while holding orphans’ money, and Shmuel goes to seek him among the dead.
After Shmuel identifies his father more precisely, the dead say he is in the heavenly academy.
Shmuel finds Levi outside and asks why he has not entered.
Levi says he is excluded for having offended R. Afes by failing to attend his academy.
Shmuel’s father arrives, visibly both crying and laughing.
Shmuel asks why his father is crying.
His father says Shmuel will die soon.
Shmuel asks why he is laughing.
His father says Shmuel is greatly esteemed in this world.
Shmuel asks that Levi be admitted to the heavenly academy, and he is.
Shmuel asks where the orphans’ money is.
His father identifies the millhouse hiding place and distinguishes the orphans’ money from his own.
Shmuel asks why the money was arranged that way.
His father put his own money at either exposed end so theft or ground damage would first affect him.
The story again suggests that the dead know future events.
Perhaps Shmuel’s importance caused an exceptional advance announcement.
R. Yonatan later teaches that the dead speak with each other.
He cites God’s words to Moses about the oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
Why does the verse say “saying”?
Moses is told to report to the Patriarchs that God fulfilled the oath to their descendants.

19a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If the dead know nothing, why would Moses’ message to the Patriarchs matter?
If they already know, why would he need to tell them?
The message gives Moses credit for bringing the news.
R. Yitzḥak compares speaking ill of the dead to speaking to stone; either they do not know or they do not care.
Rav Pappa reports that a man who maligned Mar Shmuel after death was struck by a falling reed.
A scholar is different: God defends his honor.
R. Yehoshua ben Levi says disparaging deceased scholars leads to Gehenna.
A Psalm says God leads those on crooked paths away even when Israel has peace.
The school of R. Yishmael says not to suspect a scholar by day over a sin seen at night.
Is repentance only a possibility?
One should assume he has repented.
For a property offense, that assumption waits until restitution.
R. Yehoshua ben Levi says courts impose ostracism in twenty-four cases of dishonoring a teacher found in the Mishnah.
R. Elazar asks where those cases are.
He is told to search for them.
R. Elazar finds three: slighting handwashing, maligning departed scholars, and acting arrogantly toward Heaven.
What is the example involving a deceased scholar?
Akavya excludes converts and freed women from the bitter-water rite; the sages disagree.
They cite a freed maidservant treated by Shemaya and Avtalyon; Akavya disparages their action.
The account says he died under a ban and the court stoned his coffin.
What is the example involving handwashing?
R. Yehuda disputes the report of Akavya’s ban, praising his wisdom and piety.
He identifies Elazar ben Ḥanokh, who slighted handwashing, as the person banned.
A large stone on his coffin demonstrates the rule for someone who dies under a ban.
What is the example of arrogance toward Heaven?
Shimon ben Shataḥ tells Ḥoni that his conduct would ordinarily warrant a ban.
Ḥoni is spared because God grants his pleading as a father indulges a son.
Proverbs is cited in praise of the joy he brings.
Are there no further instances?
A baraita says Theodosius of Rome was threatened with a ban over Passover-like roasted goats.
That case is in a baraita, while the count concerns the Mishnah.
Is there no other example in the Mishnah?
The Mishnah records the dispute over the oven of akhnai.
Why is it called the oven of akhnai?
The sages surrounded it with arguments like a snake and ruled it impure.
A baraita says they burned what R. Eliezer had declared pure and then banned him.
The ban itself is still not taught in the Mishnah.
Then how does R. Yehoshua ben Levi count twenty-four cases?
He infers analogous cases; R. Elazar counts only those stated explicitly.
The discussion returns to pallbearers and their replacements.
A baraita says not to begin a funeral close to Shema time, but not to interrupt one already begun.
Rav Yosef’s funeral did begin near Shema time.
An important person receives different treatment.
The discussion turns to those before and behind the bier.
Eulogizers leave one at a time to recite Shema when the deceased lies before them.
Otherwise they recite Shema and pray while the mourner remains silent and accepts judgment.
A prayer acknowledges sins and asks God to repair the breaches of Israel with mercy.
Abaye says not to recite it, because one should not invite misfortune by one’s words.
Rav Yosef cites Isaiah’s comparison with Sodom and the prophet’s sharp reply.
The mishnah’s rule for returning after burial is recalled.
Must there be time to finish all of Shema, rather than even one chapter or verse?
A baraita allows beginning if even a chapter or verse can be completed.
The mishnah is explained the same way: begin if one can finish even a verse before the condolence row.

19b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita exempts mourners who can see inward from the condolence row; others must read Shema.
R. Yehuda distinguishes those present for the mourner from those present for themselves.
Rav requires a person who finds prohibited mixed fabric in his garment to remove it even publicly.
Proverbs says no wisdom or counsel stands against God.
Where God’s name is profaned, honor for a teacher does not take precedence.
A baraita permits mourners to follow an honored mourner even along an impure path.
Why does the principle about God’s honor not prohibit this?
The path is an uncertain field whose impurity is only rabbinic.
One may blow dust aside and walk through such a field.
A well-trodden field of this kind is treated as pure.
A priest reports crossing over coffins to greet kings, apparently placing royal honor over impurity law.
Why does the principle about God’s honor not forbid this?
Rava distinguishes coffins with a handbreadth of space, which block impurity, from those without it.
Most coffins have that space; the sages set aside their precaution for the honor of kings.
A baraita says human dignity can override a Torah prohibition.
How can that stand against the principle that no counsel opposes God?
Rav bar Shaba identifies the prohibition as “do not deviate” from the sages’ ruling.
Students object that “do not deviate” is itself a Torah prohibition.
Rav Kahana tells them not to dismiss Rav bar Shaba’s explanation.
Rabbinic rules rest on “do not deviate,” but the sages may waive them for human dignity.
A baraita cites “you may disregard” a lost object, apparently allowing honor to override return.
Examples include a priest facing a cemetery or an elder for whom retrieval is undignified.
Why does the principle about God’s honor not require retrieval anyway?
The verse explicitly permits disregarding the object in some cases.
Could that exception be generalized?
A monetary duty does not establish a rule for other prohibitions.
Another baraita asks what the Nazirite verse’s mention of a sister teaches.
Someone on the way to offer a Paschal lamb or circumcise a son does not turn back to become impure for a relative.
Does the same rule bar impurity for a dead person with no one to bury them?
“His sister” begins the distinction: he avoids impurity for her; the exception continues on the next daf.

20a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The duty to bury a person with no one else to do so overrides the usual impurity rule.
Why does the principle that no counsel stands against God not prevent this?
The verse’s mention of a sister creates a specific exception.
Can that exception establish a general rule?
Refraining from an action is a distinct case and cannot establish a broader override.
Rav Pappa asks why earlier generations saw miracles but his generation did not.
The difference cannot simply be breadth of study: Rav Yehuda’s generation studied Nezikin, while theirs studied all six orders.
Rav Yehuda struggled with a teaching in Uktzin and called it a difficult dispute of Rav and Shmuel.
The later generation studied many versions of Uktzin.
Yet rain came when Rav Yehuda removed a shoe, while their fasting and cries went unanswered.
Abaye attributes the difference to earlier generations’ greater dedication to sanctifying God’s name.
Rav Adda tore a woman’s garment, believing she was a Jew wearing something forbidden; she was not Jewish.
He was assessed four hundred zuz for embarrassing her.
He asks her name and makes a wordplay on Matun and the amount owed.
Rav Giddel sat near the immersion area and instructed women how to immerse.
The sages ask whether he fears temptation.
He says he regards them as white geese.
R. Yoḥanan sat near the immersion area hoping women would see him and bear beautiful children.
The sages ask whether he fears the evil eye.
He says Joseph’s descendants are not subject to it.
Genesis describes Joseph as flourishing by a spring, with a word that can also mean eye.
R. Abbahu reads the verse as placing Joseph above the eye.
R. Yosei cites Jacob’s blessing that Joseph’s descendants multiply.
As fish are hidden by water from the evil eye, so are Joseph’s descendants protected.
Alternatively, Joseph’s restraint from looking at what was not his protects him.
The next mishnah opens: women, slaves, and minors are exempt from Shema.

20b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishnah ends: women, slaves, and minors are exempt from phylacteries but obligated in prayer, mezuzah, and Grace after Meals.
Why state their exemption from Shema when it is a time-bound positive commandment?
Its acceptance of Heaven’s kingship might have suggested an exception.
Why state the exemption from phylacteries?
Their link to mezuzah might have suggested an obligation.
Prayer is a plea for mercy, so they are obligated.
Could its fixed times in the Psalm make it a time-bound commandment?
The mishnah teaches that they are still obligated.
Why state the obligation of mezuzah?
Its link to Torah study might have suggested an exemption.
Why state the obligation of Grace after Meals?
A verse about eating morning and evening might have made it seem time-bound.
Rav Adda bar Ahava says women have a Torah obligation in Shabbat kiddush.
Why, when kiddush is a time-bound positive commandment?
Abaye proposes a rabbinic obligation.
Rava objects that Rav Adda called it a Torah obligation, and that this logic would obligate women in every such commandment.
Rava connects remembering Shabbat to observing it; women included in observance are included in kiddush.
Ravina asks whether women’s obligation in Grace after Meals is biblical or rabbinic.
What practical difference follows?
Only an obligation at the same level would let a woman discharge another person’s biblical duty.
What source can resolve Ravina’s question?
A baraita permits a son, slave, or wife to recite Grace after Meals for the relevant family member.
The sages criticize someone who must rely on his wife or children to recite it.
The baraita seems to require women’s obligation to be biblical if they can discharge a biblical duty.
But a minor in the same baraita has no biblical obligation.
The case concerns someone who ate only enough to incur a rabbinic duty; a rabbinic obligation can discharge it.
Rav Avira transmits a teaching under two possible attributions.
The angels ask why God favors Israel when the Torah says God shows no favoritism.
God says Israel blesses even after a small amount of food, beyond the stated duty after satisfaction.
The next mishnah says one impure from a seminal emission contemplates Shema without its blessings.
After eating he recites the later blessing but not the earlier one.
R. Yehuda permits both preceding and following blessings.
Ravina infers that silent contemplation counts as speech.
Otherwise the mishnah’s requirement to contemplate Shema would be pointless.
If contemplation counts as speech, why not speak aloud?
The precedent is the revelation at Sinai.
Rav Ḥisda holds the opposite view: contemplation is not speech.
If it counted as speech, the person should recite Shema aloud.
If it does not count, why does the person contemplate it?
R. Elazar says this prevents someone from sitting idle while everyone else recites.
Why not study some other passage instead?
Rav Adda says one should engage with the matter occupying the community.

21a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Prayer also occupies the community, yet the mishnah lets an impure person continue only if already praying.
Prayer differs because it does not express acceptance of Heaven’s kingship.
Grace after Meals also lacks that element, yet the mishnah requires its later blessing.
Shema and Grace after Meals are Torah duties; prayer is rabbinic.
Where does the Torah require a blessing after eating?
Deuteronomy commands blessing after eating and satisfaction.
Where does the Torah require a blessing before Torah study?
The verse calls for giving God greatness before proclaiming God’s name.
R. Yoḥanan proposes two inferences: a blessing after Torah and one before food.
If food needs a later blessing, Torah, already blessed beforehand, should too.
If Torah needs an earlier blessing, food, already blessed afterward, should too.
Food’s physical enjoyment makes its rule distinctive.
Torah’s promise of eternal life likewise makes its rule distinctive.
The mishnah explicitly requires a later food blessing but not an earlier one.
Rav Yehuda rules that doubtful Shema is not repeated, while doubtful Emet Veyatziv is.
He treats Shema as rabbinic and Emet Veyatziv as a Torah duty.
Rav Yosef cites the verse about lying down and rising as evidence for Shema.
Abaye reads that verse as referring to Torah study generally.
The mishnah makes an impure person contemplate Shema but omit its blessings, while blessing after food.
If Emet Veyatziv is biblical, why omit the blessing after Shema?
Its remembrance of the exodus is already present in Shema.
Why not recite Emet Veyatziv instead of Shema?
Shema supplies both remembrance of the exodus and acceptance of Heaven’s kingship.
R. Elazar requires repeating doubtful Shema but not doubtful prayer.
R. Yoḥanan favors additional prayer and wishes a person could pray all day.
Shmuel says someone who realizes during prayer that he already prayed must stop, even mid-blessing.
But a student who mistakenly begins a weekday blessing on Shabbat is told to finish that blessing.
On Shabbat the person remains obligated in prayer; one who already prayed has fulfilled the duty.
Shmuel allows a second prayer with a congregation only if it includes a new element.
The Gemara begins explaining why both of Shmuel’s rulings are needed; the explanation continues next daf.

21b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Both rules about repeating prayer are needed: joining a congregation and stopping a prayer already begun differ.
Rav Huna permits starting prayer only if it can finish before the leader reaches Modim.
R. Yehoshua ben Levi instead requires finishing before the leader reaches Kedusha.
What underlies their disagreement?
They disagree whether an individual may recite Kedusha alone.
Rav Adda reads “I shall be sanctified among Israel” as requiring ten for a sacred response.
How does the verse imply ten?
A verbal analogy links “among” here to the congregation elsewhere, understood as ten.
All agree that one does not interrupt prayer for Kedusha.
May one interrupt for “May His great name be blessed”?
A reported view allows that response even during lofty study.
The Gemara rejects that reported view as the ruling.
R. Yehuda’s permission to say blessings before and after is recalled.
Does that mean he permits someone with a seminal emission to study Torah?
R. Yehoshua ben Levi derives a restriction from Torah study placed beside Sinai’s requirements.
R. Yehuda cannot simply reject juxtaposed verses, since he uses them in Deuteronomy.
How do we know he does not use juxtaposition throughout the Torah?
Ben Azzai derives a sorceress’s stoning from its position beside bestiality.
R. Yehuda rejects that placement as proof and derives stoning by analogy to mediums.
How do we know he does use juxtaposition in Deuteronomy?
R. Eliezer permits marriage to a woman raped or seduced by one’s father or son.
R. Yehuda forbids the father’s former partner in those cases.
Rav explains his reading of the verse forbidding uncovering a father’s skirt.
The adjacent passage about rape shows which case he reads into that verse.
Why then not derive the Torah-study restriction from the adjacent Sinai verses?
R. Yehuda uses that juxtaposition for another teaching about teaching a son Torah.
The verse about teaching children sits beside the verse about standing at Horeb.
A mishnah requires immersion after seminal impurity in several cases; R. Yehuda exempts them.
Perhaps his exemption applies only when another impurity already prevents full purification.
Perhaps he also exempts a person with seminal impurity alone, and the case merely highlights the sages’ stricter view.
The mishnah’s last case nevertheless requires immersion after intercourse followed by bleeding.
That requirement would be obvious if attributed to the sages, who require immersion even in the harder case.
It appears instead to be R. Yehuda’s deliberately stated distinction; the discussion continues.

22a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The previous argument concludes that one with seminal impurity alone still requires immersion.
Perhaps R. Yehuda meant silent contemplation rather than spoken blessings.
But does R. Yehuda accept silent contemplation as a solution?
A baraita has R. Meir permit Shema and later food blessing while leaving other blessings to thought.
R. Yehuda in that baraita permits uttering the blessings aloud.
Rav Naḥman likens his treatment of blessings to the rules of proper conduct.
The verses about Sinai are read to require awe and reverence during Torah study.
A baraita permits many forms of impurity to study but restricts one who had a seminal emission.
R. Yose permits familiar teachings without a new exposition.
R. Yonatan permits expounding Mishnah but not Gemara.
R. Natan permits Gemara as well, provided divine names are not pronounced.
R. Yoḥanan the Cobbler bars interpretive study, with a variant barring study-hall entry.
R. Yehuda permits study of the rules of proper conduct.
R. Yehuda immersed before teaching those rules to students beside a river.
His students ask why he immersed when he had permitted that study.
He is lenient for others but stringent for himself.
R. Yehuda ben Beteira says Torah words do not become impure.
He urges a hesitant student to speak Torah clearly despite impurity.
Jeremiah likens God’s word to fire, which does not receive impurity.
The allowance to explain Mishnah but not Gemara supports a reported ruling from R. El’ai.
Another baraita records views allowing Mishnah only, forbidding both forms, or permitting both.
The stricter and more permissive versions align with R. Yoḥanan the Cobbler and R. Yehuda ben Beteira.
Rav Naḥman lists three accepted rulings, including R. Yehuda ben Beteira’s view of Torah study.
R. El’ai limits the first shearing duty to the Land of Israel.
R. Yoshiya requires wheat, barley, and a grape seed sown together for that vineyard prohibition.
R. Yehuda ben Beteira says Torah words do not receive impurity.
Ze’iri reports that immersion, or in another version handwashing, was set aside.
The immersion version follows R. Yehuda ben Beteira.
The handwashing version fits Rav Ḥisda’s criticism of seeking water during prayer time.
A baraita allows nine kav of water poured over someone with seminal impurity.
The teaching passes in whispers to ben Azzai, who in one version teaches it publicly.
Two sages preserve different versions: ben Azzai taught it aloud or whispered it.
Public teaching prevents loss of Torah study and marital procreation.
Whispering avoids encouraging excessive marital activity among scholars.
R. Yannai reports both lenient and strict practice and praises personal stringency.
Why would R. Yehoshua ben Levi question morning immersion if he himself restricts Torah study after emission?
He questions needing forty seah of immersion when nine kav poured may suffice.
R. Ḥanina says the immersion rule created a strong safeguard.
A woman’s reminder that forty seah would be needed deters a man seeking misconduct.
Rav Huna asks why the sages neglect immersion if heated baths are available.
Rav Ḥisda questions whether immersion in heated water is valid.
Rav Huna points to R. Adda as supporting Rav Ḥisda’s concern.
R. Zeira, already in a bath, asks for nine kav to be poured over him.
R. Ḥiyya asks why that is needed while he is already in the water.
R. Zeira distinguishes immersion in forty seah from pouring nine kav.
Rav Naḥman prepares a nine-kav vessel.
A later report limits nine kav to a sick person with an involuntary emission.
Rav Yosef says this makes Rav Naḥman’s vessel useless.
Ravin begins a further report of an incident in Usha, continued on 22b.

22b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: At Rav Oshaya’s place, Rav Asi says an involuntary emission during illness requires no purification.
Rav Yosef says this restores a use for Rav Naḥman’s nine-kav vessel.
What exactly did Ezra’s original immersion decree require?
Abaye assigns forty seah to healthy voluntary cases and nine kav to healthy involuntary cases.
The later sages disagree how those categories apply to a sick person.
Rava objects that Ezra instituted immersion, not the later option of pouring nine kav.
Rava assigns Ezra’s decree to healthy voluntary cases and nine kav to a later rabbinic enactment.
The sages still dispute which purification, if any, applies in cases of illness.
Rava rules: voluntary cases need forty seah; a healthy involuntary case needs nine kav; a sick involuntary case needs none.
A baraita permits nine kav for oneself but requires forty seah when teaching others.
R. Yehuda requires forty seah in every case.
Sages disagree whether a sick involuntary case needs nine kav or forty seah when teaching others.
They also disagree whether R. Yehuda’s forty seah may be held in vessels.
If vessels are excluded, what does R. Yehuda’s “in every case” add?
It includes drawn water gathered in the ground.
Rav Pappa, Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua, and Rava bar Shmuel eat together.
Rav Pappa asks to lead Grace after Meals because nine kav were poured over him.
Rava bar Shmuel invokes the forty-seah rule for acting on others’ behalf and claims the lead.
Rav Huna claims the lead because he had no need for either purification.
Rav Ḥama immersed before Passover to discharge others’ obligations.
The Gemara rejects his practice as the ruling.
A new mishnah says to shorten prayer, not stop it, on recalling seminal impurity.
Someone about to immerse reads Shema before sunrise if able, even while covered in water.
Foul or flax-soaking water cannot serve as covering without added water; one keeps four cubits from urine or feces.
A baraita repeats the rule to shorten rather than interrupt prayer.
A Torah reader who recalls seminal impurity continues with less careful diction.
R. Meir permits no more than three verses in that state.
A baraita directs a worshipper who sees feces ahead to move until it is four cubits behind.
Another baraita permits moving aside.
Moving aside applies when moving forward is impossible.
Rabba says prayer where feces is later found was improper but still valid.
Rava cites Proverbs against counting a wrongly performed act of worship.
Rava rules that the prayer is invalid.
A baraita says to pause prayer until a flow of urine stops, then resume.
Where should the person resume?
Rav Ḥisda and Rav Hamnuna differ: restart or continue from the stopping point.
The Gemara begins asking what principle explains their dispute.

23a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Do the two views on resuming interrupted prayer differ over whether a long delay requires restarting?
Rav Ashi says that reading does not explain why the delay itself was never specified.
Both require restarting after enough time to finish the prayer; they dispute a shorter pause.
One treats the person as unfit to pray, while the other considers the prayer valid.
A baraita says someone who needs to relieve himself must not pray; prayer in that state is improper.
The rule applies when he cannot restrain himself; otherwise his prayer counts.
How long must he be able to wait?
Rav Sheshet says a parasang’s travel time.
A variant attaches the same distinction to the baraita and gives the time measure in Rav Zevid’s name.
R. Yonatan says a person needing relief should not pray.
Amos calls on Israel to prepare to meet God.
R. Yonatan interprets Ecclesiastes as urging guarded conduct and an offering after sin.
Rava praises sages who repent when they bring an offering.
His initial reading contrasts fools who offer sacrifice without repentance.
If fools do not know how to do evil, would they not be righteous?
They bring offerings without recognizing whether their conduct was good or bad.
Another reading connects guarding one’s steps with bodily readiness for prayer.
A baraita requires removing phylacteries four cubits before entering a bathroom.
Rav Sheshet limits the advance removal to a regular bathroom, not a makeshift one.
After use, the makeshift site is treated as a bathroom, so he waits four cubits before putting them on.
May one wear phylacteries into a regular bathroom merely to urinate?
Ravina permits it; Rav Adda bar Mattana forbids it.
Rava forbids it, fearing defecation or, in another version, passing wind while wearing them.
Beit Shammai require leaving phylacteries in a window and redonning them four cubits away.
Beit Hillel allow holding them in one’s hand while entering.
R. Akiva says to hold them with one’s garment.
A garment alone may let them slip and fall.
He means holding them in both garment and hand.
Nearby recesses are preferable to public-side recesses where theft could create suspicion.
A student left phylacteries near the street; a woman took them and falsely claimed he paid her with them.
On hearing the accusation, the student went up to a roof and died in a fall.
The sages then required holding phylacteries in garment and hand.
Another baraita traces the change from recesses threatened by mice, then passersby, to holding them.
R. Meyasha rules to roll the phylacteries and hold them opposite the heart.
Rav Naḥman limits how far a strap may hang below the hand.
If there is no daylight left to wear them again, a handbreadth pouch may be used.
R. Yoḥanan likewise distinguishes carrying them by day from placing them in a pouch at night.
Abaye requires a handbreadth only for their usual container; another container can be smaller.
Small sealed vessels can protect contents from corpse impurity.
R. Yoḥanan handed over an aggadic book before entering but kept his phylacteries, invoking the sages’ permission; the explanation continues.

23b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: R. Yoḥanan’s statement continues, and Rava reports that Rav Naḥman likewise kept his phylacteries for protection.
A baraita forbids praying, urinating, or sleeping while holding phylacteries or a Torah scroll.
Shmuel applies the distraction concern to a knife, money, a bowl, or bread.
Rav Sheshet rejects the baraita as Beit Shammai’s view, since Beit Hillel allow holding phylacteries in a regular bathroom.
A baraita’s contrast between permitted and forbidden cases seems to concern holding phylacteries in different bathrooms.
Perhaps it instead contrasts rules about uncovering one or two handbreadths.
The proposed distinction is between relieving oneself and urinating.
That cannot explain why urination would require uncovering behind.
Both cases involve defecation; the difference is between a man and a woman.
That reading does not explain the baraita’s claim of an unanswerable inference.
The baraita therefore concerns phylacteries and refutes Rav Sheshet’s attribution.
Why allow holding them in a regular bathroom but not a makeshift one?
Seated use avoids urine droplets, while standing use may soil the hands.
Then the distinction seems an adequate answer to the supposedly unanswerable inference.
The rule must be understood by its specific reason, not by that abstract inference.
Before a full meal, one should walk to prompt bodily relief and attend to it.
R. Yitzḥak says to remove phylacteries before a full meal.
R. Ḥiyya instead permits placing them on the table and calls that fitting.
Until when should they remain off?
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak says until Grace after Meals.
Two baraitot disagree whether phylacteries may be wrapped with money.
The difference is whether the cloth was designated for phylacteries.
Rav Ḥisda requires both designation and actual use before the cloth is barred to coins.
For Abaye, designation alone is enough to bar use for money.
Rav Yosef asks whether phylacteries may be put under the head, since underfoot is disrespectful.
Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel permitting it even when one’s wife is present.
A baraita permits them under the head but forbids it with a wife present unless placed separately.
The baraita is acknowledged as a refutation of Shmuel.
Rava nevertheless rules in accordance with Shmuel.
The Gemara asks for Rava’s reason; the answer follows on 24a.

24a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Keeping phylacteries nearby for their protection is preferable.
Where under the head should they be placed?
R. Yirmeya says between pillow and mattress, away from the head’s direct position.
R. Ḥiyya’s teaching seems to place them in a pouch directly beneath the head.
The pouch’s bulge protrudes beyond the head.
Bar Kappara and Rav Sheisha each arrange the phylacteries so they are covered but set aside.
Rav Hamnuna finds Rava’s phylacteries beside his head on a night of marital relations, taught as practical law.
May two people sharing a bed turn away from each other and recite Shema?
Shmuel permits it even with one’s wife.
Rav Yosef says a wife is more like one’s own body than another person is.
One baraita permits two bedmates to turn away and recite.
Another requires a separating garment beside family members unless they are minors.
Rav Yosef can distinguish a wife from another person, but Shmuel still faces a difficulty.
Shmuel cites another baraita whose language challenges Rav Yosef’s distinction too.
Both sides must treat the rules about a wife as a tannaitic dispute.
Would exposed buttocks prevent the bedmates from reading Shema?
The allowance supports Rav Huna’s view that buttocks are not treated as nakedness here.
A rule allowing a seated unclothed woman to separate challah is proposed as support.
Rav Naḥman reads the case as one where her body is fully covered by the ground.
The earlier baraita permits reading beside minor family members.
Until what age are they considered minors for this rule?
Rav Ḥisda gives an age of three years and one day for a girl and nine for a boy.
A variant gives eleven years and one day for a girl and twelve for a boy.
The determining sign is physical maturity, supported by Ezekiel’s verse.
Does Rava’s ruling for Shmuel in the phylactery case also decide this bed-sharing case?
Rav Ashi says the cases cannot be assumed to share one ruling.
Rav Mari asks about hair protruding from a garment.
Rav Pappa dismisses that as excessive hairsplitting.
R. Yitzḥak says an exposed handbreadth of a woman counts as nakedness.
For looking with improper intent, even a little finger is already prohibited, so why specify a handbreadth?
The measure concerns reciting Shema in the presence of one’s wife.
Rav Ḥisda applies the rule to an exposed leg and cites two verses of Isaiah.
Shmuel cites the Song of Songs concerning a woman’s voice.
Rav Sheshet cites the Song of Songs concerning a woman’s hair.
R. Ḥanina reports seeing Rabbi hang his phylacteries.
A baraita and a verse condemn hanging phylacteries.
Hanging them by their straps differs from hanging them by the boxes.
Alternatively, both forms are barred; Rabbi hung them inside their pouch.
Why report that incident if it was in a pouch?
It teaches that a pouch need not be set down as a Torah scroll is.
R. Ḥanina begins another account of Rabbi’s conduct during prayer.

24b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The report of Rabbi’s prayer continues: he adjusts clothing but covers his mouth when yawning.
A baraita condemns audible prayer, deliberate yawning, sneezing, and spitting during prayer.
Involuntary belching or yawning differs from deliberate behavior.
How can the conflicting statements about sneezing be reconciled?
Sneezing from above differs from passing wind below.
Rav Zeira praises a sneeze during prayer as a sign of comfort granted above.
What about the conflicting statements on spitting?
Rav Yehuda permits absorbing saliva in a garment or head covering while praying.
Rav Ashi spits behind him during prayer while Ravina stands nearby.
Ravina asks why he did not use the head covering as Rav Yehuda taught.
Rav Ashi says that would disturb his concentration.
The rule against audible prayer is recalled.
Rav Huna allows a louder voice when silent prayer prevents concentration.
The permission applies alone, since a congregation would be disturbed.
R. Abba avoids Rav Yehuda because he intends to leave Babylonia for Israel against his teacher’s view.
He decides to hear one teaching before departing.
He hears a rule to pause prayer after passing wind until the odor goes away.
A variant says to step away, wait, offer a short supplication, and resume where one stopped.
R. Abba says that teaching alone justified his visit.
A baraita permits reading Shema under a garment in cold weather after making a barrier at the neck, or in another view at the heart.
Does the first view allow the heart to face one’s nakedness?
Yes; it requires a barrier at the mouth rather than the heart.
Rav Huna permits reading Shema in a filthy alley with a hand over the mouth.
Rav Ḥisda rejects that allowance emphatically.
A variant attributes the permissive ruling to R. Yehoshua ben Levi.
Rav Ḥisda likewise rejects that version.
Rav Huna elsewhere forbids a scholar even to stand in filth because Torah thoughts are unavoidable.
The earlier prohibition concerns standing still; the allowance concerns walking.
R. Yoḥanan elsewhere bars Torah thought in bathhouse and bathroom, casting doubt on the permissive report.
Perhaps the difference again is between standing and walking.
But R. Abbahu stopped Shema while walking through filth, and R. Yoḥanan advised him where to resume.
R. Yoḥanan merely answered according to R. Abbahu’s view, without adopting it himself.
A baraita supports Rav Huna: cover the mouth and continue Shema while walking.
Another supports Rav Ḥisda: stop Shema on entering a filthy alley.
If one refuses to stop, what judgment follows?
A verse in Ezekiel is cited against that conduct.
Further verses condemn bringing sin upon oneself and dishonoring God’s word.
What reward follows for one who stops?
A verse in Deuteronomy promises long life.
Rav Huna allows Shema when a garment covers the waist.
A baraita extends the rule to cloth, leather, or sack garments.

25a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: For prayer, unlike Shema, one must cover the heart.
Rav Huna says one who entered a bathroom wearing phylacteries should cover them by hand until finishing.
Can he really wait until he finishes entirely?
Only until the first discharge is complete.
Why not stop and step out at once?
A baraita warns that restraining a bowel movement or urine flow can cause harm.
Rav Huna permits Shema with feces on the skin or a hand in a bathroom; Rav Ḥisda forbids it.
Rav Huna invokes the Psalm in which every breathing being praises God.
Rav Ḥisda invokes the Psalm in which all one’s bones speak praise.
For odor with a source, Rav Huna measures four cubits from the source.
Rav Ḥisda measures four cubits beyond where the odor ends.
