A baraita supporting Rav Ḥisda lists human and animal waste and a foul refuse heap as obstacles to Shema.
A ten-handbreadth height difference separates the domains; otherwise the filth must be out of sight.
The baraita places a reader four cubits beyond a source-based odor.
Rava declines to follow that baraita in these rulings.
He cites a narrower rule for human and pig waste, and dog waste used with tanning hides.
What if a foul smell has no visible source?
Rav Sheshet points to students studying while others sleep on nearby mats.
This permits Torah study only for another person’s odor, not Shema or one’s own odor.
Abaye permits Shema opposite passing feces, while Rava forbids it.
Abaye cites a leprosy-impurity rule distinguishing a stationary source from one merely passing.
Rava distinguishes fixed leprosy impurity from the requirement that a camp be holy.
Rav Pappa treats a pig’s mouth like passing feces.
Why state the obvious?
The rule holds even just after the pig leaves a river.
Rav Yehuda forbids uncertain feces but permits uncertain urine.
A variant permits doubtful feces at home but forbids it at a refuse heap; doubtful urine remains permitted.
Rav Hamnuna says the Torah’s urine restriction applies only to the flowing stream.
R. Yonatan sets the verse about leaving camp beside the verse requiring waste to be covered.
The covering duty concerns feces; the other verse concerns urine.
After urine reaches the ground its restriction is rabbinic, and the sages did not extend it to doubtful cases.
How long does known urine remain an obstacle?
Several sages say as long as it remains wet enough to moisten.
Geniva reports a stricter measure: as long as its mark is visible.
Rav Yosef questions that view by comparing Rav’s leniency once feces forms a dry crust.
Abaye counters with another report from Rav forbidding even earthenware-dry feces.
Two descriptions define when feces remains firm rather than crumbling.
Ravina recalls two versions of a teacher’s instruction to inspect the dryness of feces.
What ruling follows from the conflicting reports?
Ameimar forbids and Mar Zutra permits recitation opposite earthenware-dry feces.
Rava forbids that feces and forbids urine while it can moisten.
A baraita on absorbed or dried urine might imply that a visible mark still forbids even without moisture.
The baraita also supports the opposite inference, so neither can be drawn.
Another baraita contrasts absorbed urine with R. Yosei’s moisture-based rule.
If “absorbed” merely means no moisture, how does R. Yosei differ from the first view?
One reading treats “absorbed” as no visible mark, leaving a genuine dispute over a dry mark.
The Gemara responds that both views may instead use moisture as the criterion.

25b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The earlier two views differ over moisture sufficient to dampen something else.
The mishnah’s time for Shema after immersion is recalled.
Does its sunrise deadline assume R. Eliezer’s view?
It can also follow R. Yehoshua if it addresses the early practice of the vatikin.
How can someone covered only by water read Shema if the heart sees nakedness?
The ruling concerns murky water, which blocks that view like earth.
A baraita permits reading up to the neck in clear water; another view requires clouding it.
The first view allows the heart to face nakedness.
It also allows the heel to face nakedness.
Abaye and Rava dispute whether a heel touching nakedness prevents Shema.
A variant agrees touching is barred but disputes merely seeing.
The conclusion forbids touching but permits merely seeing.
Rava permits Shema facing feces behind transparent glass but forbids it facing nakedness there.
Feces is governed by covering, which glass supplies.
Nakedness is governed by visibility and remains visible through glass.
Abaye permits covering a tiny amount of feces with spittle.
Rava requires thick spittle.
Rava allows covering feces in a hole with a sandal before reading.
Feces stuck to the sandal remains an unresolved case.
Rav Yehuda forbids Shema facing a naked non-Jew.
Why specify a non-Jew when a Jew’s nakedness is also barred?
The rule makes clear that a non-Jew’s nakedness also counts, despite a possible reading of Ezekiel.
The mishnah’s rule about foul or flax-soaking water is recalled.
How could a small addition of water remedy a large quantity of foul water?
Those waters cannot serve at all; adding clean water applies to urine.
A baraita disputes whether any added water or a quarter-log is needed.
Rav Naḥman limits the dispute to water added after urine is present.
Rav Yosef places the dispute before the urine and requires a quarter-log afterward.
Rav Yosef asks for a quarter-log of water, following R. Zakkai.
A Tosefta bars Shema facing even empty waste vessels and repeats the dispute over water added to urine.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel distinguishes a vessel behind a bed from one in front.
R. Shimon ben Elazar requires removing or placing the vessel beneath the bed even in a large room.
Does the former view allow immediate reading behind the bed, or still require distance?
A second baraita gives the views in different names and describes the behind-bed case.
The baraitot now contradict one another on the names attached to the views.
One proposal reverses the later baraita.
Why reverse it rather than the earlier one?
R. Shimon ben Elazar elsewhere treats an entire house as four cubits.
Rav Yosef asks whether a bed raised three to nine handbreadths separates the space beneath it.
Abaye confirms that ten handbreadths certainly creates a separate domain.
Rava summarizes: below three is joined, ten separates, and the middle range was unresolved.
Rav and another report follow R. Shimon ben Elazar, while Rava rejects his rule.
Rav Aḥai finds a Torah scroll near his son’s marriage bed and says its presence endangered him.
A baraita forbids marital relations near a Torah scroll or phylacteries unless removed or doubly covered.
Abaye says ordinary storage vessels count as one covering even if many are nested.
Rava begins a further qualification that continues on 26a.

26a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A chest atop the scroll is treated as one vessel inside another.
R. Yehoshua ben Levi requires a ten-handbreadth partition around a Torah scroll during marital relations.
Mar Zutra observes such a partition around a Torah scroll in Mar bar Rav Ashi’s room.
He asks why a partition is used when another room is available for the scroll.
Mar bar Rav Ashi says he had not thought of moving it.
The mishnah requires four cubits of distance from urine and feces.
Rav Huna limits four cubits to filth behind the person; in front, it must be out of sight, even for prayer.
A report that prayer is allowed opposite a privy appears to contradict that rule.
The first response treats the privy as empty.
A baraita treats an empty privy and empty bathhouse as restricted too.
The privy may be newly built and unused.
Ravina’s unresolved question about merely designating a privy challenges that distinction.
Ravina asked about prayer inside it; praying opposite it was permitted.
Rava treats Persian privies as sealed because waste passes away from the visible place.
The mishnah requires immersion for three cases of secondary seminal impurity; R. Yehuda exempts them.
Does R. Yehuda also exempt a seminally impure person who subsequently becomes a zav, despite being initially eligible for immersion?
The mishnah’s woman who has intercourse before menstruation supplies the same sequence, yet R. Yehuda exempts her.
R. Ḥiyya explicitly teaches that R. Yehuda exempts the corresponding male case.
The chapter closes with a return formula.
The mishnah gives noon or four hours as the respective deadlines for the morning prayer.
It gives evening or mid-afternoon as the respective deadlines for the afternoon prayer.
The evening prayer has no fixed time; the additional prayer lasts all day or until seven hours.
A baraita about prayer at sunrise seems at odds with the later morning deadline.
The sunrise practice is the special practice of the vatikin.
A rule allowing a missed morning prayer to be made up in the afternoon challenges noon as an absolute limit.
Later prayer remains possible, but only prayer by noon earns the reward of its appointed time.
May someone who missed the afternoon prayer recite two evening prayers?
Perhaps evening and morning can be paired only because Scripture calls them one day.
If prayer substitutes for sacrifice, crossing into the next day may invalidate compensation.
Alternatively, prayer is supplication and could be made up whenever needed.
A tradition permits two evening prayers after missing afternoon prayer, rejecting the expired-sacrifice objection.
A baraita uses Ecclesiastes to describe missed Shema or prayer as an irreparable omission.
That baraita concerns deliberately missing prayer.
Rav Ashi supports the distinction from its wording: “omitted,” rather than “erred.”

26b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita gives the makeup prayers for missed Friday or Shabbat Minḥa and locates havdala in the first post-Shabbat prayer.
Does missing havdala in that first prayer really make the prayer invalid?
A teaching requires repetition for omitted rain formulas but not for omitted havdala, which can be said over wine.
The contradiction remains difficult.
R. Yosei attributes the daily prayers to the Patriarchs; R. Yehoshua ben Levi links them to the daily offerings.
Baraitot are introduced in support of both explanations.
Abraham’s early standing and a verse equating standing with prayer support his institution of morning prayer.
Isaac’s late-day conversation and a verse connecting conversation with prayer support afternoon prayer.
Jacob’s evening encounter and Jeremiah’s use of encounter for prayer support evening prayer.
The offering schedule explains the competing noon and four-hour deadlines for morning prayer.
The afternoon offering explains the competing evening and half-afternoon deadlines for Minḥa.
Burning offering parts overnight explains why the evening prayer has no fixed hour.
The additional offering explains the all-day and seven-hour deadlines for Musaf.
The baraita defines the earlier Minḥa as beginning six and a half hours into the day.
It defines the later Minḥa as beginning nine and a half hours into the day.
Which Minḥa does R. Yehuda mean when setting his midpoint deadline?
A baraita identifies the later midpoint, eleven hours minus a quarter.
The offering-based times appear to refute the Patriarchs explanation.
R. Yosei can say the Patriarchs instituted prayer while the Sages set its times by offerings.
Musaf, with no Patriarchal origin, shows that offerings also shape the system.
The Gemara repeats the combined account of Patriarchal institution and offering-based times.
The mishnah’s four-hour deadline is recalled.
Does R. Yehuda’s “until four hours” include the fourth hour?
The midpoint deadline for Minḥa is offered as evidence that “until” excludes the endpoint.
The alternative inclusion reading begins an objection that continues on the next daf.

27a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Including the endpoint seems to erase the difference from the Rabbis.
Excluding the endpoint creates a difficulty from the mishnah’s Musaf deadline.
A baraita orders overlapping Minḥa and Musaf differently according to frequency or the approaching deadline.
Without an inclusive seventh hour, how could the two prayer times overlap at all?
But including the endpoint renews the earlier problem about R. Yehuda and the Rabbis.
“Half of Minḥa” means the first half ending at eleven hours minus a quarter, preserving a distinct deadline.
R. Yehuda ben Bava’s five testimonies include a morning offering brought in the fourth hour.
That testimony confirms that “until four hours” includes the fourth hour.
Rav Kahana follows R. Yehuda because Eduyyot supports his ruling.
The discussion asks which tanna fits a teaching that the manna melted when the sun heated at four hours.
A verse about the heat of the day at six hours places the manna’s earlier melting at four.
Neither view of the morning prayer’s endpoint initially seems to fit this definition of morning.
The teaching can be reconciled with either R. Yehuda or the Rabbis.
For the Rabbis, the repeated “morning” divides the longer morning into two parts.
For R. Yehuda, the extra “morning” advances the collection deadline by one hour.
How is the four-hour time derived from “the sun grew hot”?
At four hours the sun is hot while shade is still cool, explaining the verse.
The mishnah’s afternoon prayer deadline is recalled.
Rav Ḥisda asks whether R. Yehuda’s Minḥa deadline is law; Rav Yitzḥak offers no ruling.
Rav’s early Shabbat evening prayer seems to support R. Yehuda’s earlier Minḥa cutoff.
Rav Huna and the Sages waited until evening, supporting the contrary practice.
With no decisive ruling, either consistent practice is valid.
Rav prays the Shabbat service before nightfall and avoids crossing in front of R. Yirmeya, who prays behind him.
The incident shows that Shabbat evening prayer can be said before sunset.
It also shows a student can pray behind a teacher.
Rav’s conduct supports the prohibition on crossing in front of someone praying.
R. Ami and R. Asi apparently crossed in front of people praying.
They passed beyond four cubits, outside the prohibited area.
A separate rule appears to prohibit R. Yirmeya’s prayer position behind Rav; discussion continues on 27b.

27b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rules against praying behind one’s teacher, with a baraita’s severe warning, challenge R. Yirmeya’s conduct.
R. Yirmeya was Rav’s colleague as well as student, shown by his informal question about accepting Shabbat.
Rabbi’s early Shabbat prayer followed by a bathhouse visit challenges the claim that labor had ceased.
Rava says he entered merely to perspire, before the later decree.
Abaye nevertheless allowed basket work after an early Shabbat prayer.
That early prayer had been recited in error.
A congregation’s mistaken early post-Shabbat prayer was nevertheless left in force.
Rabbi ruled that their prayer, once recited, counted.
A congregation is spared the burden of repeating prayer.
Rav prayed Shabbat evening early, while R. Yoshiya prayed the post-Shabbat service early.
May kiddush over wine also be recited before Shabbat begins after an early prayer?
Shmuel permits early Shabbat prayer and kiddush over wine; the ruling follows him.
May havdala over wine likewise follow an early post-Shabbat prayer?
Shmuel permits early post-Shabbat prayer and havdala over wine.
A transmitted report places R. Yishmael’s early Shabbat prayer beside a pillar.
Ulla gives a different place, person, and occasion: a palm tree and an early post-Shabbat prayer by R. Elazar.
The mishnah says evening prayer has no fixed time.
If this only meant any hour of the night, why was it worded “no fixed time”?
The wording fits the view that evening prayer is optional.
Rabban Gamliel calls evening prayer obligatory; R. Yehoshua calls it optional.
Abaye rules for obligation, while Rava rules for optional status.
A student asks R. Yehoshua, who answers that evening prayer is optional.
Rabban Gamliel answers “obligatory” and tells the student to raise the disagreement in the study hall.
Before the Sages, Rabban Gamliel repeats his position and R. Yehoshua initially denies dissenting.
Rabban Gamliel confronts R. Yehoshua with the student’s report and orders him to stand.
R. Yehoshua admits his earlier ruling because the living student can testify to it.
R. Yehoshua remains standing through the lecture until the crowd stops the interpreter.
The crowd recalls repeated humiliations and resolves to remove Rabban Gamliel.
They consider R. Yehoshua, but his involvement in the incident disqualifies him.
They consider R. Akiva, but fear he lacks ancestral merit against possible harm.
They choose R. Elazar ben Azarya for wisdom, wealth, and Ezra lineage.
His wisdom would let him answer scholarly challenges.
His wealth would support dealings with the imperial court.
His ancestry would protect him from punishment.
Asked to lead the academy, R. Elazar consults his household; his wife’s reply continues on 28a.

28a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: R. Elazar answers his wife’s concern about removal: even brief tenure is worth taking.
When she notes his youth, a miracle gives him white hair, explaining “as if seventy.”
The door guard is removed, admitting students whom Rabban Gamliel had screened.
Accounts disagree whether four hundred or seven hundred benches were added.
Rabban Gamliel fears he held back Torah study; a dream shows white vessels full of ashes.
The dream only served to ease his distress; it did not show the new students were unworthy.
Eduyyot was taught that day, pending rulings were explained, and Rabban Gamliel kept attending.
An Ammonite convert asks whether he may enter the congregation.
Rabban Gamliel prohibits him, while R. Yehoshua permits him.
Rabban Gamliel invokes the Torah’s ban on Ammonites and Moabites.
R. Yehoshua argues that Sennacherib displaced the nations, so an individual follows the permitted majority.
Rabban Gamliel cites the prophecy that Ammon’s exiles will return.
R. Yehoshua answers that a promised return of Israel has also not yet occurred.
The convert is immediately permitted.
Rabban Gamliel goes to appease R. Yehoshua and notices his blackened walls.
R. Yehoshua rebukes him for not knowing the hardships of scholars.
Rabban Gamliel apologizes; R. Yehoshua accepts for his father’s honor.
The Sages ask who will tell the study hall; a launderer volunteers.
R. Yehoshua sends a message supporting restoration of the original officeholder.
R. Akiva orders the gates shut to keep Rabban Gamliel’s servants from troubling the Sages.
R. Yehoshua comes himself and restates the hereditary-office argument with the image of a sprinkler.
R. Akiva confirms his forgiveness and proposes visiting Rabban Gamliel.
Removing R. Elazar would violate the principle that sacred status is raised, not lowered.
Alternating weekly leadership equally would stir rivalry.
They assign Rabban Gamliel three weeks and R. Elazar one, then identify the original student as R. Shimon ben Yoḥai.
R. Yoḥanan calls postponing Musaf until late in the day negligent.
A baraita prioritizes the frequent Minḥa prayer over Musaf when both are due.
R. Yehuda instead prioritizes Musaf because its appointed time will expire sooner.
R. Yoḥanan rules to pray Minḥa first.
R. Zeira sits by the academy to honor passing scholars and asks R. Natan for its latest ruling.
R. Natan reports R. Yoḥanan’s ruling against R. Yehuda’s Musaf-first order.
R. Zeira confirms the attribution to R. Yoḥanan and repeats it forty times.
The attribution is new to him because he had been uncertain whether it came from R. Yehoshua ben Levi.
R. Yehoshua ben Levi applies Zephaniah’s verse to late Musaf under R. Yehuda’s deadline.
Rav Yosef’s translation supports reading the verse’s “nugéi” as destruction for missed times.
R. Elazar applies the same verse to late morning prayer under R. Yehuda.
A Psalm supports reading “nugéi” as sorrow.
Rav Naḥman supplies another verse in Lamentations for the sorrow meaning.

28b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: After Rav Avya misses a lecture due to illness, Abaye asks about his absence to placate Rav Yosef.
Why did Rav Avya not eat first and attend?
He cites Rav Huna’s ban on eating before Musaf.
Abaye suggests praying Musaf alone, eating, and attending.
Rav Avya cites the rule against praying before the congregation.
Abaye limits that rule to someone praying in a communal setting.
The Gemara rejects both the pre-Musaf eating ban and a similar pre-Minḥa ban.
R. Neḥunya prays briefly on entering and leaving the study hall.
The students ask why these prayers are appropriate.
He seeks freedom from error on entry and gives thanks on departure.
A baraita gives his entry prayer against mistaken rulings by himself and his colleagues.
His exit prayer thanks God for a life of Torah study and its reward.
R. Eliezer’s students ask him for a path to life in the world to come.
He urges respect for peers, sound upbringing, learning from scholars, and awareness before God in prayer.
R. Yoḥanan ben Zakkai weeps in illness, and his students ask why.
Even judgment by a mortal ruler with limited power would make him weep.
He fears enduring divine judgment and uncertainty between Eden and Gehenna.
His students ask for a blessing.
He blesses them to fear Heaven as they fear human beings.
The students wonder whether that is the full extent of the blessing.
He says people already hide wrongdoing from others, showing how much such fear would mean.
Before death he orders vessels removed from impurity and a chair prepared for Hezekiah.
The mishnah presents full or abbreviated daily Amidah according to Rabban Gamliel, R. Yehoshua, and R. Akiva.
R. Eliezer says fixed routine alone is not supplication.
R. Yehoshua gives a short prayer for travel in danger.
A traveler unable to face the Temple directs the heart toward the Holy of Holies.
Why were the Amidah’s blessings set at eighteen?
One explanation matches eighteen divine mentions in Psalm 29.
Rav Yosef matches eighteen divine mentions in Shema.
R. Yehoshua ben Levi matches eighteen spinal vertebrae.
The vertebrae explanation accompanies a rule to bow until they protrude.
Ulla measures a sufficient bow by sight of a coin opposite the heart.
R. Ḥanina allows a head movement for one who strains to appear to bow.
The Amidah now has nineteen blessings, challenging the count of eighteen.
The anti-heretic blessing was added later at Yavne.
What corresponds to the added blessing in each numerical scheme?
For the Psalm scheme, it matches “the God of glory thunders.”
For the Shema scheme, it matches the word “one.”
For the spine scheme, it matches a small vertebra.
Shimon HaPakuli orders the blessings; Shmuel HaKatan composes the added blessing at Rabban Gamliel’s request.
The next year Shmuel forgets the blessing; the account continues on 29a.

29a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Shmuel HaKatan paused for hours over the added blessing but was not removed as prayer leader.
A rule removes a leader who misses that blessing because omission may signal heresy.
Shmuel himself composed the blessing, so suspicion did not arise.
Could he have since changed his beliefs?
Abaye invokes a tradition that a good person does not become wicked.
Ezekiel describes a righteous person turning from righteousness.
Abaye limits that verse to someone originally wicked.
The warning about Yoḥanan the High Priest becoming a Sadducee challenges that limit.
Abaye identifies Yoḥanan with Yannai; Rava separates them and calls Yoḥanan originally righteous.
Rava’s view makes the case difficult.
Rava allows that even an originally righteous person may change.
Why, then, was Shmuel HaKatan left in place?
He began the blessing; only failure to begin triggers removal.
What corresponds to the seven Shabbat blessings?
They match seven divine voices in the Psalm.
What corresponds to the nine Rosh HaShana blessings?
They match Hannah’s nine divine mentions and her remembrance then.
What corresponds to the twenty-four fast-day blessings?
They match Solomon’s twenty-four prayers at the Ark’s entry.
Why are those blessings not said every day?
Solomon said them on a day of mercy, so they are used on such days.
What is R. Yehoshua’s abridged eighteen-blessing prayer?
Rav requires an abbreviation of every blessing.
Shmuel supplies the single “Havineinu” blessing covering the middle petitions.
Abaye criticizes routine use of Havineinu.
Shmuel excludes Havineinu after Shabbat and festivals because havdala belongs in the knowledge blessing.
Rabba bar Shmuel suggests a separate fourth havdala blessing, citing a tannaitic view.
A separate blessing is not standard; the abridged service likewise should not gain an eighth blessing.
Mar Zutra asks why havdala cannot be inserted into Havineinu; the objection remains unresolved.
Rav Beivai bars Havineinu in the rainy season because the rain request belongs in the blessing of years.
Mar Zutra proposes adding a rain petition to the abbreviated wording.
Such an insertion might confuse the worshipper.
Havdala could cause the same confusion.
Havdala comes at the beginning; a rain insertion comes amid the prayer.
Rav Ashi asks why rain cannot be requested in the later “Hear prayer” section, citing the missed-rain rule.
A remedy for an error does not establish the normal initial practice.
R. Tanḥum’s rule distinguishes omitted rain praise, rain request, and havdala.
A Tosefta instead requires repetition after a missed rain request.
One attempted distinction separates individual and communal prayer.
That does not fit the stated reason: communal prayer would be remedied by the leader, not “Hear prayer.”
Both cases concern individuals; recalling the omission before “Hear prayer” permits repair there, with the account continuing on 29b.

29b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The contrasting case recalls the rain omission only after the “Hear prayer” blessing.
An omitted New Moon addition sends the worshipper back to Temple service, or to the prayer’s start if it ended.
Rav Pappa says the prayer ends for this purpose only after the feet move.
He traces that distinction from his father to Rav.
Rav Naḥman allows return to Temple service even after moving when further supplications are habitual.
A variant says returning to Temple service before moving also depends on habitual supplications.
The mishnah’s warning against fixed prayer prompts the question: what counts as fixed?
One view calls prayer fixed when it feels like a burden.
The Rabbis say it lacks the tone of supplication.
Rabba and Rav Yosef say the person adds nothing personal.
R. Zeira could add something but fears confusion.
Another view points to prayer near sunrise or sunset, supported by a verse.
In the West they criticized prayer at sunset lest the time slip away.
The mishnah’s short danger prayer raises the meaning of “parashat ha-ibbur.”
One reading asks for Israel’s needs even when God is filled with anger.
Another asks for their needs even when they transgress Torah.
A baraita introduces short prayers for a place of beasts and robbers.
R. Eliezer asks God to do His will and ease those who fear Him.
R. Yehoshua asks God to hear Israel’s cry and answer swiftly.
R. Elazar ben Tzadok offers a similar short plea.
Others ask God to supply each person’s many needs despite limited understanding.
Rav Huna rules for the version given by Others.
Elijah advises avoiding anger and drunkenness and consulting God before travel.
What does consulting the Creator before travel mean?
It means the traveler’s prayer, required before a journey.
What is the traveler’s prayer?
Its wording asks for safe travel, rescue from enemies, blessing, and favor.
Abaye begins a further rule that continues on 30a.

30a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Abaye frames the traveler’s prayer in the plural, including the congregation.
When is the traveler’s prayer said?
It begins after setting out.
How far a journey requires it?
At least a parasang.
Rav Ḥisda requires standing; Rav Sheshet permits saying it while moving.
On a journey Rav Sheshet stands to pray after hearing that Rav Ḥisda did so, choosing the better practice when easy.
What distinguishes Havineinu from the short prayer in danger?
Havineinu needs the first and last three blessings but no later repeat.
The danger prayer needs neither set of blessings but must later be repeated.
Havineinu is said standing; the danger prayer can be said while walking.
A baraita says a rider dismounts to pray if someone can hold the donkey.
Rabbi says to remain seated either way so the mind stays settled.
The ruling follows Rabbi.
A blind person or one unable to find directions directs the heart toward Heaven.
From abroad, one directs the heart toward the Land of Israel.
Within the Land, one directs the heart toward Jerusalem.
Within Jerusalem, one directs the heart toward the Temple.
Within the Temple, one directs the heart toward the Holy of Holies.
Within or behind the Holy of Holies, one faces the Ark cover.
The directions converge so all Israel direct their hearts to one place.
A verse about talpiyyot is read as the hill toward which all mouths turn.
Shmuel’s father and Levi prayed early before travel, then recited Shema at its time.
A baraita supports early performance of travel-day duties and later Shema.
R. Shimon ben Elazar instead joins Shema to prayer even when traveling.
The views prioritize standing prayer or placing redemption next to prayer.
Mareimar and Mar Zutra assembled a quorum before their festival lecture.
Rav Ashi prayed seated with the congregation and later again standing at home.
He declines the proposed alternatives as burdensome or unsupported by senior practice.
The mishnah presents three views of Musaf and whether a communal setting exempts an individual.
How does R. Yehuda’s report differ from the first version of R. Elazar’s view?
They differ over an individual where no quorum is present.
A tradition rules for R. Yehuda’s report in R. Elazar’s name.
Shmuel’s practice of avoiding an individual Musaf is cited in support; discussion continues on 30b.

30b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Shmuel recalls one day without a quorum, when he prayed Musaf alone.
R. Yannai rejects the claim that the law follows R. Yehuda’s report about communal Musaf.
R. Yoḥanan observed R. Yannai praying two successive prayers.
Perhaps the second was a repeat for lack of concentration, not Musaf.
R. Zeira trusts the precision of R. Yoḥanan’s testimony.
R. Ami and R. Asi prayed in their study place despite many synagogues in Tiberias.
A contrary tradition rules according to R. Yehuda’s report.
R. Zeira asks why R. Ḥiyya prayed twice and rules out lack of initial concentration.
He suggests that the New Moon addition was omitted.
A baraita permits omission of New Moon mention if it can be included in the next prayer.
R. Yoḥanan limits that leniency to communal prayer.
How long should one pause between two prayers?
Enough to regain a pleading or beseeching frame of mind.
Both formulations draw support from verbs for Moses’ petitions.
Rav says an omitted New Moon mention in evening prayer needs no repeat because months are sanctified only by day.
Ameimar tries limiting that rule to a full month.
Rav Ashi rejects the distinction because Rav’s day-only reason applies to either month.
The chapter closes with a return formula.
The new mishnah requires solemnity and recalls the pious waiting an hour to focus before prayer.
The mishnah says prayer should not be interrupted even for a greeting or a snake on the heel.
Hannah’s bitter-hearted prayer is first offered as a source for solemn prayer.
Her unusual distress may make that example exceptional.
A verse about bowing in reverence is offered instead.
David’s unusual self-affliction could also make his case exceptional.
Another verse is read as calling for trembling in holiness.
The wording may instead mean beauty, as when Rav Yehuda dressed for prayer.
The verse “Serve the Lord in fear and rejoice with trembling” supplies a further source.
Rabba explains that joy should retain reverent trembling.
Rabba cites the verse when Abaye appears too cheerful.
Abaye says wearing tefillin keeps his reverence in place.
R. Zeira similarly challenges R. Yirmeya’s excessive cheer with a verse.
R. Yirmeya likewise points to his tefillin.
A wedding story about excessive rejoicing begins and continues on 31a.

31a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: At two weddings, a valuable cup is broken to temper excessive rejoicing.
Rav Hamnuna sings of mortality and asks what Torah and mitzvot will protect them.
R. Yoḥanan postpones unrestrained laughter until the verse’s future joy among the nations.
Reish Lakish followed that teaching throughout his life.
A baraita prescribes approaching prayer from a settled ruling, not active legal dispute.
What is an example of such a settled ruling?
Abaye cites the accepted seven-clean-days practice after even a small blood sighting.
Rava cites bringing grain in its chaff so an animal can eat it without tithes.
Another example prohibits benefit from blood drawn from a consecrated animal.
The Sages followed the mishnah; Rav Ashi followed the baraita.
Prayer begins with joy in a mitzva rather than grief, laziness, frivolity, or idle talk.
One should part from a friend with a matter of law, as the prophets closed with praise and comfort.
A further teaching says parting with law helps one remember the companion.
Rav Kahana accompanies Rav Shimi and asks about an old saying on Babylonian palms.
A verse about land no one crossed yet no one settled prompts a question about its redundant wording.
The tradition links settlement to Adam’s decree about each land.
Another report gives the route on which Rav Mordekhai accompanied Rav Shimi.
A verse supports focusing the heart toward Heaven in prayer.
R. Akiva prayed briefly with a congregation but extensively alone, moving through bows and prostrations.
Daniel’s open windows support praying in a room with windows.
Daniel’s three daily prayers limit the number of daily set prayers.
His earlier habit shows this schedule preceded exile.
His facing Jerusalem establishes prayer’s direction.
David’s evening, morning, and noon prayers separate the times.
Hannah’s inaudible voice supports quiet prayer.
Solomon’s “song and prayer” places praise before requests.
Requests are not inserted before the Amidah, but can be added after it at length.
Rav likewise allows extensive personal requests after the Amidah.
Hannah’s speaking in her heart teaches focus during prayer.
Her moving lips teaches spoken articulation.
Her unheard voice teaches prayer should not be raised aloud.
Eli’s impression that she was drunk teaches that intoxication bars prayer.
Eli’s rebuke opens another inference, continued on 31b.

31b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Eli’s rebuke of Hannah is read as a duty to correct apparent misconduct.
Hannah’s “no, my master” challenges Eli’s insight in suspecting her.
A variant asks why Eli judged her guilty rather than recognizing distress.
Her denial of wine teaches a falsely suspected person to explain their innocence.
The shared word beliya’al links drunken prayer to the severity of idol worship.
Eli’s peace wish and blessing teach a false accuser to appease and bless the person.
Hannah is identified as the first to address God as Lord of Hosts.
She asks why one son is difficult among all God’s hosts.
A poor guest asking the king for one slice of bread illustrates her appeal.
The doubled “see” in Hannah’s prayer is read as insisting God will see her plight.
The proposed route is a false sota suspicion leading to the Torah’s promise of offspring.
That reading depends on whether the sota promise includes fertility for a barren woman.
R. Yishmael’s baraita says an innocent barren woman is granted children.
R. Akiva objects that this would encourage seclusion and limits the promise to improved childbirth.
What does Hannah’s doubled “see” mean on R. Akiva’s reading?
It is ordinary biblical phrasing.
Three uses of “your maidservant” recall menstruation, dough separation, and lamp lighting, which Hannah says she observed.
What does Hannah mean by asking for “offspring of men”?
Rav reads it as a distinguished man among men.
Shmuel reads it as the one who anoints Saul and David.
R. Yoḥanan reads it as Samuel’s stature equaling Moses and Aaron.
The Rabbis read it as a child who blends among others.
Rav Dimi explains that Hannah asked for neither extreme in height, appearance, or intellect.
Hannah’s standing beside Eli supports not sitting within four cubits of prayer.
Why does “for this youth I prayed” follow the verse about slaughtering the offering?
Samuel had ruled before Eli that a non-priest may slaughter the offering.
The verse assigns priestly service from receiving the blood onward, not slaughter itself.
Eli accepts the law but says ruling before a teacher incurs death.
Hannah pleads for this very son despite Eli’s offer to pray for another.
Hannah’s words “on her heart” are read as a plea to use her capacity to nurse a child.
A separate teaching says a Shabbat fast may avert a decree but violates Shabbat delight.
Its remedy is a further fast to atone for that violation.
Hannah’s phrasing is read as challenging Heaven directly.
Elijah’s prayer is offered as a parallel challenge to Heaven.
The next question asks how God acknowledged Elijah’s claim, continuing on 32a.

32a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Micah’s verse is cited as God’s acknowledgment of responsibility for Israel’s evil.
Three verses about divine shaping of Israel and its heart temper the case against them.
Rav Pappa adds Ezekiel’s promise that God’s spirit will cause obedience.
Moses’ prayer is read as a direct challenge to God by exchanging el and al.
The school of R. Yannai asks how “Di Zahav” supports the same claim.
Moses argues that the abundance of gold God gave Israel helped cause the calf.
A lion’s roar over meat rather than straw illustrates excess leading to unruliness.
A well-fed cow kicking its owner provides a second illustration.
A pampered son given money near temptation supplies a third illustration.
A proverb and Hosea connect satiety with forgetting God.
Further verses connect wealth and fullness with pride and idolatry.
Hosea’s “silver and gold ... for Baal” is read as God conceding Moses’ claim.
The words “go, descend” after the calf require explanation.
God tells Moses his stature existed for Israel and seems lost after their sin.
When God says “leave Me,” Moses realizes his prayer can avert destruction.
A king’s hint to a bystander about saving his son illustrates Moses’ insight.
“Leave Me” is read as Moses holding God’s garment until Israel is forgiven.
Moses rejects replacing Israel with his own nation: one ancestral merit cannot withstand what three could not.
He also fears shame before the forefathers for seeking his own advancement.
The unusual word vayḥal in Moses’ prayer invites several readings, first illness from exertion.
Rava reads it as Moses releasing a divine vow, by analogy to vow language.
Shmuel reads it as Moses offering his life for Israel.
Another reading says he activated divine mercy.
The Rabbis read his plea as calling destruction of Israel a sacrilege.
A baraita reads the prayer as continuing until Moses was seized by fever.
What does it mean that God swore to the forefathers “by You”?
Moses argues that an oath by God’s eternal name cannot expire like heaven and earth.
Why does Moses’ quotation say “the land of which I spoke” rather than “You spoke”?
R. Elazar assigns the later words to God instead of Moses.
R. Shmuel keeps them as Moses’ plea about what he has already told Israel in God’s name.
Why does Numbers use the feminine noun for God’s ability?
Moses fears the nations will say God’s strength has weakened.
God replies that the nations saw His power at the sea.
Moses says they could still claim the Canaanite kings were beyond that power.
God’s “I have forgiven according to your word” confirms Moses’ argument.
The teacher’s acknowledgment and God’s “you gave Me life” are further praise of Moses’ plea.
R. Simlai teaches that praise of God should precede personal requests.
Moses’ prayer begins with God’s greatness before his request to enter the land.
A mnemonic introduces the next series of teachings.

32b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Moses’ limited answer through prayer shows prayer’s importance even beyond good deeds.
R. Elazar ranks bodily fasting above charity given from wealth.
Isaiah’s sequence places prayer above sacrifices.
Isaiah’s bloodied hands support barring a killer priest from blessing.
Verses describe prayer gates as shut after the Temple’s fall, yet tears still heard.
Rava avoids ordering a fast on a cloudy day because a verse describes clouds blocking prayer.
Ezekiel’s iron wall represents separation between Israel and God after destruction.
Moses’ prolonged prayer followed by divine hearing supports sustained prayer.
Another teaching warns that prolonged prayer with expectation can bring heartache; Torah is its remedy.
Length is praised when one does not insist on a guaranteed answer.
A Psalm’s repeated “hope” supports praying again if not answered.
Torah, good deeds, prayer, and work all require strengthening.
Joshua’s charge supports strength in Torah and good deeds.
The repeated call to hope supports persistence in prayer.
A verse about defending the people supports strength in work.
Why does Zion say both forsaken and forgotten?
Israel says even a human remembers a former wife, whereas God seems to have done neither.
God describes vast constellations created for Israel and denies having forgotten her.
God recalls Israel’s offerings and firstborn animals in the wilderness.
Israel fears God will likewise remember the golden calf.
“These” are promised to be forgotten.
Israel then fears Sinai will also be forgotten.
“I will not forget” preserves Sinai; the paired verses are explained as calf and revelation.
A Psalm is read to support waiting before prayer.
Another Psalm supports waiting after prayer.
A baraita brings both verses for waiting before and after prayer.
The early pious spent an hour before, during, and after each prayer.
How could they maintain Torah and work with nine hours spent on prayer?
Their Torah endured and their labor was blessed on account of piety.
The mishnah forbids answering even a king’s greeting during prayer.
Rav Yosef limits that rule to Israelite kings; danger from foreign rulers permits interruption.
A baraita says to shorten prayer rather than stop for an approaching violent man or carriage.
Shortening is preferred when possible; otherwise one interrupts.
A pious traveler does not answer an officer’s greeting until prayer ends.
The officer cites the duty to guard one’s life and challenges the dangerous silence.
The traveler begins a comparison with standing before a human king, continued on 33a.

33a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The traveler argues that silence before an eternal King is more fitting than silence before a mortal king.
The officer is appeased and the traveler reaches home safely.
The mishnah’s rule against interruption for a snake is recalled.
Rav Sheshet allows interruption for a scorpion, which poses greater danger.
A baraita treating a pit of snakes and scorpions as fatal seems to challenge the snake rule.
In the pit, the falling person presses on the snakes and provokes attack.
Approaching oxen warrant stopping prayer; distance depends on the ox’s history.
A warning about an ox is narrowed to a black ox in Nisan.
R. Ḥanina ben Dosa lets an arvad bite him; the creature dies.
He tells the study hall that sin, not the arvad itself, kills.
The Sages praise his survival and the arvad’s defeat.
The mishnah locates rain praise, rain request, and havdala within Amidah blessings and records two alternatives.
Why is rain praise placed in the resurrection blessing?
Rain is likened to reviving the dead.
Why is the rain request placed in the blessing of years?
Rain sustains livelihood, matching that blessing.
Why is havdala placed in the knowledge blessing?
Distinguishing sacred from ordinary requires understanding.
Another view places it there as the first weekday blessing.
R. Ami praises knowledge as the opening weekday theme.
Knowledge appears between divine names in a verse; another verse criticizes lack of understanding.
The Temple also appears between divine names in a verse.
R. Elazar compares a person with knowledge to a rebuilt Temple through that shared pattern.
Vengeance too appears between divine names; does that make it great?
Yes, in its proper place; two references express favorable and adverse vengeance.
Where did the Great Assembly originally put havdala within its prayer ordinances?
Practice shifted from prayer to wine and back, then required wine even after prayer.
A second transmission repeats that development and requirement.
Rabba and Rav Yosef likewise require havdala over wine after prayer.
A Tosefta says omission in prayer need not be repeated because it “can” be said over wine.
Read the Tosefta as saying it “is” said over wine.
A direct question to R. Yoḥanan yields the same requirement for the cup.
Does havdala over the cup also require havdala in prayer?
An a fortiori argument requires prayer too, since that was the primary enactment.
A baraita praises prayer havdala and seems to bless one who performs both.
The baraita seems self-contradictory: if prayer suffices, a second blessing would be unnecessary.
The blessing is instead for havdala in one place but not the other.
What if someone erred in both prayer and cup havdala?
Rav Sheshet says to return to the beginning.

33b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Ravina asks for the ruling on havdala in prayer and over wine.
Rava likens it to kiddush: prayer does not replace the cup.
R. Zeira asks whether R. Yoḥanan follows R. Eliezer for a festival after Shabbat.
Does calling it “law” imply a genuine dispute in that case?
The Rabbis may dispute him during ordinary weekdays but agree for a festival.
R. Akiva’s separate blessing still appears to differ.
His extra blessing is not adopted; neither weekday nor festival Amidah adds one.
The report is corrected from “law” to “inclined toward.”
Traditions vary among “law,” “inclined,” “agree,” and “appears correct.”
R. Zeira prefers R. Ḥiyya’s precise transmission, comparing him to Raḥava’s wording on the Temple Mount.
Rav Yosef sets aside those reports for Rav and Shmuel’s Babylonian formula.
The “You have made known” prayer distinguishes Shabbat from festival within the festival blessing.
The mishnah silences three problematic additions to communal prayer.
Repeating “We give thanks” suggests two authorities.
Remembering God only for good conflicts with blessing Him for harm too.
Why silence a plea invoking mercy on a bird’s nest?
One view says it implies favoritism among creatures.
Another says it turns commandments into mere expressions of mercy.
A prayer leader says the bird-nest plea and Rabba seems to praise him.
Abaye cites the mishnah that silences such a prayer.
Rabba was testing Abaye’s understanding.
Another prayer leader extends the customary divine praises with many more adjectives.
R. Ḥanina says even the standard three are said only because Moses and the Assembly established them.
Praising a king of gold coins with silver illustrates the inadequacy of extra praises.
R. Ḥanina says fear of Heaven alone is in human hands, citing Moses.
How can fear be treated as small if it is God’s treasured possession?
For Moses, who had it, fear seemed small; what one lacks seems large.
Repeating “Shema” is compared with repeating “We give thanks.”
A baraita calls repetition reprehensible, but does not say to silence it.
Word-by-word repetition is reprehensible; repeating a whole verse suggests two authorities.
Could the second recitation simply repair lack of attention the first time?
Abaye’s reply begins on the next daf.

34a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Abaye objects that careless prayer shows improper familiarity with Heaven.
One who failed to concentrate should be made to focus before repeating it.
The mishna disapproves a blessing restricted to the good.
An erring prayer leader is replaced immediately without the customary refusal.
Where does the replacement begin?
At the start of the blessing in which the first leader erred.
The leader should not answer amen after the priestly blessing, lest he lose his place.
Even as the only priest, the leader normally does not raise his hands.
He may do so if certain he can resume his prayer.
Ordinarily a prospective leader should decline at first; no refusal is like food without salt.
Excessive refusal is like food spoiled with too much salt.
How should the prospective leader act?
Decline once, hesitate the second time, and take the place on the third request.
Leaven, salt, and polite refusal help in small amounts but harm in excess.
Rav Huna sends an erring worshipper back to the beginning of the affected group of blessings.
Rav Asi disagrees about the middle blessings, saying they have no fixed order.
Rav Sheshet cites the rule to restart at the particular blessing where the error occurred.
This appears to refute Rav Huna.
Rav Huna treats all middle blessings as a single blessing for this purpose.
Rav Yehuda confines requests for personal needs to the middle blessings.
R. Hanina compares the three sections to a servant praising, petitioning, and departing from his master.
A student led an unusually long prayer before R. Eliezer.
His students ask why the prayer is so long.
R. Eliezer points to Moses praying forty days and nights.
Another student led an unusually short prayer before R. Eliezer.
His students ask why the prayer is so short.
R. Eliezer cites Moses’s brief plea to heal Miriam.
Rav Hisda teaches that prayer for another need not mention the person’s name.
Moses says “heal her” without naming Miriam.
A baraita prescribes bowing at the beginning and end of the Patriarchs and Thanksgiving blessings.
One who tries to bow at the beginning and end of every blessing is taught not to do so.
Bar Kappara begins a distinction: an ordinary person follows that rule.

34b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A High Priest bows at the end of each blessing and a king at its beginning and end.
R. Yitzhak reports a different account: a High Priest bows at each beginning.
A king stays bowed throughout, as Solomon rose only when his prayer ended.
Kidda is bowing face down, as Bathsheba did.
Keria is kneeling, as Solomon did.
Hishtahavaya means full prostration, as Jacob’s words to Joseph show.
Abaye and Rava were seen leaning to one side in prayer.
Two baraitot disagree whether bowing at thanksgiving is praiseworthy.
They distinguish its beginning from its end.
Rava nevertheless bowed at both points.
The Sages ask why he acts this way.
He cites the example of Rav Nahman and Rav Sheshet.
A baraita still condemns bowing at thanksgiving.
That baraita refers to thanksgiving in Hallel.
Another baraita separately condemns bowing in thanksgiving and in Hallel.
Its first thanksgiving refers to Grace after Meals.
The mishna calls an error in prayer a bad omen for the worshipper or leader’s congregation.
R. Hanina ben Dosa predicted whether sick people would live after praying.
They ask how he knows.
Fluent prayer signals acceptance; disrupted prayer signals rejection.
The Gemara asks which blessing the omen concerns.
Rav Safra’s tradition identifies the Patriarchs blessing.
Another version cites a baraita requiring concentration in all blessings, or at least one.
Rav Safra identifies that one as the Patriarchs blessing.
What is the source for R. Hanina’s sign that prayer is accepted?
Isaiah links the creation of fluent speech on the lips with healing.
R. Yohanan reserves the unseen reward for scholars themselves; prophetic promises concern their supporters.
R. Yohanan also limits the prophets’ visions to the messianic era, not the World-to-Come.
Shmuel disagrees: only political subjection separates the messianic era from this world.
R. Yohanan limits prophetic promises to penitents; the fully righteous have unseen reward.
R. Abbahu places penitents higher, reading “the distant” before “the near.”
R. Yohanan reads the distant as one always far from sin and the near as one formerly close to it.
What is the unseen reward?
R. Yehoshua ben Levi identifies wine preserved since creation.
R. Shmuel bar Nahmani identifies Eden, unseen by any creature.
Did Adam not see it?
Adam was in the Garden.
Are Garden and Eden the same?
A river flows from Eden to water the Garden, so they differ.
R. Hanina prays for Rabban Gamliel’s ill son and says his fever has left.
The messengers ask if he is a prophet.
He claims no prophecy, only the tradition that fluent prayer shows acceptance.
The messengers record the time; Rabban Gamliel confirms his son recovered then.
R. Yohanan ben Zakkai’s son recovers after R. Hanina prays with his head between his knees.
R. Yohanan says his own prolonged prayer would not have been heeded so readily.
His wife asks whether Hanina is greater.
He compares Hanina to a servant before the king and himself to a minister.
R. Yohanan requires a room with windows for prayer, citing Daniel’s windows toward Jerusalem.
Rav Kahana calls prayer in an open field presumptuous.
He also discourages detailing one’s sin, citing the blessing of covered transgression.
The chapter concludes.

35a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna prescribes “fruit of the tree” for tree fruit.
Wine receives the distinct blessing “fruit of the vine.”
Produce of the ground receives “fruit of the ground.”
Bread receives the distinct blessing “who brings forth bread.”
Vegetables receive “fruit of the ground.”
R. Yehuda prescribes “varieties of herbs” for vegetables.
What is the source for blessings before food?
“Holy for praises” is read to require blessings before and after fourth-year fruit.
R. Akiva therefore forbids tasting anything before blessing.
Is that really what the verse teaches?
Both expressions are needed for redemption and for distinguishing fruit associated with song.
R. Yonatan’s tradition asks why Temple song is said only over wine.
The vine’s wine gladdens God and people; its Temple libation receives song.
This works for all fourth-year plantings, but what of the view limiting it to vineyards?
R. Hiyya and R. Shimon bar Rabbi differ whether the rule says planting or vineyard.
How can the vineyard view leave a word for blessing?
A verbal analogy of “produce” restricts fourth-year fruit to vineyards.
That frees one expression of praise to teach blessing.
Without the analogy, where is blessing derived?
Even with it, the verse yields blessing afterward; what requires blessing beforehand?
An a fortiori inference: if one blesses when full, all the more when hungry.
How does the rule extend beyond vineyards?
Any enjoyed food should require blessing as vineyard produce does.
Vineyards differ because they require leaving incomplete clusters for the poor.
Standing grain also requires a blessing.
Grain differs because it requires separating hallah.
Vineyard and grain together establish a common factor: enjoyment requiring blessing.
Both have a connection with offerings on the altar.
That common factor would at least include olives, also used at the altar.
Why invoke the altar for olives when Scripture calls their orchard a vineyard?
Rav Pappa distinguishes an “olive vineyard” from an unqualified vineyard.
The shared connection to the altar still blocks a general inference.
Try deriving other foods from the seven species, which are enjoyed and blessed over.
The seven species differ because they require first fruits.
Also, that source provides an after-blessing, not a before-blessing.
Again, the blessing before eating follows a fortiori from blessing after satiation.
Even the planting view cannot explain meat, eggs, and fish from fruit laws.
Reason supplies the rule: enjoying this world without blessing is forbidden.
A baraita calls unblessed enjoyment misuse of consecrated property.
What remedy is offered? Go to a Sage.
How can a Sage undo the violation already committed?
Rava says to learn blessings from a Sage beforehand to avoid the violation.
Shmuel likens unblessed enjoyment to using sacred property, citing God’s ownership of the earth.
R. Levi contrasts God’s ownership of the earth with its gift to humanity.
The first verse speaks of the time before a blessing; the resolution continues on 35b.

35b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The earth is given to people after they bless.
R. Hanina bar Pappa likens unblessed enjoyment to stealing from God and Israel.
Scripture calls God father and Israel mother, explaining the verse about robbing parents.
Who is the “companion of a destroyer”?
One who eats without blessing is compared with Jeroboam, who led Israel astray.
R. Hanina contrasts God’s “my grain” with Israel’s “your grain.”
The latter applies when Israel does God’s will; the former when they do not.
How can gathering grain coexist with constant Torah study?
R. Yishmael permits customary work alongside study.
R. Shimon asks what becomes of Torah if one works through every season.
When Israel does God’s will, others do its work, as Isaiah says.
Otherwise Israel works for itself, and may even serve its enemies.
Abaye says many succeeded with R. Yishmael’s approach but not R. Shimon’s.
Rava tells students to work during the key agricultural months to secure the year’s food.
Earlier generations centered Torah and managed both study and work; later ones centered work and lost both.
Earlier generations brought produce through the gate to incur tithes; later ones avoided that entrance.
R. Yannai says produce becomes liable when it enters the house, citing the tithe declaration.
R. Yohanan says even a courtyard establishes liability, citing “within your gates.”
Why does wine differ in blessing? Perhaps its improvement through processing explains it.
Olive oil also improves in processing yet retains the tree-fruit blessing.
A distinct olive blessing seems difficult: the fruit itself is already called olive.
One could instead bless “fruit of the olive tree.”
Mar Zutra proposes that wine nourishes but oil does not.
A vow permits only water and salt, implying other foods, including oil, nourish.
Rav Huna explains the vow concerns anything that nourishes, unlike the special grain blessing.
Oil nourishes; wine instead satisfies while oil does not.
Rava drank wine before Passover to stimulate appetite, seemingly not to satisfy it.
Much wine stimulates; a little satisfies.
Scripture calls bread satisfying and wine gladdening, casting doubt on wine’s satiety.
Wine both satisfies and gladdens; bread satisfies without gladdening.
Why not recite the three after-blessings over wine?
People do not base meals on wine.
What if someone does base a meal on wine?
Until Elijah resolves whether it can be a meal, personal practice yields to the norm.
The teaching that olive oil receives the tree-fruit blessing is restated.
If drunk plain, oil harms the drinker.
Teruma law distinguishes damaging oil by drinking from benefiting by anointing.
Perhaps the oil is eaten with bread.
Then bread is primary, and its blessing exempts the secondary oil.
The case is oil drunk with anigeron, a beet broth; its description continues.

36a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If anigeron is the main food, its blessing should cover the secondary oil.
The case is a sore throat treated by swallowing much oil in anigeron.
Why is a blessing necessary to state?
Perhaps medicinal intent would remove the obligation.
Pleasure from the oil still requires a blessing.
Rav Yehuda and Rav Nahman dispute the blessing on wheat flour.
Rava supports Rav Yehuda from olive oil, whose blessing stays tied to its original fruit.
Unlike oil, flour can improve further into bread.
Does further improvement really require the general blessing?
Shmuel says barley flour gets the general blessing, suggesting wheat flour may get the ground-fruit blessing.
Wheat flour also gets the general blessing.
Why mention barley rather than the more ordinary wheat?
One might otherwise think barley flour needs no blessing at all.
Even salt and salt water receive a blessing; why not barley flour?
Unlike customary salt, barley flour can harm, yet enjoyment still obligates blessing.
Rav Yehuda and Shmuel dispute the blessing on heart of palm.
Rav Yehuda treats it as fruit; Shmuel uses the general blessing because it hardens.
Shmuel initially favors Rav Yehuda by comparing a radish that hardens yet keeps its produce blessing.
Radishes are planted for that food, unlike palms planted for their hearts.
Caper leaves and shoots receive a produce blessing despite the plant being grown for fruit.
Caper is also grown for its shoots, unlike palm for its heart.
Despite Shmuel’s praise of Rav Yehuda, the ruling follows Shmuel.
Outside Israel, Rav discards orla caper berries but permits the buds.
A prior mishna calls both berries and buds tree fruit for blessings.
Rav follows R. Akiva, who treats only the berries as fruit for tithes.
Why not simply announce the law follows R. Akiva?
That might wrongly extend the leniency to Israel; it applies outside Israel.
Why not say explicitly that R. Akiva governs outside Israel?
One might limit that ruling to rabbinic tithes and exclude Torah-based orla.
Ravina sees Mar bar Rav Ashi eat the buds and discard the berries.
Why not follow Beit Shammai, who appear more lenient about caper?
The mishna says Beit Shammai classify caper as vineyard mixed species, yet both schools apply orla.
These rulings seem to call caper both a vegetable and a tree.
Beit Shammai are uncertain and rule strictly in both areas.
But uncertain orla is permitted outside Israel; the argument continues on 36b.

36b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The rule for uncertain orla outside Israel concludes: buying is allowed if picking is unseen.
R. Akiva’s leniency may be followed against R. Eliezer; Beit Shammai’s against Beit Hillel may not.
Caper buds may be orla as protection secondary to the fruit under the Torah’s wording.
Rava initially requires a protector to remain attached after harvest; the bud does not.
Abaye cites pomegranate blossom, excluded from food size yet included in orla.
Rava revises the rule: protection must remain when the fruit ripens; caper buds fall off.
Date coverings count as protection even when present only on immature fruit.
Rav Nahman follows R. Yosei, who treats the grape bud as fruit.
The Rabbis disagree about grapes, but do they disagree for other trees?
The seventh-year cutting rules protect other trees once fruit begins to emerge.
Rav Asi explains the measure for an unripe grape as the size of a white bean.
The Rabbis exclude a grape bud but protect fruit of other trees from emergence.
Rava finally defines protection by whether removing it kills the fruit; caper fruit survives.
Pomegranates wither when their blossom is removed; caper fruit remains.
Mar bar Rav Ashi’s practice is adopted: eat caper buds outside Israel and bless as ground produce.
Rav Sheshet and Rava differ whether chewed peppers need a blessing.
Rava exempts chewed pepper or ginger from Yom Kippur liability.
A baraita treats pepper as edible fruit subject to orla and part of Israel’s abundance.
Fresh peppers are edible; dry ones are not treated as food here.
The Sages cite edible Indian ginger blessed as ground produce against the Yom Kippur exemption.
Fresh ginger differs from dry ginger.
Rav Yehuda and Rav Kahana dispute the blessing for a cooked grain dish.
For plain pounded grain all agree on the grain blessing; the dispute concerns a honey mixture.
Rav Yehuda treats the honey as primary, while Rav Kahana treats grain as primary.
Rav Yosef supports Rav Kahana from Rav and Shmuel: any dish containing the five grains gets their blessing.
Why do Rav and Shmuel separately say “contains grain” and “is grain”?
The second formula establishes grain’s blessing alone; the first extends it to mixtures.

37a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: “Contains grain” includes a mixture.
Would that alone imply pure rice or millet gets the grain blessing?
“Is from the five grains” excludes rice and millet even when unadulterated.
A baraita compares rice and millet bread to cooked grain dishes, whose blessing is mezonot.
The comparison concerns blessings before and after; the formulas differ for rice or millet.
Another baraita explicitly lists rice among cooked dishes.
That follows R. Yohanan ben Nuri, who treats rice as grain even for Passover.
Do the Rabbis really exclude rice from this category?
A baraita distinguishes intact cooked wheat bread from dissolved pieces and their blessings.
It gives cooked rice the mezonot blessing even when its pieces remain intact.
R. Yohanan ben Nuri would instead require the bread blessing and full Grace.
The baraita follows the Rabbis and refutes Rav and Shmuel.
The refutation is accepted.
The wheat-chewing baraita says ground-fruit blessing, while another says seed blessing.
That is the dispute between R. Yehuda’s specific plant blessing and the Rabbis’ general one.
The earlier baraita gives ground-fruit on chewed rice and mezonot on cooked rice.
Another baraita denies the special after-blessing.
Rav Sheshet attributes the two rulings to Rabban Gamliel and the Rabbis.
They differ whether seven-species food gets full Grace or one abridged blessing.
R. Akiva blesses briefly after dates in Rabban Gamliel’s presence.
Rabban Gamliel rebukes him for entering the dispute.
R. Akiva invokes the rule that the majority prevails over an individual.
R. Yehuda begins a variant report of the seven-species rule.

37b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: In R. Yehuda’s report, Rabban Gamliel requires full Grace for seven-species fruit or unbaked grain.
For rice or millet bread, he requires one abridged blessing; the Rabbis require none of those.
The earlier wheat-bread clause cannot follow Rabban Gamliel, who requires full Grace even for dates.
But if it follows the Rabbis, their two teachings conflict.
Keep the Rabbis as the source and amend the rice after-blessing to no special blessing.
Rava initially gives flour-heavy farmers’ porridge the grain blessing because flour dominates.
He initially gives honey-heavy Mehoza porridge the general blessing because honey dominates.
Rava revises both to the grain blessing, citing Rav and Shmuel on any mixture containing grain.
Rav Yosef treats a cooked dish with olive-sized bread pieces as bread for both blessings.
Smaller pieces, he initially says, receive the grain blessing and one abridged after-blessing.
What supports Rav Yosef’s distinction?
A meal-offering is blessed as bread and is crumbled into olive-sized pieces.
Abaye asks whether flour-fine meal-offering crumbs then lose the bread blessing.
A baraita still treats gathered crumbs as leavened or unleavened bread on Passover.
Perhaps those crumbs were pressed into a mass.
The baraita speaks of eating “them,” plural, so they were not one mass.
The crumbs originally came from a large loaf.
What is the final ruling?
Rav Sheshet gives the bread blessing even for crumbs smaller than an olive.
Rava requires that the crumbs still look like bread.
Authorities disagree whether terokanin requires separating hallah.
Abaye identifies terokanin as a ground-oven preparation.
Abaye says terita is exempt from hallah.
Terita is variously described as poured batter, Indian bread, or bread for kutah.
R. Hiyya likewise exempts bread made for kutah.
Another baraita requires hallah for that bread.
R. Yehuda distinguishes it by how its preparation reveals its intended use; the explanation continues.

38a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Bread for kutah requires hallah if shaped as loaves, not if shaped as boards.
Abaye asks what blessing is said over the ground-oven preparation.
Rav Yosef calls it dough rather than bread and prescribes the grain blessing.
Mar Zutra, using it as a meal, recites the bread blessing and full Grace.
Mar bar Rav Ashi says it fulfills matza because it counts as bread of affliction.
He gives date honey the general blessing.
It is merely liquid exuded by the dates.
R. Yehoshua exempts one who consumes fruit liquids of teruma from the added fifth.
A Sage asks Rava about pressed terima.
Rava initially does not understand the term.
Ravina asks which sort of pressed substance is meant.
Rava recalls that teruma dates may be pressed, though not brewed into beer.
The ruling gives pressed dates the tree-fruit blessing because they retain their identity.
Rav and Shmuel dispute the blessing for shetita.
Rav Hisda distinguishes thick food from thin medicinal drink.
Rav Yosef asks how medicinal shetita could be prepared and drunk on Shabbat.
Abaye cites the rule allowing ordinary food and drink for healing on Shabbat.
Another version says eating is intended and the cure comes incidentally.
Why teach a blessing if shetita is ordinary food? Perhaps deliberate medicinal use would exempt it.
Pleasure from consuming it still requires a blessing.
A baraita records the Rabbis’ hamotzi and R. Nehemya’s motzi formulas for bread.
Rava says all agree motzi describes a past act, as in the verse on Egypt.
The Rabbis read hamotzi as past, citing water brought from the rock.
R. Nehemya reads hamotzi as present or future from the Exodus promise.
The Rabbis explain that the verse promises later recognition of what God had brought about.
Sages praise Rav Zevid’s son as skilled in blessings, and R. Zeira asks to meet him.
When served bread, the visitor says motzi.
R. Zeira questions his expertise, beginning a preference for hamotzi.

38b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: What did choosing the undisputed motzi teach?
He avoided the disagreement.
The ruling nevertheless follows the Rabbis’ hamotzi.
The mishna places vegetables beside bread, suggesting both keep their blessing after cooking.
Rabbenai infers that boiled vegetables retain the ground-fruit blessing.
Rav Hisda cites Rav for the ground-fruit blessing on boiled vegetables.
Ulla reports R. Yohanan’s contrary general blessing.
Rav Hisda distinguishes vegetables improved by boiling from those diminished by it.
Cabbage, chard, and pumpkin illustrate vegetables improved by boiling.
Which vegetables lose their quality when boiled?
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak names garlic and leeks.
Rav Nahman cites Shmuel for the ground-fruit blessing on boiled vegetables.
Ulla again reports R. Yohanan’s contrary general blessing.
Rav Nahman compares a dispute whether boiled matza fulfills Passover.
The matza dispute concerns taste; even R. Yosei may retain the produce blessing for vegetables.
R. Hiyya bar Abba and R. Binyamin bar Yefet transmit conflicting rulings from R. Yohanan.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak says Ulla adopted the mistaken report.
R. Zeira favors R. Hiyya’s careful, frequently reviewed transmission over R. Binyamin’s.
R. Yohanan explicitly gave repeatedly boiled lupins the ground-fruit blessing.
R. Hiyya saw R. Yohanan bless both before and after a salted olive.
If salted produce retains its status, the olive gets tree-fruit and abridged after-blessings.
If it loses that status, what after-blessing applies?
The general “creatures and their needs” after-blessing could apply.
A baraita bars cooked bitter herbs for Passover; do they really retain their status?
Passover requires the bitter taste, which cooking removes.
R. Yirmeya asks how a pitted salted olive warranted an after-blessing.

39a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Does removing the pit leave too little olive for an after-blessing?
The measure is a medium olive; the large one before R. Yohanan still met it after pitting.
A mishna defines the measure as a medium aguri olive, named for its stored oil.
Two students before bar Kappara disagree when one first blesses the poultry.
Bar Kappara rebukes the student who ridiculed his companion’s preference.
He then rebukes the one who blessed without consulting the elder.
Both students fail to live through the year.
Did they dispute whether cooked vegetables retain a specific blessing and outrank poultry?
Both may assign the general blessing and dispute preference versus nourishment.
Rav Huna gives coarsely cut turnips the ground-fruit blessing but finely cut ones the general blessing.
Rav Yehuda keeps the ground-fruit blessing for both; fine cutting improves taste.
Rav Kahana initially distinguishes beet stew from flour-rich turnip stew.
He later treats both as vegetables because the flour merely binds the dish.
Rav Hisda praises beet stew for heart, eyes, and intestines.
Abaye specifies that it must be well cooked.
Rav Pappa gives vegetable cooking water the status of its vegetables.
Is dill broth meant for flavor or merely to remove residue?
Dill loses food status after flavoring a pot, showing it was added for flavor.
Rav Hiyya bar Ashi allows the bread blessing on dried bread soaked in a bowl.
This seems to oppose R. Hiyya’s requirement that the blessing end as bread is broken.
Rava notes that even a whole loaf is sliced when the blessing ends.

39b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava says to bless before breaking bread.
Nehardea follows R. Hiyya’s timing, while other Sages follow Rava.
The final ruling follows Rava: bless, then break.
Rav Huna permits blessing pieces; R. Yohanan prefers a whole loaf.
All prefer a piece of wheat bread over a whole barley loaf.
R. Yirmeya compares a dispute over whole small versus half large onions for teruma.
Is this a dispute between importance and wholeness?
With a priest present, quality wins; without one, durability matters to the first tanna.
Rav Nahman cites Mar son of Ravina, who combines a piece with the whole loaf.
A baraita also instructs placing the piece inside the whole and blessing.
Rav Nahman praises the teaching for reconciling the students’ views.
On Passover all combine broken and whole matza, citing “bread of affliction.”
On Shabbat two loaves are required, citing the double portion of manna.
Rav Kahana held two loaves but broke one.
R. Zeira broke a large piece for the whole meal.
Ravina asks whether that looks gluttonous.
Its unusual use on Shabbat shows it honors the day.
Rav Ami and Rav Asi used eruv bread for the meal to perform another mitzva with it.

40a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav distinguishes speech about sharing bread from requesting salt after a blessing.
R. Yohanan allows a salt request, but considers preparing ox feed an interruption.
Rav Sheshet says even directing ox feed needs no new blessing.
Animals must be fed before people eat, as the order in Deuteronomy suggests.
Rava bar Shmuel says a bread breaker waits for salt or relish for everyone.
At the Exilarch’s house he breaks the bread immediately, and they ask why.
That quality bread needed no condiment.
Advice on urination: sitting, loose earth, or a raised spot prevents interruption or splashing.
Rava bar Shmuel advises salt after food and water after drink.
A baraita repeats the advice.
Another warns of bad breath by day and illness by night without them.
A baraita recommends water with meals for the intestines.
Rav Hisda specifies one jug per loaf.
Lentils monthly are said to prevent illness, but daily use harms breath.
Mustard monthly is said to prevent illness, but daily use weakens the heart.
Rav credits small fish with intestinal and general health benefits.
R. Hama credits black cumin with preventing heart pain.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel warns that its odor can be deadly.
Its odor harms while its taste helps; R. Yirmeya’s mother used and removed it accordingly.
The mishna records R. Yehuda’s blessing for varieties of herbs.
R. Zeira rules against that view.
He explains it from giving each day its own blessing, and by analogy each food type.
He contrasts a full human vessel, which holds no more, with a full learner who can receive more.
“If you listen, you will hear” links present attentiveness with further learning.
Reviewing older learning leads to new learning; turning away prevents it.
The mishna validates a ground-fruit blessing said over tree fruit.
It invalidates a tree-fruit blessing said over ground produce.
The general “by whose word” blessing works for all foods.
Who holds that earth is the tree’s primary source?
Rav Nahman points to R. Yehuda, who still reads the first-fruits declaration after a tree is cut.
Why state the obvious invalidity of a tree blessing on ground produce?
It is needed even for R. Yehuda, who calls wheat a tree.
R. Meir identifies Adam’s tree as the vine, citing wine’s ill effects.
R. Nehemya identifies the fig, whose leaves repaired their shame.
R. Yehuda identifies wheat, which enables a child to call its parents.
Would R. Yehuda’s designation of wheat as a tree require a tree-fruit blessing?
Only a plant whose branch remains and fruits again takes that blessing.

40b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If the branch does not survive fruit removal to produce again, the blessing is ground-fruit.
Rav Huna excludes bread and wine from the general blessing; R. Yohanan includes them.
A Tosefta contrasts R. Meir’s acceptance of improvised blessings with R. Yosei’s fixed formula.
Does each amora simply follow one of those tannaim?
Rav Huna says even R. Meir requires explicitly naming bread in an improvised blessing.
R. Yohanan says even R. Yosei accepts the established general blessing.
Binyamin the shepherd recites an Aramaic bread blessing, which Rav accepts.
Rav elsewhere requires God’s name in every blessing.
His Aramaic wording included “the Merciful.”
How could one sentence fulfill the three blessings of Grace?
It fulfilled only the first blessing.
Is Rav teaching merely that a vernacular language works?
A mishna already permits Grace and other recitations in any language.
Rav teaches that even a vernacular paraphrase of the formula can suffice afterward.
Rav requires God’s name; R. Yohanan also requires mention of sovereignty.
Abaye favors Rav from the tithe confession, which mentions blessing and the Name but not sovereignty.
R. Yohanan would read both Name and sovereignty into that teaching.
The mishna gives the general blessing to food not nourished by the ground.
It also assigns that blessing to vinegar, inferior dates, and locusts.
R. Yehuda denies a blessing over produce associated with a curse.
R. Yehuda prioritizes one of the seven species; the Rabbis allow any preferred item.
A baraita lists animal foods, spoiled foods, salt, and mushrooms under the general blessing.
A vow distinguishes mushrooms from earth-fruit yet includes them among earth-grown things.
Abaye says mushrooms grow from earth without drawing nourishment from it.
But the baraita says they do not grow from earth.
Read it as “do not draw nourishment from earth.”
What are novelot? The amoraim differ between sun-burnt and wind-fallen dates.
Wind-fallen dates are not obviously a cursed kind, as R. Yehuda calls them.
His “curse” may refer to the other listed foods.
Another version asks why wind-fallen dates get the general, rather than tree-fruit, blessing.
