Plain novelot means heat-damaged dates; the dispute concerns novelot temara.
A demai mishna lists novelot temara among produce treated leniently.
The Gemara identifies the other fruits on that list.
R. Ila and R. Zeira dispute whether novelot temara are heat-damaged or wind-fallen.
If wind-fallen dates are ownerless, why would certainly untithed ones owe tithes?
Gathering them into a finished pile can create tithe liability, as with gathered gifts to the poor.
Another version of the discussion begins on the next daf.

41a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A variant cannot explain why one mishna says plain novelot and another novelot temara; the difficulty remains.
Ulla limits the seven-species priority dispute to foods sharing a blessing; differing blessings each require their own.
A baraita says a radish blessing can exempt an olive.
The radish is primary in that case.
Then why would R. Yehuda prefer the olive, contrary to the primary-food rule?
R. Yehuda himself says a radish blessing covers an olive brought for its sake.
Read the baraita as primary radish first, but separate blessings when neither food is secondary.
For two foods with the same blessing, R. Yehuda chooses the olive; the Rabbis allow either.
R. Ami and R. Yitzhak report the view that this dispute applies only to equal blessings.
Another view extends the dispute even to different blessings.
If both blessings must be recited, what can the dispute concern?
R. Yirmeya says it concerns which goes first.
A tradition ranks blessings by the order of the seven species in Deuteronomy.
R. Hanan instead reads the entire verse as legal measures.
Wheat sets the eating time for clothing to become impure in an afflicted house.
A barley-sized bone transmits impurity by touch or carrying.
A quarter-log of wine sets the Nazirite measure.
A dried fig sets the Shabbat carrying measure.
Pomegranate begins a measure for household vessels, continued on 41b.

41b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Household vessels lose impurity at a hole the size of a pomegranate.
R. Yosei bar Hanina links “olive oil” to olive-sized measures.
Not every measure is an olive; earlier examples differ.
Most measures are olive-sized.
“Honey” alludes to the large-date measure for Yom Kippur.
The measures are not written explicitly there; the verse serves as a rabbinic support.
Rav Hamnuna blesses dates before pomegranates at a meal.
Rav Hisda asks why the earlier-listed pomegranate does not take priority.
Dates are second after the nearer “land,” while pomegranates are fifth.
Rav Hisda praises Rav Hamnuna’s insight.
Rav Huna and Rav Nahman require a before-blessing on meal-time fruit, but no separate after-blessing.
Rav Sheshet requires both, except that pastry may be covered by Grace.
R. Hiyya says bread exempts all foods and wine all drinks.
Rav Pappa exempts food integral to the meal from both separate blessings.
Fruit brought during the meal needs a before-blessing but no separate after-blessing.
Food brought after the meal requires both blessings.
Students ask why bread exempts food integral to the meal.
Ben Zoma says the bread blessing covers it.
Then why does bread not also exempt wine?
Wine is different; its explanation continues on 42a.

42a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Wine has its own blessing even during a meal.
Rav Huna eats many dessert loaves without full Grace.
Rav Nahman says food on which people base a meal requires full Grace.
At a wedding, Rav Yehuda questions the bread blessing said over dessert pastry.
The diners cite R. Mona and a supposed ruling of Shmuel in his favor.
Rav Yehuda corrects the report: Shmuel did not rule like R. Mona.
They cite his own report that wafers get the bread blessing.
That applies when a meal is based on them.
Rav Pappa eats food served after the meal is said to be finished.
Why does he not treat the meal as ended?
The relevant threshold is removal of the table.
After a table is removed at the Exilarch’s house, Rava eats more but R. Zeira does not.
R. Zeira asks why Rava eats after table removal.
The guests still depend on the Exilarch’s continuing table.
Rav and Rav Ashi say customary post-meal oil delays the meal’s end.
The Gemara instead follows the rule that handwashing is followed immediately by Grace.
Abaye adds that blessing follows scholars, citing Laban and Joseph.
The mishna says a blessing over wine before a meal covers wine afterward.
The same applies to appetizers before and after.
Bread covers appetizers, but appetizers do not cover bread.
Beit Shammai say appetizers do not even cover a cooked dish.
Individuals bless separately while sitting; a reclined group can be covered by one.

42b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna separates individual wine blessings during a meal from one group blessing after it.
The wine blesser also blesses the incense brought after the meal.
R. Yohanan limits one wine blessing to Shabbat and festivals; weekdays require each cup blessed.
R. Yehoshua ben Levi adds bathhouse and bloodletting occasions to the one-blessing rule.
Rava blesses before and after a weekday meal, and Rabba bar Mari approves.
Abaye blesses each cup on a festival, prompting a challenge from that rule.
His intent to drink changed with each cup.
Does a blessing on wine drunk to moisten food cover wine drunk afterward for pleasure?
Rav and Rav Nahman say yes; Rav Kahana, Rav Sheshet, and other students say no.
Rava cites the mishna’s separate blessing over wine after the meal.
Rav Nahman reads that clause as a case with no wine during the meal.
The mishna’s rules on bread, appetizers, and Beit Shammai are restated.
Does Beit Shammai dispute the first or last clause?
Perhaps they deny that bread covers even cooked food.
Or perhaps they deny that an appetizer covers cooked food.
The dilemma remains unresolved.
The mishna seems to require reclining before one blesses for all.
A baraita lets one bless for a seated group, even with separate loaves.
They may have planned in advance to eat together at a named place.
Rav’s students face the same doubt after arranging to eat at a river.
Rav Adda bar Ahava begins a response on the next daf.

43a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A student mourns Rav again and laments that they had not mastered Grace after Meals.
An elder resolves their doubt: agreeing on a place to eat counts as reclining.
Rav says only bread needs reclining for a shared blessing; R. Yohanan includes wine.
Another version has Rav say reclining works only for bread; R. Yohanan says it works for wine too.
A Tosefta has guests bless wine separately before reclining and together afterward.
The first version of Rav conflicts with the separate blessings before reclining.
Guests in the waiting area intend to move, so have not formed a fixed group.
The second version of Rav conflicts with the joint wine blessing after reclining.
Reclining for bread also establishes the group for wine.
Why does each diner bless wine during the meal, but one blesses for all afterward?
While eating, their throats are not free to respond together.
Why does the wine blesser also bless incense if another diner outranks him?
He washed first after the meal.
The first to wash after a meal is designated for Grace.
Rabbi asks Rav to wash, and R. Hiyya explains this assigns him Grace.
The scent blessing is said when the incense smoke rises.
But the fragrance has not yet been smelled.
Like bread, the blessing may precede enjoyment when one intends to enjoy it.
A teaching gives woody incense the tree-spice blessing, except animal musk.
A baraita restricts that blessing to balsam and myrtle, refuting the broad rule.
Rav Hisda asks which blessing applies to balsam oil.
Rav Yehuda says “Creator of the oil of our land.”
What should those without his attachment to Israel say?
R. Yohanan says “Creator of fragrant oil.”
R. Adda allows the tree-spice blessing on costus but not infused oil.
Rav Kahana includes infused oil but excludes oil with ground spices.
The Nehardeans include even oil with ground spices.

43b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav gives jasmine the fragrant-tree blessing.
He gives seaside spikenard the same blessing.
Flax stalks are called “trees” in Joshua.
Garden daffodil takes the tree-spice blessing; wild daffodil takes the herb-spice blessing.
Violets take the herb-spice blessing.
Citron or quince fragrance takes the fruit-fragrance blessing.
A blessing is said on blossoming trees seen in Nisan.
The soul’s enjoyment of scent explains why fragrance is blessed over.
Hosea describes Israel’s young men as fragrant like Lebanon.
God makes each person’s work pleasing to him, as Ecclesiastes suggests.
A proverb about a pig and a palm heart illustrates differing tastes.
A torch counts like two travelers and moonlight like three on a dark path.
Do those counts include the traveler?
The moon’s count and the demon rule show that the traveler is included.
The tradition urges accepting a furnace rather than publicly humiliating another person.
Tamar avoids publicly identifying Judah while facing punishment.
Beit Shammai bless scented oil before myrtle; Beit Hillel reverse the order.
Rabban Gamliel favors oil because it serves for scent and anointing.
R. Yohanan rules like Rabban Gamliel’s decision.
Rav Pappa nevertheless blesses myrtle before oil.
His host asks why he does not follow that decision.
Rav Pappa attributes a contrary ruling to Rava.
The Gemara says he offered that attribution to avoid embarrassment.
Beit Shammai hold oil in the right hand and bless it before wine.
Beit Hillel instead hold wine in the right hand and bless it first.
The perfumed oil is rubbed on the attendant or a wall if the attendant is a scholar.
A baraita lists conduct considered unbecoming for a Torah scholar.
Perfume in the market is restricted where it raises suspicion of sexual impropriety.
The concern chiefly applies to perfumed clothes; authorities differ about hair.
Walking alone at night raises suspicion unless the scholar has a known study appointment.
A teaching regards patched shoes as unbecoming.
But R. Hiyya bar Abba himself wore patched shoes.
The concern is repeated upper patches, outdoors in summer, when conspicuous.
Public conversation with a woman can raise suspicion even when she is a relative.
Eating with the unlearned may draw the scholar after their conduct.
Arriving last at the study hall may make him seem negligent.
Long strides are said to impair eyesight.
The Shabbat-eve kiddush wine is given as a remedy.
An upright gait is likened to crowding God’s presence, which fills the earth.

44a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna says a blessing over primary salted food exempts secondary bread.
In general, blessing the primary food covers what accompanies it.
When would salted food be primary to bread?
For those eating the exceptionally sweet Genosar fruit.
Rabba bar bar Hana describes the large quantities R. Yohanan ate.
He claimed not to have tasted sustenance, rather than no food at all.
Further exaggerated accounts describe how much other Sages ate.
Rav Dimi describes a royal city supplying vast amounts of salted fish to fig pickers.
Ravin describes a royal tree yielding many pigeons.
R. Yitzhak recounts eighty priestly sibling pairs in Gufnit, unmatched in Babylonia.
Rav says a meal without salt is not a meal.
R. Yohanan says the same of a meal without a cooked dish.
Rabban Gamliel requires full Grace after seven-species fruit; the Rabbis require one abridged blessing.
R. Akiva requires full Grace even after vegetables when they form the meal.
The mishna disputes which blessing is said when drinking water for thirst.
Why does Rabban Gamliel require three blessings?
The verses place the seven species, bread, and blessing in one passage.
The Rabbis say a repeated “land” separates the bread rule from the fruit list.
Rabban Gamliel uses that separation to exclude raw wheat.
Grain products take mezonot first and an abridged threefold blessing afterward.
Seven-species fruit takes the tree-fruit blessing first and the abridged blessing afterward.
Abaye asks for the wording of that abridged blessing.
Rav Dimi recites its fruit formula, praising the land and praying for Jerusalem.
For the five grains, the wording begins “for nourishment” and ends “for the land and nourishment.”
How should the fruit blessing conclude?
Rav Dimi cites Rav’s New Moon formula as a precedent for naming two themes.
Rav Hisda and R. Yohanan differ between “its fruits” and “the fruits.”
Rav Amram assigns different formulas to Babylonia and Israel.
Rav Nahman objects that Babylonians should not claim Israel’s fruits as their own.
Reverse the attributions: Israel says “its fruits”; Babylonia says “the fruits.”

44b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav requires an after-blessing for eggs and meat, but not vegetables.
R. Yitzhak extends it to vegetables, but not water.
Rav Pappa extends the after-blessing even to water.
The Sages describe whose view they followed in practice.
The mishna distinguishes foods needing both blessings from items needing only a prior blessing.
The earlier opinions can read the exception as vegetables or water.
What remains excluded according to Rav Pappa?
The exception refers to commandments.
Western Sages bless after removing tefillin; what is excluded for them?
Fragrances need a blessing before smelling, but none afterward.
An egg is said to be more nourishing than an equal amount of most foods, except meat.
Can boiled vegetables really serve as a whole meal, as R. Akiva says?
Rav Ashi identifies a nourishing cabbage stalk.
A baraita lists the bodily effects of spleen, leeks, vegetables, small creatures, cabbage, beets, and turnips.
How can one gain the benefit of spleen without harming the intestines?
Chew the spleen and discard it.
How can one gain the benefit of leeks without hurting the teeth?
Boil leeks and swallow them.
The warning about raw vegetables concerns the first meal after bloodletting.
R. Yitzhak forbids speaking with one who ate vegetables before four hours.
The reason is the smell.
R. Yitzhak also forbids eating raw vegetables before four hours.
Ameimar and Rav Ashi eat early raw vegetables; Mar Zutra abstains.
They challenge his abstention: if the problem is odor, why can he speak with them?
Mar Zutra follows the separate rule forbidding the eating itself.
Rav Hisda applies the warning about small animals to a goat below one-quarter growth.
Rav Pappa includes even fully grown small marsh fish among restorative creatures.
Rav Aha identifies the neck as restorative; Rava seeks meat near the slaughter site.
Does the teaching imply cabbage nourishes but does not heal?
A baraita names cabbage among remedies for the sick.
Cabbage serves even as nourishment, as well as healing.
How can turnips be harmful when Rava prized them for a meal?
The harm depends on lacking meat, wine, or sufficient cooking.
Rava asks how Rav Pappa counteracts turnips without abundant wine.
He uses wood: his wife cooked them thoroughly with many pieces of palm wood.
A baraita warns that small salted fish can be dangerous at particular intervals.
The warning applies to insufficiently roasted fish without beer afterward.
What does the mishna exclude by saying one drinks water for thirst?
Rav Idi begins the answer, continued on the next daf.

45a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The thirst qualification excludes water taken to clear food choking the throat.
R. Tarfon gives a different formula for the blessing over water.
Rava bar Rav Hanan asks which opinion governs practice.
Observe the practice of the people.
The preceding chapter concludes.
The mishna requires three joint diners to make a zimmun and lists permitted foods and diners who count.
Those who ate prohibited untithed or unredeemed food, an insufficient amount, or a gentile do not count.
Women, slaves, and minors do not combine with the men for this zimmun.
The mishna disputes whether an olive-bulk or egg-bulk is the minimum meal.
What is the scriptural source for zimmun?
Rav Asi cites the invitation to praise God together.
R. Abbahu cites the call to give praise to God.
Rav Hanan derives that one answering amen must not speak louder than the leader.
R. Shimon ben Pazi cites Moses and God to limit the translator’s volume.
Why does the verse specify a voice?
It means a voice matching that of Moses.
A baraita confirms that the reader and translator should match their volumes.
Rav and R. Yohanan dispute whether two diners may voluntarily make a zimmun.
The mishna specifies three diners, implying two may not make a zimmun.
Three are obligated; the proposed two-person zimmun is optional.
A baraita forbids three diners to separate, suggesting two cannot form a zimmun.
A three-person group already incurred an obligatory zimmun.
A waiter may join two diners without permission but needs permission to join three, suggesting two are insufficient.
The Gemara begins to distinguish the waiter case, continuing on the next daf.

45b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The waiter may join two diners because they prefer an obligatory zimmun.
A baraita permits separate women’s or slaves’ zimmun but forbids mixing the groups.
Even many women are likened to two men for a quorum, yet may make their own zimmun.
Three women still constitute three separate participants.
Then why may women and slaves not join despite separate participants?
The mixed group is barred because of impropriety.
Rav’s rule about calling back a third diner appears to identify Rav as rejecting voluntary two-person zimmun.
The three already incurred an obligatory zimmun.
R. Yohanan allows one of two diners to fulfill Grace through the other, suggesting no two-person zimmun.
Why teach this, when hearing a blessing without responding already fulfills the obligation?
R. Zeira infers that the two have no zimmun between them.
Western Sages permit voluntary two-person zimmun; perhaps they learned it from R. Yohanan.
They might have learned it from Rav before he reached Babylonia.
Rav permits a three-person zimmun when a diner has left but can be called back.
Abaye requires the absent diner to answer the call.
Mar Zutra requires physical presence for a ten-person zimmun invoking God’s name.
Rav Ashi reasons that nine resemble ten more closely than two resemble three.
The law follows Mar Zutra because God’s name should not be invoked with fewer than ten present.
Two learned diners should each say Grace separately.
If one diner is unlearned, the learned diner may recite for both.
One diner interrupts for two others to form zimmun; two do not interrupt for one.
Rav Pappa and another interrupted for his son.
Rav Pappa went beyond the strict requirement.
Three equally learned Sages wonder whether, without a senior leader, separate blessings are preferable.
Mareimar says their separate blessings fulfilled Grace but not zimmun.
A missed zimmun cannot be made up after Grace.
How does a newcomer answer when finding a group reciting zimmun?
Rav Zevid says to bless; Rav Pappa says to answer amen.
There is no dispute: respond with a blessing after “let us bless,” and amen after “blessed be.”
Two baraitot disagree whether answering amen after one’s own blessing is laudable.
It is proper after the Jerusalem blessing, but improper after other blessings.
Abaye answers aloud to signal that workers may stop before the later, rabbinic blessing.
Rav Ashi answers softly so people will not slight that later blessing.

46a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: R. Abbahu hosts a feast when R. Zeira recovers.
The host asks R. Zeira to break bread.
R. Zeira cites R. Yohanan’s rule that the host breaks bread, and the host does so.
The host then asks R. Zeira to recite Grace.
R. Zeira cites Rav Huna’s rule that the one who breaks bread recites Grace.
Whose view supports the host’s request?
R. Yohanan says the host breaks bread generously while a guest recites Grace to bless the host.
The guest asks that the host avoid shame in this world and the next.
Rabbi adds wishes for success and protection from sin.
Where does the zimmun formula end?
Rav Nahman ends it at “let us bless”; Rav Sheshet includes the first blessing of Grace.
Two baraitot give different numbers of blessings; the proposal assumes the final blessing is rabbinic.
Their differing counts may reflect the dispute about whether zimmun includes the first blessing.
Each Sage can reconcile both baraitot with his own view.
Rav Nahman explains the shorter count by the abbreviated Grace said by laborers.
Rav Sheshet explains the longer count by treating the final blessing as scriptural.
Rav Yosef argues the final blessing is not scriptural because laborers omit it.
Rav Yitzhak argues its opening and closing form shows it is not scriptural.
A baraita lists the usual opening and closing forms and their exceptions.

46b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The final blessing opens but does not close with “Blessed,” marking it as separate.
Rav Nahman argues that omitting the blessing in mourning shows it is not scriptural.
R. Akiva instead names the true Judge.
Does that mean the true Judge is omitted under the first opinion?
The first opinion includes “who is good and does good” as well.
Mar Zutra combines the blessing of God’s goodness with acceptance of judgment in mourning.
Where does a diner resume after interrupting for a zimmun?
Rav Zevid says to return to the beginning.
The Rabbis and the final ruling say to resume where he stopped.
The Exilarch describes Persian seating customs, placing the greater diner centrally.
Rav Sheshet asks how the greater diner can converse with one seated above him.
Persian diners communicate with gestures.
Where does the first washing begin?
With the greatest diner.
Must the greatest then wait with washed hands for everyone?
His table is brought immediately.
Where does the final washing begin?
With the least significant diner.
Must the greatest then wait with soiled hands?
His table remains until the water reaches him.
Rav Sheshet cites a baraita prescribing the Jewish order of reclining.
The baraita orders washings and assigns Grace to the greatest among the last five to wash.
This supports Rav’s rule that the first to wash at the end leads Grace.
Rabbi tells Rav to wash first, indicating that Rav will lead Grace.
A baraita begins a rule about when diners should not defer to rank.

47a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The previous rule also withholds deference during the final handwashing.
Ravin passes Abaye on the road but offers him precedence at the synagogue door.
Ravin cites R. Yohanan’s rule to defer at a doorway with a mezuzah.
Would that exclude synagogue and study hall doorways without mezuzot?
The rule concerns a doorway fit for a mezuzah.
Rav says diners may not eat before the bread breaker tastes.
Rav Safra insists on his teacher’s exact word, “taste.”
The distinction teaches precise quotation of a teacher.
Two sharing a dish wait for each other; the bread breaker takes first unless deferring to a superior.
Rabba bar bar Hana teaches that bread breaking waits for the respondents’ amen.
Rav Hisda requires waiting only for most respondents.
Why does an unfinished amen from the minority not likewise delay the blessing?
An excessively prolonged amen is treated as an error.
A baraita forbids hasty, cut-off, or uninformed amen and careless blessing.
Ben Azzai warns about defective amen and praises a properly prolonged amen.
Rav says a late diner cannot join their zimmun because they have finished eating.
Shmuel says they could still eat if appealing food came, so the meal is not over.
Rav’s students expect the newly arrived Rav Aha to lead Grace.
Rav Aha argues that a principal diner, rather than the greatest person, should lead.
The final ruling assigns Grace to the greatest, even if he arrived last.
How can one who ate demai count if that produce is forbidden?
He could relinquish his property and eat demai as a pauper.
Rav Huna reports Beit Shammai’s dissent about feeding demai to paupers and soldiers.
Why specify first tithe after its teruma was removed?
Even when the Levite took grain on stalks before teruma gedola, the tithe can be permitted.
The verse requires the Levite to separate a tenth of the tithe, not teruma gedola.
Rav Pappa asks why the same exemption does not apply after the grain is piled.
Abaye begins a scriptural distinction, continued on the next daf.

47b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The verse requires teruma gedola after grain has been piled, not while still on stalks.
Why specify redeemed second tithe and consecrated property?
Paying their principal redeems them even if the additional fifth remains unpaid.

ranges.en: One who eats only a fig may join zimmun but cannot discharge others without eating grain.

Moses instituted the food blessing with manna; Joshua instituted the land blessing upon entry.

A baraita orders the four blessings and places Shabbat’s mention in the Jerusalem blessing.

What is the scriptural source for Grace after Meals?
A baraita reads the blessings of food, zimmun, land, Jerusalem, and God’s goodness from the verse.
An inference from blessing after satiety yields blessing before eating.

Rabbi derives the earlier food blessing from “that He gave you.”
R. Yitzhak derives a blessing before bread from a reading of “bless your bread.”

R. Yohanan says Saul’s reign could not begin before Samuel’s ended.

His student instead links God’s giving of land and Torah through matching verses.

R. Yehuda ben Beteira derives Torah and Jerusalem from two readings of “the good.”
R. Eliezer requires mention of the good land and David’s dynasty in Grace.

ranges.en: Circumcision is said to have thirteen covenants, more than Torah’s three.

Omitting covenant, Torah, or David’s house prevents fulfillment of Grace.
R. Il’a transmits the same requirement.
Sages dispute whether the final blessing needs God’s sovereignty, tied to whether it is rabbinic.
R. Yosei permits concluding the Jerusalem blessing with “who saves Israel.”
Does this exclude the usual conclusion about building Jerusalem?
It permits the alternative as well.
Rabba bar Rav Huna begins with one theme and ends with two.
Rav Hisda cites Rabbi’s ban on ending a blessing with two themes.
Rabbi states that a blessing should not end with two themes.
Levi cites “for the land and for the food.”
It means the land producing food.
Levi cites “for the land and for the fruit.”
It means the land producing fruit.
Israel sanctifies the festivals and new moons, so each formula is one theme.
Levi cites the combined Shabbat and festival conclusion.
Rabbi treats that formula as an exception.
Why is the disputed conclusion different?
Jerusalem’s rebuilding and Israel’s redemption are separate themes.
Why should a blessing avoid two themes?
Distinct commandments should not be bundled.
What conclusion should the Jerusalem blessing have?
Rav Sheshet aligns its conclusion with whether the opening names Israel or Jerusalem.
Rav Nahman always allows “builds Jerusalem,” linking its rebuilding to Israel’s ingathering.
Rav Hisda recalls Rav Sheshet objecting to his Grace at the Exilarch’s house.
He had omitted covenant, Torah, and sovereignty.

R. Zeira faults him for choosing Rav against many other authorities.
R. Yohanan requires God’s sovereignty in the final blessing.
What new rule is taught, given R. Yohanan’s earlier statement?

Why not require a third mention for the land blessing, or none for the adjacent Jerusalem blessing?

Rav Pappa instead requires two added mentions besides the final blessing’s own.
Rav Giddel gives an abridged Shabbat formula when Shabbat was omitted in Grace.
He gives a parallel formula when a festival was omitted.
For New Moon he gives a formula, but R. Zeira is unsure of its exact wording and source.
The next account begins with Rav Nahman’s omission of a special Grace formula.

ranges.en: Rav Nahman repeats Grace after omitting Shabbat, following Rav’s rule.

Yes: Rav says to repeat Grace after such an error.
But Rav Huna permits a short replacement blessing.
It works only before the final blessing has begun.
Why does the mishna require an olive-bulk for R. Meir but an egg-bulk for R. Yehuda when another source reverses them?

There R. Meir requires an egg-bulk while R. Yehuda requires only an olive-bulk.
R. Yohanan reverses the attributions in one source.

For consecrated meat, they compare the return duty to either impurity or prohibition.
The mishna gives different zimmun invitations for groups of three or ten.

The group answers with a blessing corresponding to the leader’s formula.

R. Akiva cites the synagogue’s uniform invitation regardless of group size.

The Gemara begins a reinterpretation on the next daf.

ranges.en: “Let us bless” is allowed and preferred because it includes the leader.

A request is different.
Another verse invites a full request.
That invitation concerns Torah learning.

There the divine referent is obvious.

Why does the mishna both equate ten with ten thousand and prescribe different larger formulas?

Rava chides him for disputing customary wording that accommodates both opinions.

Even three who have sat together but not yet eaten may not separate.
Another reading includes diners eating from separate loaves.
A further reading includes three diners arriving from three different groups.
Rav Hisda limits this to original groups of at least three.
Rava begins a further qualification on the next daf.

ranges.en: Three diners from prior groups form a new zimmun only if their original groups did not already include them.
Rava compares a divided bed that regains susceptibility to impurity only after reassembly.

A shared waiter can join two otherwise separate dining groups.
R. Eliezer treats undiluted wine as fruit juice for blessing and handwashing.

The Gemara assigns it to R. Eliezer.

The teaching may predate that proclamation or have another role, continued on the next daf.

A vessel does not contaminate a person.

A second-degree table affects ordinary food only through liquids.

ranges.en: Permitted Shabbat flames for childbirth or illness can receive the later blessing.

If a new flame replaced the old, carrying a flame on Shabbat should not incur liability.
The old flame persists, but blessing concerns its permitted new addition.

The Sages barred it because of the original gentile flame.
A baraita links blessing over a city’s fire to a Jewish majority.
The two clauses conflict about a city split evenly.
An even split permits blessing; the second clause mirrors the first clause’s wording.
A child carrying a torch is checked for Jewish identity before blessing.

Just after sunset, an adult carrier is evidently gentile, but a child may have taken the torch by chance.
A furnace-sized flame seen outside the city may receive a blessing.
Baraitot disagree about blessing over a furnace fire.
Its early heating stage differs from its later lighting use.
Baraitot also disagree about an oven or stove fire.
Again the early heating stage differs from the later use.
Baraitot disagree about a synagogue or study-hall flame.
A light for an honored person differs from one used for illumination.
Alternatively, a caretaker’s presence determines whether it serves for light.
Alternatively, moonlight determines whether the caretaker needs the flame.
Beit Hillel favor one public fire blessing to honor God before the assembled group.
Why does Beit Shammai require each person to bless separately?
A common blessing interrupts study; Rabban Gamliel’s house likewise avoided interruptions.

Bathroom spices and cleansing oil are not blessed for fragrance.
Must a scent be intended for fragrance to receive a blessing?
A perfumer’s shop receives repeated blessings on separate visits, though the scent seems commercial.
The seller wants passersby to enjoy the scent and enter.

Together with garment perfuming, those uses form a majority not intended for fragrance.

53b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna requires some benefit from the havdala flame.

Seeing without using seems to mean being too far away.
The flame might instead be dimming.
Smoldering coals qualify when they can ignite a wood chip unaided.
Which spelling describes the dimming coals?
A verse supports the spelling with ayin.
Rava requires actual benefit from the flame.
The benefit must allow distinguishing similar coins or weights.
The Sages describe the lights from which they made the blessing.

All agree an intentional failure to say Grace requires returning to the eating place.
Does the mishna not already say “forgot”?

The houses dispute whether one who descended from a high place must return to bless.
Two students’ different returns are followed by a gold purse for one and a lion for the other.
Rabba bar bar Hana returns by telling his caravan he forgot a golden dove, and finds one.

The dove evokes Israel’s protection through commandments.
R. Yohanan and Reish Lakish give hunger and thirst measures for digestion.
A report gives Reish Lakish’s measure as walking four mil.
The measures differ for large and small meals.
How can one answer amen without hearing the whole blessing and thereby fulfill an obligation?
The rule concerns one who did not eat with the blessing group.
Rav and Rav Huna urge their sons to lead the blessing.
A baraita says answering amen is more rewarded than reciting the blessing.
R. Nehorai compares the responder to the warriors who secure victory.

Sages disagree whether cleansing oil is required before Grace and whether dirty hands disqualify.
Rav Nahman cites a verse read as first washing, final washing, oil, and Grace.
The chapter concludes.

ranges.en: The mishna prescribes a blessing at a place of miracles for Israel.

A new house or possessions prompt the blessing for reaching this time.

Love God with both inclinations, one’s life, wealth, and every measure received.
The mishna requires reverence near and on the Temple Mount.

What is the source for blessing on a miracle?

A baraita lists miracle sites that call for thanksgiving.

ranges.en: The Arnon tradition describes an ambush crushed as the Ark passed, prompting Israel’s song.

R. Yohanan cites God remembering Abraham while rescuing Lot.
How could Jericho’s wall be swallowed when the verse says it fell?
Its great width made its collapse a sinking into place.
Four who were saved must give thanks: seafarers, desert travelers, the healed, and released prisoners.
Psalm 107 describes sailors rescued from a storm and then thanking God.
The psalm likewise describes desert travelers led to safety.
It describes the sick healed after crying out.
It describes prisoners brought out of darkness.
What blessing is recited?
Rav Yehuda gives the blessing for God’s good acts.
Abaye requires a gathering of ten, citing the psalm’s congregation.
Mar Zutra adds two Sages, citing its assembly of elders.
Rav Ashi asks whether all ten must be Sages.
The verse instead says a congregation of people.
Perhaps the ten people are joined by two further Sages; the objection remains difficult.
After Rav Yehuda recovers, visitors bless God and he says their words exempted him.
Did Abaye not require ten listeners?
Ten people were present.
But Rav Yehuda himself did not speak the blessing.
His answer of amen counts as his thanks.
Rav Yehuda lists people said to need protection, with additional variants.
He names prayer, the table, and the bathroom as three practices prolonged for long life.
Is prolonged prayer truly beneficial? A contrary teaching begins on the next daf.

55a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Expecting prolonged prayer to be answered leads to heartache and scrutiny of one’s sins.
Long prayer is beneficial when one does not insist on its acceptance.
One may instead increase supplication.
A long meal gives a poor visitor a chance to receive food; a verse links altar and table.
The Sages say a person’s table now atones as the altar once did.
A baraita warns that lingering improperly in the bathroom can be harmful.
The warning concerns straining while lingering, not taking time without strain.
R. Yehuda describes regularly using the many bathrooms along his route.
Rav Yehuda says refusing a Torah reading or blessing, or acting superior, shortens life.
Verses support the Torah and blessing cases; Joseph’s early death is tied to superiority.
Three things require mercy: a good ruler, year, and dream, each linked to Scripture.
R. Yohanan says God proclaims famine, plenty, and a good leader, citing verses.
R. Yitzhak derives consultation before appointing a communal leader from Bezalel’s selection.
God, Moses, and Israel each affirm Bezalel’s suitability.
Bezalel’s wisdom is shown when Moses reverses the Tabernacle’s construction order.
Bezalel reasons that a house must precede its vessels and restores the intended order.
Moses says Bezalel seems to have known God’s intention directly.
Shared words for wisdom, understanding, and knowledge connect Bezalel’s craft with creation.
R. Yohanan cites a verse that God grants wisdom to those already wise.
R. Abbahu offers a different verse about wisdom placed in wise hearts.
Rav Hisda says any dream is preferable to a fast, and an uninterpreted dream resembles unread mail.
He says dreams are not fulfilled wholly, and their sadness or joy may suffice.
Rav Yosef says even his good dream can be offset by its joy.
A bad dream can induce fear, even more than lashes.
Jeremiah compares dreams and prophecy to straw and grain.
What is the connection between straw and grain in the verse about dreams?
Like grain with straw, a dream cannot be free of empty material.
R. Berekhya says Joseph’s dream shows that only part of a dream is fulfilled.

55b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Joseph’s mother had already died when he dreamed of the moon bowing.
R. Levi says a good dream may take twenty-two years to be fulfilled, as Joseph’s did.
Joseph was seventeen at the dream, thirty before Pharaoh, then seven years of plenty and two of famine elapsed.
Rav Huna says a good person is not shown a good dream, nor a bad person a bad dream.
A baraita says David never saw a good dream and Ahitophel never saw a bad one.
A verse and its interpretation say a righteous person is spared frightening dreams, apparently opposing Rav Huna.
Others saw troubling dreams about David; he did not see them himself.
If seeing no dream is good, why does R. Zeira call seven dreamless nights a sign of evil?
David saw dreams but did not know what he had seen.
One distressed by a dream should go before three people.
Why invite interpretation when Rav Hisda says an uninterpreted dream is like an unread letter?
He should have three people make the dream good by declaring and repeatedly blessing its good outcome.
The three then recite three verses each about reversal, redemption, and peace.
Three cited verses describe turning mourning or a curse into joy or blessing.
Three cited verses speak of redemption or rescue.
Three cited verses speak of peace.
A sage advises someone who cannot recall a dream to pray during the priestly blessing.
The prayer asks God to strengthen good dreams and heal and transform troubling ones.
He should finish with the congregation’s amen, or recite a shorter prayer for peace.
Another sage gives a hand gesture and declaration for someone fearing the evil eye on entering a city.
Joseph’s blessing is read as placing his descendants above the evil eye.
R. Yosei derives the same protection from the comparison of Joseph’s descendants to fish hidden in water.
One concerned about one’s own evil eye should look at the left side of the nose.
Another sage advises disclosing illness after the first day, lest disclosure initially weaken one’s fortune.
Rava initially concealed illness, then announced it so friends would pray and enemies rejoice.
A verse warns against rejoicing at an enemy’s fall, supporting Rava’s hope that such joy would end his suffering.
Shmuel cited a verse dismissing false dreams after bad dreams, but questioned it after good dreams.
The verse about God speaking in a dream challenges a blanket claim that dreams are false.
Rava asks how the verse about divine dreams fits the verse about false dreams.
Dreams conveyed by an angel differ from false dreams conveyed by a demon.
R. Bena’a reports that twenty-four different interpretations of his dream all came true, suggesting dreams follow the interpreter’s words.
Is the saying that dreams follow the mouth actually a biblical verse?
R. Elazar grounds it in the cupbearer’s report that Joseph’s interpretations came to pass.
Rava limits this principle to interpretations fitting the dream, citing Joseph’s interpretation of each man’s dream.
How did the baker know Joseph’s interpretation of the cupbearer’s dream was good?
Each official was shown his own dream and the interpretation of the other’s dream.
A verse that comes to mind upon waking is a minor prophecy, says R. Yohanan.
He lists three dreams likely to be fulfilled: a morning dream, a friend’s dream about someone, and one interpreted within a dream.
A further view includes a repeated dream, citing Pharaoh’s doubled dream.
A person dreams only of thoughts already in the heart, according to R. Shmuel bar Nahmani.
Verses in Daniel link the king’s dreams to thoughts that arose on his bed and in his heart.
Rava observes that people do not dream of a golden palm or an elephant passing through a needle’s eye.

56a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The emperor asks R. Yehoshua to predict what he will dream.
R. Yehoshua describes a feared Persian captivity; the emperor thinks of it all day and dreams it that night.
King Shapur likewise asks Shmuel to predict his dream.
Shmuel describes Roman captivity; Shapur dwells on it all day and dreams it at night.
Bar Haddaya interprets dreams favorably for a fee and unfavorably without one; Abaye pays, but Rava does not.
Abaye and Rava report dreaming of the verse about an ox slaughtered before its owner.
Bar Haddaya reads it as loss and sorrow for Rava.
He reads the same verse as profit and overwhelming joy for Abaye.
They report the verse about bearing children who are taken away.
He gives Rava its adverse, literal sense.
He tells Abaye his many daughters will marry away from home.
They report the verse about sons and daughters given to another people.
For Abaye, it means his wife’s relatives will be chosen for their children’s marriages.
For Rava, it means his wife will die and a stepmother will take charge of his children; a teaching identifies the other people as a stepmother.
They report a dream verse bidding one eat bread joyfully.
For Abaye, the verse points to profitable business and a joyful meal.
For Rava, it points to loss and reciting Scripture to calm his fear.
They report a verse about carrying much seed into the field.
Bar Haddaya applies the favorable beginning to Abaye and the adverse ending to Rava.
They report a verse about olive trees across their borders.
Again he applies its beginning to Abaye and its ending to Rava.
They report the verse about all peoples seeing God’s name upon them.
Abaye is told he will become a famed and feared head of the academy.
Rava is told he will be suspected after a royal theft; the next day the theft and arrest occur.
They describe lettuce seen on the mouth of barrels.
He predicts expanding business for Abaye but bitterness for Rava.
They describe meat seen on the mouth of barrels.
He predicts desirable wine for Abaye but spoiled wine for Rava.
They describe a barrel hanging from a palm tree.
He predicts Abaye’s business will rise but Rava’s wares will sell cheaply.
They describe a pomegranate growing on a barrel.
He predicts flourishing business for Abaye but souring business for Rava.
They describe a barrel falling into a pit.
He predicts sought-after merchandise for Abaye but ruined merchandise for Rava.
They describe a braying donkey foal by their heads.
He predicts Abaye’s leadership but tells Rava a letter has vanished from his tefillin; Rava’s objection elicits the precise letter.
Rava comes alone and reports that his outer door fell in a dream.
Bar Haddaya predicts Rava’s wife will die.
Rava reports dreaming of his teeth falling out.
Bar Haddaya predicts the death of Rava’s children.
Rava reports two flying doves.
Bar Haddaya predicts two divorces.
Rava reports two turnip heads.
Bar Haddaya predicts two blows.
Two blind men fighting in the study hall strike Rava twice, as foretold; he refuses a third blow.
After paying the interpreter, Rava reports a fallen wall.
Bar Haddaya now predicts property without boundaries.
Rava reports Abaye’s house falling and covering him with dust.
He predicts Rava will inherit leadership of Abaye’s academy.
Rava reports his own house falling and its bricks being taken.
He predicts Rava’s teachings will spread widely.
Rava reports his head splitting and his brain falling out.
He benignly interprets this as a feather falling from a pillow.
Rava reports hearing the Egyptian Hallel in his dream.
He predicts miracles for Rava.
On a boat, Bar Haddaya fears Rava’s miracle; Rava finds his book saying dreams follow the interpreter’s words.
Rava confronts him and forgives all but the prediction about Rav Hisda’s daughter, then curses him with merciless capture.
Bar Haddaya fears a sage’s justified curse and decides on exile to atone.
In Rome a royal wardrobe keeper reports dreaming of a needle in his finger.
Bar Haddaya asks for a fee and gives no interpretation when refused.
The keeper reports a worm between two fingers.
Bar Haddaya again refuses to interpret without payment.
The keeper reports a worm on his whole hand.
Bar Haddaya finally says the worm signifies destruction of all the royal silk.
As the keeper faces execution, he identifies Bar Haddaya as one who withheld the warning; the court blames the interpreter’s greed.

56b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The royal court executes Bar Haddaya by tying his legs to two bent cedar trees and releasing them.
Ben Dama asks R. Yishmael about his dream of two fallen cheeks.
R. Yishmael says two Roman units plotting against him have died.
Bar Kappara tells Rabbi his nose fell off in a dream.
Rabbi reads this as anger departing from him.
Bar Kappara reports that his hands were severed.
Rabbi says he will no longer need manual labor.
Bar Kappara reports his legs were severed.
Rabbi says he will ride a horse.
Bar Kappara reports hearing that he would die in Adar before Nisan.
Rabbi reads the words as dying with honor and avoiding temptation.
A heretic reports dreaming of watering olives with oil.
R. Yishmael says the dream points to incest with his mother.
The heretic reports plucking a star.
R. Yishmael says he kidnapped an Israelite.
The heretic reports swallowing a star.
R. Yishmael says he sold the captive and spent the money.
The heretic reports his eyes kissing each other.
R. Yishmael accuses him of incest with his sister.
The heretic reports kissing the moon.
R. Yishmael says he had relations with an Israelite woman.
The heretic reports treading in myrtle shade.
R. Yishmael says he had relations with a betrothed woman.
He reports the shade above him and tree below.
R. Yishmael says his sexual conduct was inverted.
He reports ravens circling his bed.
R. Yishmael says his wife was unfaithful with many men.
He reports doves circling his bed.
R. Yishmael says the dreamer had relations with many women.
He reports holding two doves that flew away.
R. Yishmael says he married two women and released them without divorce documents.
He reports peeling eggs.
R. Yishmael says he stripped the dead of clothing.
The dreamer denies this last claim, but a woman identifies the deceased man’s cloak on him.
The dreamer says he was told his father left property in Cappadocia.
With no Cappadocian connection, R. Yishmael reads the name as a clue to money in the tenth beam.
The dreamer finds the coins in that beam.
R. Hanina says a well in a dream means peace, citing Isaac’s servants finding living water.
R. Natan reads the well as Torah through verses associating both with life.
Rava says the well signifies actual life.
R. Hanan names river, bird, and pot as signs of peace, drawing on verses for each.
R. Hanina limits the favorable pot to one without meat, citing a verse where meat in a pot signals harm.
For a river dream, R. Yehoshua ben Levi advises saying its peaceful verse before a threatening one comes to mind.
For a bird dream, say the verse of divine protection before the verse of a bird wandering.
For a pot dream, say the verse of peace before a verse of judgment involving a pot.
For grapes, say the favorable verse about Israel before the verse about poisonous grapes.
For a mountain, say the verse of good tidings before the verse of lamentation.
For a shofar, say the verse of gathering before the verse of a war alarm.
For a dog, say the verse of Israel’s safety before the verse of greedy dogs.
For a lion, say the verse of prophecy before the verse of a destroying lion.
For a shave, say the verse of Joseph’s release before the verse of Samson losing strength.
For a well, say the verse of living water before the verse likening wickedness to a well.
For a reed, say the verse protecting a bruised reed before the verse about an unreliable reed.
The Sages connect a reed with acquiring wisdom and reeds with acquiring understanding.
R. Zeira names four similar-sounding objects auspicious in dreams.
A baraita associates seeing a pumpkin with strong reverence for Heaven.
For an ox, recite its favorable verse of majesty before the verse about a goring ox.
A baraita gives five ox dream omens: wealth, scholarly sons, suffering, travel, and advancement.
A baraita instead says riding an ox in a dream means death.
The favorable case is riding the ox; the dire case is the ox riding the person.
Seeing a donkey means salvation, supported by the verse of a king riding one.
A cat dream has a favorable or unfavorable wordplay depending on its local name.
White grapes are favorable in or out of season; black grapes are favorable only in season.
A white horse is favorable whether still or running, while a running red horse is unfavorable.
A dream of Ishmael son of Abraham means one’s prayer will be heard.
A camel dream means a death decree was averted.
Two sages offer verses whose wordplay connects the camel with being brought up or spared death.
A dream of Pinehas or an elephant signifies miracles; multiple elephants signify many miracles.
A baraita instead excludes elephants and monkeys from good animal omens.
The Gemara begins a distinction to reconcile the elephant reports.

57a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A saddled elephant is a good dream omen; an unsaddled one is not.
Dreaming of Huna signifies a miracle, and of names with two nuns, many miracles.
A written eulogy in a dream signifies that Heaven spared the dreamer.
Answering “May His great name be blessed” in a dream promises a share in the World-to-Come.
Reciting Shema in a dream signals worthiness for the Divine Presence, though the generation is unworthy.
Putting on tefillin in a dream portends greatness, supported by a verse and its interpretation.
Dreaming of prayer is favorable if the prayer was not yet finished.
Dreamed relations with one’s mother signify understanding through a wordplay on “if.”
Dreamed relations with a betrothed woman signify Torah through a wordplay on inheritance and betrothal.
Dreamed relations with a sister signify wisdom through the verse calling wisdom a sister.
Dreamed relations with an unknown married woman signify the World-to-Come only if she was not on one’s mind before sleep.
Wheat in a dream signifies peace, as both appear in a verse.
Barley signifies removal of sin by wordplay; R. Zeira recalls seeing it before moving to Israel.
A laden vine signifies that one’s wife will not miscarry, like the fruitful vine in a psalm.
A vine branch signifies the Messiah, linked to Jacob’s blessing.
A fig tree signifies retained Torah, supported by the verse about tending a fig.
Small or large pomegranates signify the growth of business.
A split pomegranate signifies Torah for a scholar and mitzvot for an unlearned person, with verses for each.
Olive fruit signifies growing business; olive trees signify many children, as in the psalm.
Another view says an olive tree signifies a good name, based on Jeremiah’s olive image.
Olive oil signifies the light of Torah, linked to the oil for the lamp.
Dates signify the end of sins through a wordplay on the verse.
A goat or goats signify blessed year or years, linked to a verse about goats’ milk.
Myrtle signifies success or inheritance, provided the dreamer sees it still on its stem.
An etrog signifies honor before God through the verse’s word for beauty.
A lulav signifies a single heart directed to the Father in heaven.
A goose signifies wisdom; Rav Ashi recounts a goose dream before becoming head of the academy.
Roosters signify sons, while a hen signifies a fine garden and rejoicing.
Eggs signify a pending request; broken eggs and other fragile objects signify its fulfillment.
Entering a city signifies fulfilled wishes, supported by a verse about the desired haven.
Shaving one’s head is favorable; shaving both head and beard favors the whole family.
A small boat signifies a good name for the dreamer, a large boat for the family, if it rides high.
Relieving oneself is favorable if the dream does not include wiping afterward.
Climbing a roof signifies ascent; Abaye and Rava say later descent does not undo it.
Tearing one’s clothes in a dream signifies the tearing up of one’s decree.
Nakedness signifies freedom from sin in Babylonia but lack of mitzvot in Israel.
Being guarded or chained signifies protection, but an ordinary rope does not.
Entering a marsh signifies academy leadership; a forest signifies leadership of advanced students.
Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua each receive the positions associated with their dreams.
Another account distinguishes their positions by whether a drum hung in the marsh dream.
Rav Ashi reports dreaming of a marsh and drum before his own leadership.
A tanna says dream bloodletting signifies forgiveness of sins.
Another baraita says dream bloodletting means sins are counted.
They are counted for forgiveness.
A snake dream signifies accessible livelihood; a bite doubles it, while killing it loses it.
Rav Sheshet argues that killing the snake should increase livelihood even more.
The Gemara attributes his positive reading to his own snake dream.
Drinks are favorable in dreams except ambiguous wine; verses connect wine with joy or bitter sorrow.
R. Yohanan says wine is always favorable for a Torah scholar, citing wisdom’s invitation to drink.

57b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: R. Yohanan again calls a verse falling into one’s mouth upon waking a minor prophecy.
Dreams of David, Solomon, or Ahab respectively signify piety, wisdom, or calamity.
Dreams of Kings, Ezekiel, Isaiah, or Jeremiah signify greatness, wisdom, comfort, or calamity.
Dreams of Psalms, Proverbs, or Job signify piety, wisdom, or calamity.
Dreams of Song of Songs, Ecclesiastes, Lamentations, or Esther signify piety, wisdom, calamity, or a miracle.
Dreams of Rabbi, R. Elazar ben Azarya, or R. Yishmael ben Elisha signify wisdom, wealth, or calamity.
Dreams of Ben Azzai, Ben Zoma, or Aher signify piety, wisdom, or calamity.
Animals are generally auspicious in dreams except an elephant, monkey, or ape.
The earlier teaching calls an elephant dream a sign of a miracle.
The favorable elephant is saddled; the unfavorable one is unsaddled.
Metal objects are generally favorable except destructive tools seen with handles.
Fruits are generally favorable except unripe dates.
Vegetables are generally favorable except turnip heads.
Rav says a dream of turnip heads preceded his becoming wealthy.
Rav saw them attached to their stems.
Colors are favorable except tekhelet; birds are favorable except three named nocturnal birds.
A mnemonic introduces lists about the body, the World-to-Come, and mental ease.
Three foods enter the body without benefiting it: cherries, poor dates, and unripe dates.
Washing, anointing, and bodily use benefit the body without entering it.
Shabbat, sunlight, and bodily use are foretastes of the World-to-Come.
What kind of bodily use is meant? Intercourse seems to weaken the body.
The reference is to relieving oneself.
Pleasant sound, sight, and smell restore one’s mind.
A fine dwelling, spouse, and utensils broaden one’s mind.
Fire, honey, Shabbat, sleep, and dreams are each described as one-sixtieth of a greater reality.
Six signs favor a sick person: sneezing, sweat, diarrhea, emission, sleep, and dreaming.
Verses support each of the six favorable signs for the sick.
Six foods or organs, with small fish added by some, promote lasting recovery from illness.
Ten foods or acts may cause a recovered person to relapse; some add nuts and cucumbers.
R. Yishmael’s school explains “cucumbers” as a wordplay on their harm to the body.
A verse and tradition say the tables of Antoninus and Rabbi always had cucumbers, suggesting they are desirable.
Large cucumbers are harmful; small ones are the prized kind.
A deceased person in a dream may signal peace, but taking vessels from the house is unfavorable.
Rav Pappa limits the warning to shoes or sandals and lists exceptions to favorable items taken or given by the dead.
The mishna introduces a blessing for a site from which idolatry has been removed.
A baraita prescribes a blessing for seeing the idol Mercury.
At a place cleared of idolatry, one blesses God and prays for its removal across Israel and for worshippers’ return.
Outside Israel one need not include the request about the worshippers’ hearts.
R. Shimon ben Elazar includes the request abroad too, citing future worship by all peoples.
Rav Hamnuna lists five blessings on seeing sites in ruined Babylonia.
The ruins of Babylonia or Nebuchadnezzar’s house have distinct blessings.
Daniel’s lion den or the furnace of the three companions calls for a blessing for ancestral miracles.
Seeing Mercury calls for a blessing about God’s patience with transgressors.
A place stripped of its earth calls for a blessing that God decrees and fulfills.
Rava urged earth-carrying donkeys to hurry in fulfilling the decree against Babylonia.
Mar son of Ravina threw Babylonian earth away to enact the verse about sweeping it away.
Rav Ashi says he arrived at all five blessings independently without hearing Rav Hamnuna’s teaching.

58a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: R. Yirmeya says Babylonia’s curse harmed its neighbors, while Samaria’s benefited hers.
Verses describe ruined Babylonia as a harmful wetland and Samaria as ground for vineyards.
Rav Hamnuna gives distinct responses to seeing a multitude of Israel or of gentiles.
The blessing over Israel’s multitude praises the One who knows unlike minds and faces.
Ben Zoma sees a multitude at the Temple Mount and blesses God for their individual minds and service.
Ben Zoma contrasts Adam’s long process for making bread with finding bread prepared each morning.
He likewise contrasts Adam’s labor for clothing with the many workers who supply his needs.
A good guest credits the host for all the food and effort expended on the guest’s behalf.
A bad guest minimizes the food received and says the host worked only for his own family.
Verses are applied to the appreciative and unappreciative guest.
A verse about Yishai is read as his moving and teaching among multitudes.
Ulla says Babylonia has no qualifying multitude; its minimum is six hundred thousand.
The blessing for seeing sages differs for Jewish sages and sages of other nations.
The blessing for seeing kings likewise distinguishes kings of Israel and other nations.
R. Yohanan urges greeting even foreign kings to recognize the difference between their reign and Israel’s.
Blind Rav Sheshet goes to greet a king and tells a skeptic he can discern the arrival better.
The skeptic mistakes the first two noisy troops for the king, while Rav Sheshet rejects both.
Rav Sheshet identifies the king with the arrival of the quiet third procession.
The skeptic asks how Rav Sheshet knew.
Rav Sheshet cites Elijah’s revelation in a still small voice after wind, earthquake, and fire.
As Rav Sheshet blesses the king, the skeptic challenges blessing someone he cannot see.
Accounts differ over whether the skeptic’s friends blinded him or Rav Sheshet caused his death.
R. Sheila flogs a man, who reports him to the king for judging without royal authority.
Questioned by the court, R. Sheila says the man had relations with a female donkey and claims witnesses.
Elijah appears as a human witness.
The officials ask why R. Sheila did not execute the man if the charge was proved.
R. Sheila says Jews in exile lack authority to execute and leaves judgment to the court.
R. Sheila recites the verse beginning “Yours, Lord, is the greatness.”
He tells the officials he praised earthly authority as a reflection of heavenly rule.
Pleased by his respect for royalty, the officials give him a staff and license to judge.
The accused asks whether God has worked a miracle for a liar.
R. Sheila defends his comparison by citing a verse that calls people donkeys.
Fearing another denunciation, R. Sheila invokes the rule about a pursuer and strikes the man.
After his rescue, R. Sheila undertakes to interpret the verse he had recited.
He reads “greatness” as creation, citing Job’s phrase about great works.
He reads “power” as the exodus, citing Israel’s sight of God’s great hand.
He reads “glory” as the sun and moon standing still for Joshua.
He reads “triumph” as Rome’s fall, citing Isaiah’s stained garments.
He reads “majesty” as the war at Arnon, citing the book of God’s wars.
He reads “all in heaven and earth” as the battle against Sisera, where stars fought.
He reads “kingdom” as the battle with Amalek, citing God’s throne.
He reads “exalted” as the war of Gog and Magog, citing Ezekiel.
R. Yohanan says even a local water official is appointed from heaven.
An alternative teaching in R. Akiva’s name assigns the verse’s terms to the sea, firstborn plague, Torah, Jerusalem, and Temple.

58b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita prescribes blessings or verses for inhabited and ruined houses of Israel and of other nations.
Passing the ruined home of Rav Hana bar Hanilai, Rav Hisda sighs.
Ulla asks why he sighs when Rav and R. Yohanan say sighing injures half or all the body, citing Ezekiel.
Rav Hisda recalls the home’s many cooks and its owner’s readiness to give discreetly to the poor.
Its four doors and grain set out during famine fed people without shame; its ruin warrants his sigh.
Ulla cites R. Yohanan’s teaching that righteous people’s homes were decreed to fall after the Temple’s ruin.
R. Yohanan also promises their restoration, comparing them to Zion in a psalm.
When Rav Hisda remains troubled, Ulla says a servant may be no better housed than his master.
On seeing Jewish graves, one blesses God for judgment in life, death, and resurrection.
Mar son of Ravina adds God’s knowledge of their number and the blessing of resurrection.
A verse from Jeremiah is said on seeing graves of other nations.
Seeing a friend after thirty days calls for Shehecheyanu; after twelve months, the resurrection blessing.
Rav cites a psalm to explain why twelve months makes a person forgotten from the heart.
Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua bless for meeting Rav Hanina son of Rav Ika.
Rav Hanina says he blessed for them also as for a multitude of Israel.
They marvel at his cleverness, look at him, and he dies.
R. Yehoshua ben Levi says to bless God for varied creatures when seeing spotted people.
A baraita lists spotted people among those prompting the blessing of the true Judge instead.
The differing blessings distinguish a condition present from birth from one acquired later.
A baraita gives blessings for unusual animals and for beautiful creatures or trees.
Shmuel identifies the mishna’s “zikin” as a comet.
Shmuel says a comet cannot pass Orion without destroying the world, despite his uncertainty about comets.
The Gemara objects that comets appear to cross Orion.
Their glow creates the appearance of a crossing.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua instead describes a torn firmament and light appearing through it.
Rav Ashi offers another appearance-based explanation involving stars on either side of Orion.
Shmuel asks why two verses list Orion and Pleiades in opposite orders.
Orion’s heat and Pleiades’ cold balance each other so the world can endure.
A tradition about Scorpio and a verse in Job further connect heavenly forces with human survival.
Shmuel explains Pleiades as about a hundred stars, whether clustered or scattered.
Rav Yehuda identifies Ash with the constellation called Yota.
The Gemara asks which stars Yota denotes and reports the tail of Aries or the head of Taurus.
A verse about Ash and her children favors the tail of Aries, continuing onto the next daf.

59a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Ursa Major seeks back the stars taken to fill Pleiades after two Pleiades stars were removed for the flood.
Why were the original stars not restored?
A pit cannot be filled by its own earth; a prosecutor cannot become an advocate.
Why not create two new stars?
A verse says there is nothing new under the sun.
Rav Nahman reads a verse as promising Ursa Major’s stars will one day return.
Rav Ketina identifies the mishna’s “zevaot” as earthquakes.
An earthquake occurs as Rav Ketina passes a necromancer, whom he asks its meaning.
The necromancer says God’s two tears for suffering Israel cause the earthquake.
Rav Ketina calls the explanation false because two tears should yield two quakes.
The Gemara says two quakes do occur; Rav Ketina withheld agreement to avoid encouraging followers.
Rav Ketina instead attributes quakes to God’s clapping, citing Ezekiel.
R. Natan attributes them to God’s sigh, citing another verse.
The Rabbis attribute them to a kick against the firmament, citing Jeremiah.
Rav Aha attributes them to God’s feet pressing beneath the throne, citing Isaiah.
Shmuel says thunder comes from clouds in the firmament, citing a psalm.
The Rabbis say thunder is water poured between clouds, citing Jeremiah.
Rav Aha says strong lightning in a cloud breaks hailstones.
Rav Ashi says wind blowing across hollow clouds makes the sound.
The observed sequence of lightning, rumbling, and rain supports Rav Aha.
Abaye says the mishna’s wind means a gale and maintains it does not begin at night.
Night gales appear to contradict Abaye’s rule.
They began during the day.
Abaye says gales do not last two hours, linking this to a verse about trouble.
Longer seeming gales have brief breaks between gusts.
Rava identifies the mishna’s lightning as a flash of light.
Rava lists certain lightning and cloud formations as ominous.
Their significance is to prompt prayer, and the warning applies at night, not in the morning.
R. Shmuel bar Yitzhak cites a verse to say morning clouds quickly pass.
Rav Pappa cites a proverb that morning rain can last all day.
Thick morning clouds differ from fleeting thin ones.
R. Alexandri says thunder straightens the heart through fear of God, citing Ecclesiastes.
He cites Ezekiel’s fall before a rainbow-like vision to support falling on one’s face at a rainbow.
In Israel this practice was criticized because it resembles worship of the rainbow.
Everyone agrees a rainbow calls for a blessing remembering the covenant.
R. Yishmael son of R. Yohanan ben Beroka gives the wording about faithfulness to the covenant.
Rav Pappa combines both blessing formulas.
Why single out hills and mountains as acts of creation when a verse says lightning too is made by God?
Abaye combines the formulations for all the phenomena.
Rava allows both blessings for lightning and thunder but only the creation blessing for hills and mountains.
R. Yehoshua ben Levi prescribes the creation blessing for a clear firmament.
Abaye says that occurs after a rainy night and a clearing northern wind.
Rafram bar Pappa reports Rav Hisda’s view that the firmament has not appeared pure since the Temple’s destruction.
