ranges.en: A baraita prescribes the creation blessing for the sun’s cycle, moon, planets, and constellations.
Abaye identifies the sun’s cycle with a twenty-eight-year alignment at the Nisan equinox.
Rami bar Abba defines the interval for seeing the great sea as thirty days.
The creation blessing for the Euphrates depends on seeing its original course above specified bridges.
Rami bar Abba prescribes the same blessing for the Tigris at the Shabistana bridge.
Rav Ashi explains Tigris and Euphrates by wordplays on their waters’ qualities.
Rava attributes Mehoza’s sharpness, redness, and shifting eyes to water, daytime intimacy, and dark homes.
The mishna’s blessing for rain seems to differ from R. Abbahu’s teaching about rain splashing up.
Rav Yehuda and R. Yohanan give an extended formula thanking God for every drop of rain.
Why say “abundant” rather than “all” thanksgivings?
Rava suggests saying “God of thanksgivings.”
Rav Pappa combines the two formulas.
An initial distinction assigns the mishna to hearing rain and the longer blessing to seeing it.
Hearing rain is already covered by the mishna’s rule for good news.
Both cases involve seeing rain: the longer blessing is for a little, the mishna’s for much.
Alternatively, with much rain the mishna concerns a landowner and the longer blessing a nonowner.
A sole landowner should bless Shehecheyanu, like someone acquiring a new house or vessel.
Shared land receives “good and does good”; sole ownership receives Shehecheyanu, as a baraita confirms.
A father told of a son’s birth blesses “good and does good,” though he seems the only beneficiary.
The mother shares the joy.
An heir blesses “good and does good” on inheritance, apparently benefiting alone.
The case includes brothers who inherit with him.
A blessing for changing wine types during a meal also seems to benefit only one person.
Other diners share the new wine.
Rav Huna limits Shehecheyanu for new possessions to a kind one did not already own.
R. Yohanan requires the blessing even if one owns a similar item.

60a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The first version implies both sages waive a blessing for repeated purchases.
A second version has Rav Huna waive the blessing after a prior purchase.
R. Yohanan requires it even for a repeated purchase, implying agreement about already owning a similar item.
A baraita has R. Meir waive the blessing for a similar possession while R. Yehuda requires it.
The first version fits the baraita, but whom does R. Yohanan follow under the second?
R. Yohanan says R. Yehuda also requires a blessing for repeated purchase; the baraita highlights R. Meir’s leniency.
Why not frame the dispute to highlight R. Yehuda’s stricter case?
The strength of the lenient position is preferred.
A breached dam harms the land now, though later sediment may improve it, so one blesses for present harm.
Finding an object benefits one now, though a king might later confiscate it, so one blesses for present good.
Can prayer change the sex of a fetus after the wife is already pregnant?
Rav Yosef cites Leah’s judgment about Rachel and the miraculous birth of Dina as a counterexample.
Miracles do not establish the ordinary rule.
Alternatively Leah’s prayer occurred within forty days of conception.
A baraita lists stages of pregnancy and what one may pray for at each stage.
R. Yitzhak’s teaching and a verse seem to fix a child’s sex at conception.
The prayer case is when both partners emit seed simultaneously.
Hillel hears a cry in town and trusts it is not from his home; a psalm praises such trust.
Rava reads the psalm in either direction: trust prevents fear of bad news and fearlessness follows trust.
R. Yishmael calls a fearful student sinful, citing Isaiah.
The student cites the verse praising one who fears always.
That verse concerns care in Torah study.
Rav Hamnuna warns a sighing companion that fear may invite suffering, citing Job.
The companion cites the verse praising constant fear.
The verse concerns Torah study.
Before entering a city, one prays to enter in peace.
After entering, one gives thanks for safe arrival.
Before leaving, one prays to depart in peace.
After leaving, one thanks God and prays for safety on the road.
One version of Rav Mattana limits the prayers to a city without orderly capital trials.
Another version requires prayer even where trials occur, because no advocate may be available.
A baraita gives a prayer before a bathhouse, asking for safety and possible atonement.
Abaye rejects mentioning possible death, citing the warning against opening one’s mouth to Satan.
Rav Yosef cites Isaiah’s Sodom language and the prophet’s response to illustrate this warning.
On leaving the bathhouse, Rav Aha prescribes thanks for being saved from its fire.
R. Abbahu survives a collapsing bathhouse and saves many others, affirming the thanksgiving.
Rav Aha gives a prayer before bloodletting but questions whether human healing is proper.
Abaye cites a verse authorizing physicians to heal.
After bloodletting, Rav Aha prescribes blessing God as healer without payment.

60b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Before entering the bathroom, one addresses accompanying angels and asks them to wait.
Abaye warns the angels might depart and offers a request for protection and patience instead.
On leaving, one blesses God for the body’s openings and the life sustained by their proper function.
Rav proposes ending the blessing as healer of the sick.
Shmuel objects that this implies everyone is ill and says healer of all flesh.
Rav Sheshet proposes “Who performs wondrous deeds.”
Rav Pappa combines the latter two endings.
At bedtime one recites Shema and begins the blessing over sleep.
The bedtime prayer asks for peace, Torah, good conduct, protection from harm and bad dreams, and awakening.
On waking one thanks God for the soul, its safekeeping, and its future restoration.
The rooster’s call prompts a blessing for distinguishing day and night.
Opening eyes, sitting, dressing, and standing each prompt blessings for restored faculties.
Stepping down, walking, putting on shoes, a belt, and head covering each prompt blessings.
Putting on tzitzit and arm and head tefillin each prompts a commandment blessing.
Washing hands prompts the handwashing blessing.
Washing the face prompts thanks for waking and a prayer for Torah, good company, restraint, and kindness.
Does blessing for bad as for good mean saying “good and does good” for bad news, contrary to the mishna?
Rava says the mishna concerns receiving bad news with joy, not using the same blessing text.
R. Aha cites a psalm promising song for both kindness and judgment.
R. Shmuel bar Nahmani cites a psalm that praises God in benevolence and suffering.
R. Tanhum cites verses invoking God in both salvation and distress.
The Rabbis cite Job blessing God for both giving and taking.
A teaching transmitted by Rav Huna urges saying that all God does is for good.
R. Akiva receives no lodging, sleeps outside, and repeats that all God does is for good.
Wind extinguishes his candle and animals eat his rooster and donkey; he repeats the maxim.
An army captures the town while he remains hidden; he reminds others of his saying, continuing on the next daf.

61a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: R. Akiva’s account concludes: all God does is for the good.
Rav Huna says to speak sparingly before God, citing Ecclesiastes.
Rav Nahman bar Rav Hisda reads the doubled yod in Adam’s formation as two inclinations.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak objects that animals lack that spelling yet also bite and kick.
R. Shimon ben Pazi instead reads the doubled spelling as conflict between Creator and inclination.
R. Yirmeya ben Elazar alternatively says Adam was first created with two faces.
Rav and Shmuel disagree whether the side from which Eve was made was a face or an appendage.
If it was an appendage, how does the verse say God formed Adam behind and before?
R. Ami reads this as last in creation and first in punishment.
Which punishment came first to Adam? The snake episode began with the snake, not Adam.
A baraita and verses show honor begins with the greatest, while curses begin with the least.
The first punishment refers to the flood, whose verse lists humanity before animals.
If Eve began as an appendage, why is “formed” spelled with two yods?
R. Shimon ben Pazi’s reading about Creator and inclination applies.
If she was an appendage, why does a verse say male and female were created?
R. Abbahu resolves the verses: God first considered two beings but ultimately made one.
If Eve was an appendage, why did God close flesh beneath the removed side?
That refers to the site of the incision.
If Eve was already a face, why does the verse say God built her?
R. Shimon ben Menasya reads “built” as God braiding Eve’s hair before bringing her to Adam.
Another reading compares Eve’s form to a storehouse, wider below to carry a child.
God bringing Eve to Adam teaches that a great person may serve a lesser one as best man.
If Adam and Eve were two faces, who walked in front?
Rav Nahman says the man walked first.
A baraita warns against walking behind a woman to stare at her, especially where she crosses water.
A baraita and proverb condemn handing a woman money merely to look at her.
Rav Nahman calls Manoah ignorant for following his wife, citing Judges.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak asks whether similar verses about Elkana and Elisha also mean literal walking.
Those verses concern following advice; Manoah’s verse can mean the same.
Rav Ashi says Rav Nahman’s literal reading ignores a verse where Rebecca followed the man.
R. Yohanan ranks walking behind a lion, woman, idolatry, and a praying synagogue in increasing concern.
The synagogue concern does not apply when carrying something, another entrance exists, riding, or wearing tefillin.
Rav compares the evil inclination to a fly between the heart’s openings, citing Ecclesiastes.
Shmuel compares it to wheat through wordplay on the verse about sin at the door.
A baraita says two kidneys advise good and evil, associating right and left with a verse.
A baraita begins assigning functions to kidneys, heart, tongue, mouth, esophagus, and windpipe.

61b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The baraita continues assigning organs roles in drinking, anger, laughter, digestion, sleep, and waking.
If both sleep-related organs act alike, a person immediately dies.
R. Yosei HaGelili uses verses to assign righteous, wicked, and middling people to good or evil inclinations.
Rabba calls people like himself middling.
Abaye protests that this leaves no hope for anyone else.
Rava contrasts fully wicked and fully righteous lives and urges self-examination.
Rav contrasts Ahab’s share in this world with R. Hanina ben Dosa’s in the next.
Why does the verse command love with both all one’s soul and all one’s might?
R. Eliezer says it covers one who prizes life most and one who prizes wealth most.
R. Akiva reads “all your soul” as devotion even when life is taken.
Despite a Roman ban, R. Akiva publicly gathers students to study Torah.
Pappos asks whether R. Akiva fears the authorities.
R. Akiva tells of fish fleeing nets and a fox asking them to leave the river.
The fox proposes that fish live with him on dry land.
The fish call him foolish: if water is dangerous, dry land is far worse.
Torah is Israel’s life like water to fish, so abandoning it would be worse than studying under threat.
R. Akiva and Pappos are soon arrested and imprisoned together.
Pappos says R. Akiva was arrested for Torah while he himself was arrested for idle matters.
At his execution R. Akiva recites Shema while his flesh is raked with iron combs.
His students ask whether he continues even in this suffering.
He has long awaited the chance to fulfill loving God even as his soul is taken.
He prolongs “One” until death; a heavenly voice praises him.
The angels ask whether such a death is Torah’s reward, citing a psalm.
God and a heavenly voice point to R. Akiva’s share in eternal life.
The mishna forbids irreverence facing the eastern gate aligned with the Holy of Holies.
Rav and R. Yohanan restrict the rule to a visible Temple without a barrier while the Presence dwells there.
A baraita gives different permitted directions when relieving oneself in Judea and Galilee.
R. Yosei permits it under conditions of distance, visibility, and Temple presence; the Rabbis prohibit.
How do the Rabbis differ from the first tanna?
They differ about side positions.
Another baraita repeats the regional directional rules.
R. Yosei, R. Yehuda, and R. Akiva give differing limits based on sight, Temple standing, or location.
How does R. Akiva differ from the first tanna?
He extends the prohibition beyond Israel.
Abaye rotates the bricks in Rabba’s bathroom to test his practice.
Rabba restores them and says he follows R. Akiva’s rule everywhere.

62a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: R. Akiva says he learned three bathroom practices by observing R. Yehoshua.
Ben Azzai challenges his boldness in following his teacher.
R. Akiva says it is Torah that he must learn.
Ben Azzai reports learning the same three practices by observing R. Akiva.
R. Yehuda challenges Ben Azzai’s boldness.
Ben Azzai says he must learn this Torah.
Rav Kahana hides beneath Rav’s bed and comments on Rav’s intimate behavior.
Rav tells Kahana to leave because his presence is improper.
Kahana says the conduct is Torah he must learn.
Why should one wipe with the left hand rather than the right?
Rava invokes the Torah being given by God’s right hand.
Rabba bar bar Hana says the right hand is near the mouth.
R. Shimon ben Lakish cites its use in tying tefillin.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak cites pointing to Torah accents.
Tannaim similarly give eating, writing, or Torah instruction as reasons.
R. Tanhum says modesty in the bathroom protects from snakes, scorpions, harmful forces, and perhaps troubling dreams.
R. Ami and R. Asi enter a dangerous Tiberias bathroom separately without injury.
They prescribe modesty and silence for the bathroom, and silence and prayer for suffering.
Abaye’s mother provides a lamb companion rather than a goat, which might be confused with a demon.
Rava’s wife first rattles a vessel and later guards him through a window.
Ulla says a fence permits immediate privacy, while an open field requires distance beyond hearing.
Isi bar Natan instead requires hearing distance behind a fence and visual distance in a field.
A purity-law teaching permits workers to go just behind an olive press fence.
Purity cases receive a leniency.
Another purity rule allows workers to remain within sight, apparently contrary to Isi.
Those who maintain purity receive a special leniency.
Rav Ashi says Isi only requires the other person not to see exposed parts, though the person remains visible.
Rav Nahman challenges a eulogizer’s claim that the deceased was modest without knowing his bathroom conduct.
The warning matters because false eulogies expose speakers and respondents to punishment.
A baraita defines modesty as behaving at night as one does by day when relieving oneself.
Rav’s advice and examples of Rava and R. Zeira challenge a literal same-place reading.
The rule means retaining daytime modesty at night.
Rav Ashi keeps the same-place wording but applies it to a private corner.
Rav advises relieving oneself early and late to avoid going far.
Ben Azzai gives similar timing advice and warns against sitting before preparing the body.
For someone who reversed the order, the text gives an incantation against sorcery.

62b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Ben Azzai advises avoiding sleep on the ground and sitting on a beam.
Shmuel praises dawn sleep and relieving oneself at dawn.
Bar Kappara gives short maxims about eating, drinking, bodily needs, and acting on market opportunity.
Abaye warns scholars walking to the fields not to stare at women seated nearby.
Rav Safra tells R. Abba he may enter a bathroom after hearing a cough at its door.
R. Abba criticizes speaking there and cites the Temple bathroom’s silent locked-door signal.
Rav Safra considered delay dangerous, citing harms from holding back bodily functions.
R. Elazar is pushed from a bathroom by a Roman, who is then killed by a snake; he cites Isaiah.
In David’s address to Saul, why do “he said” and “you spared” replace first-person verbs?
David says Saul deserved death as a pursuer, but Saul’s modesty spared him.
Saul chose nested enclosures for privacy and covered himself while relieving himself.
A verse about David cutting Saul’s garment is linked to David later finding no warmth in clothing.
Because David called God an inciter, God let him stumble in numbering Israel without ransom.
Verses connect the incitement, census, missing ransom, and resulting plague.
Two sages define the plague’s appointed end as the offering’s service or noon.
R. Elazar reads “many” as a great leader taken to atone; Avishai dies.
What did God see when He stopped the destruction?
Rav says God saw Jacob, citing a verse with “saw.”
Shmuel says God saw Isaac’s ashes, citing the binding narrative.
R. Yitzhak Nappaha says God saw the atonement money of the census.
R. Yohanan says God saw the Temple, citing the mountain of divine appearance.
Two further sages divide between atonement money and the Temple.
A verse about the mountain supports the Temple interpretation.
Kappandarya means a shortcut through the Temple Mount, explained by wordplay about avoiding a detour.
A synagogue entered for another purpose may later be used as a shortcut.
An original public path through a synagogue site may still be used.
Entering to pray also permits crossing through, as a verse describes worshippers using opposite gates.
Spitting on the Temple Mount is likened to spitting in God’s eye, citing His eyes being there.
Rava permits spitting in a synagogue by analogy to shoes, which are barred on the Mount but allowed in a synagogue.
An interlocutor proposes deriving synagogue spitting from the ban on using it as a shortcut instead.
Rava says the tanna used the shoe analogy.
A baraita forbids casual entry and spitting on the Mount, deriving the latter by a fortiori from shoes.
R. Yosei bar Yehuda offers a different a fortiori from the ban on sackcloth at a human king’s gate.
The interlocutor clarifies he sought a stringent rule for both Mount and synagogue, continuing on the next daf.

63a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The prior speaker asks why a synagogue should not follow the stricter shortcut analogy for spitting.
Rava says a synagogue resembles a house: shortcuts offend, but shoes and spitting are accepted.
Why did Temple blessings have a special ending?
Worshippers in the Temple did not answer amen.
Verses in Nehemiah prescribe a distinctive praise after blessing God in the Temple.
The wording requires praise for each blessing, not one response to all.
Why does the mishna provide more than Boaz’s precedent for greeting with God’s name?
An angel’s greeting to Gideon and a proverb about elders support the practice.
Rava says the verse about a time to act for God can be read in either direction.
Violation may require corrective action, and extraordinary action may justify setting aside a rule.
Hillel advises spreading Torah when cherished and holding it back when a generation disdains it.
Bar Kappara advises buying undervalued goods and stepping up where no capable person exists.
Abaye infers one should yield when an equally capable person already fills the role.
Bar Kappara calls “know Him in all your ways” a short verse embracing Torah’s fundamentals; Rava extends it broadly.
Bar Kappara urges teaching a clean, easy craft; Rav Hisda names gem cutting.
Rabbi warns against too many intimate houseguests, citing a proverb about harmful friends.
He warns against appointing a house steward, recalling Potiphar and Joseph.
The Nazirite passage follows sota to counsel abstention from wine after seeing disgrace.
The juxtaposition of sota and tithes warns that withholding priests’ gifts can lead to needing a priest for one’s wife.
The withholder may ultimately need the very gifts he kept.
Rav Nahman says giving those gifts leads to wealth, reading the adjacent verse.
Rav Huna says invoking God in distress can double livelihood, deriving it from Job’s wording.
R. Shmuel bar Nahmani reads the word as livelihood flying to the person.
R. Tavi says slack Torah study weakens one in crisis, citing Proverbs.
Shmuel extends the warning to even one neglected commandment.
Rav Safra relates that Hanina established the calendar outside Israel.
Two scholars sent from Israel say they came to study Torah with Hanina.
Hanina publicly praises their scholarship and priestly ancestry.
They contradict his purity and prohibition rulings, so he calls them worthless.
They object that he cannot undo the status he himself gave them.
Hanina asks why they consistently reverse his rulings.
They say his calendar rulings outside Israel are the reason.
Hanina points to R. Akiva, who made such rulings abroad.
They say R. Akiva had no equal remaining in Israel.
Hanina says the same was true when he left.
They say Israel’s scholars have matured and warn that refusal to heed them will bring ostracism.

63b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The scholars warn exile communities that rejecting Israel’s calendar authority severs their religious unity.
The people weep and affirm their share in Israel’s God.
The authority of Zion is grounded in Isaiah’s verse that Torah goes out from Jerusalem.
How could the visiting sages permit what Hanina prohibited, contrary to a baraita about a prior ruling?
They acted exceptionally to prevent people from following his calendar rulings.
At Yavne, four sages begin teachings honoring their hosts.
R. Yehuda argues from travel to Moses’ tent that scholars traveling to learn Torah are seekers of God.
R. Yitzhak reads “face to face” as cheerful exchange in learning law.
Another reading has Moses show Israel a cheerful face and return the tent to camp.
R. Abbahu says God urges Moses to return the tent or Joshua will replace him.
Rava says Joshua’s eventual role shows the warning was not empty.
Why does Moses say Israel became God’s people that day, forty years after Torah was given?
Torah remains as precious to its learners each day as on Sinai.
R. Tanhum compares a missed evening Shema to having never recited it.
The word “hasket” is read as forming groups for Torah study.
R. Yosei reads Jeremiah’s sword against solitary learners, who become foolish and may sin.
A verse in Isaiah offers a further link to foolishness.
Another reading urges exhausting oneself over Torah, supported by a verse about dying in a tent.
Another reading advises first listening and learning, then analyzing, as Rava teaches.
R. Yannai’s school asks how Proverbs’ milk, nose, and anger imagery applies to Torah.
The cream of Torah comes to one who labors over it from youth.
A student who silently accepts one rebuke learns to distinguish kinds of blood.
Accepting repeated rebuke leads to distinguishing monetary from capital cases.
R. Yishmael praises monetary law as a demanding source of wisdom.
R. Shmuel bar Nahmani reads Proverbs as promising elevation to humble Torah learners and warning against silencing oneself.
R. Nehemya cites Saul sparing Jethro’s descendants to honor those who host Torah scholars.
If Jethro was rewarded for self-interested kindness, a generous host merits reward all the more.
R. Yosei cites the command not to despise Egyptians because Israel lived among them.
If Egypt’s self-interested hospitality counts, hosting a scholar generously merits greater regard.
R. Eliezer cites Oved-edom’s blessing for honoring the ark.
If caring for the ark earned blessing, feeding and helping a scholar should earn more.
What blessing came to Oved-edom?
Rav Yehuda bar Zevida identifies extraordinary births in his household, continued next daf.

64a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Chronicles enumerates Oved-edom’s children and descendants and calls his large household a divine blessing.
R. Avin says forcing an opportunity pushes it away, while yielding to the moment lets it come.
Rav Yosef and Rabba are compared as breadth of learning and sharp analysis; which should lead?
The sages choose Rav Yosef’s breadth because all need a master of sources.
Rav Yosef declines the role after hearing he would lead for only two years.
Rabba leads for twenty-two years and Rav Yosef for two and a half.
During Rabba’s tenure Rav Yosef does not even summon a bloodletter to his house.
Why does a psalm invoke the God of Jacob in distress rather than also Abraham and Isaac?
The one bearing the beam shoulders its thick end; Jacob bears special responsibility for his descendants.
A verse describes a meal with Moses and the elders as eaten before God.
Eating with a Torah scholar is likened to enjoying the Divine Presence.
R. Avin prefers “go to peace” for a living person, citing Jethro’s words to Moses.
David’s “go in peace” to Absalom is contrasted with Absalom’s death.
For the dead one says “go in peace,” as the verse says to Abraham.
Moving from synagogue to study hall to learn Torah brings one before the Divine Presence, as a psalm says.
Rav reads the same psalm as scholars progressing without rest in this world or the next.
R. Elazar says Torah scholars increase peace, reading “children” as “builders.”
A chain of psalms connects Torah, Zion, friendship, divine strength, and peace.
The daf closes the chapter and tractate of Berakhot.

ranges.en: Opening position: the Shema may be read from the time priests enter to eat Terumah until the first watch, per R. Eliezer.
The Sages' rival position: the deadline is midnight.
Rabban Gamaliel's position: the deadline is the rise of dawn.
Anecdote: Gamaliel's sons come home late from a feast and report they missed the reading.
Gamaliel rules they must still read before dawn, and generalizes this to every case the Sages call midnight.
Gamaliel supports his ruling with offerings whose burning or eating must finish by dawn.
If the law runs to dawn, why would the Sages say midnight at all?
Midnight is set so that a person stays far from transgression.
Asks where the Tanna's teaching stands, and why the evening Shema is taught before the morning one.
The Tanna's source is the verse about lying down and rising up.
So the Mishnah's time marker for the bedtime Shema is when priests enter to eat Terumah.
Alternatively, the Tanna derives the order from the account of creation.
The creation wording evening then morning, one day, is quoted as the support.
If the Tanna follows that logic, why does the later clause teach morning before evening?
The Tanna starts with evening, covers morning, then returns to the evening matters.
Quotes the Mishnah phrase about priests entering to eat Terumah.
If priests eat from nightfall, why not teach that time directly?
It is an incidental teaching: priests eat Terumah from the time the stars appear.
Does this not teach something else, namely that a sin-offering does not block the meal?
Yes, the atonement of the sin-offering does not block eating Terumah.
A baraita on Leviticus 22:7 shows that sunset blocks Terumah while the sin-offering does not.
How do we know that the sunset phrase means full setting and the clean phrase means the day is over?
